## Chapter 2: The OSI Model and Why We Still Teach 7 Layers

In Chapter 1 we made one decision (packet switching) and three constraints (unreliable, unordered, asymmetric). The internet is built on top of those. But "built on top of" is a phrase that hides a lot. To talk about how the internet is built without drowning in vagueness, we need vocabulary. We need a way to say "this protocol lives there; that protocol lives there; these two are arguing because they both want to live at the same place."

The vocabulary the world settled on is the OSI 7-layer reference model. Almost no one implements the OSI model literally. Almost everyone teaches it. It is the map that everyone agrees to use even when the territory has moved on without it. The pragmatic counterpart, the TCP/IP 4-layer model, is what real protocols actually conform to. We will learn both, and we will learn the small lies in each one, because those lies are where the modern interesting questions live.

The chapter is a map chapter. It lays out the slot map for the entire book. Every later chapter introduces one or more protocols, and the first question we will always ask is: which slot does this live in? By Chapter 27 you should be able to look at any unfamiliar protocol name (HTTP/3, MASQUE, MoQ, DRDP, anything that arrives next) and place it on the map within seconds.

### 2.1 Why We Need a Layer Model At All

Imagine writing software that has to talk to another computer. The other computer might be next to you on the same Ethernet switch. It might be in a different building, reached over Wi-Fi and a corporate VPN. It might be in Tokyo, reached through fiber, ten ISPs, two undersea cables, and a CDN. The bytes you eventually deliver to the application are the same in every case. The signaling that delivered them is wildly different.

If you had to write code that handled all those cases in one giant function, the function would be unwriteable. It would have to know about voltage levels on copper, about how Wi-Fi handles collisions, about IPv6 fragmentation, about TCP retransmission timers, about HTTP request framing, and about the application's payload format. You would write one program for each (medium, transport, application) combination, and you would have hundreds of programs.

The reason you do not have to write hundreds of programs is that someone, decades ago, drew a line that said: at this point in the stack, all the medium-specific stuff is done. Above this line, you do not care whether it was copper or fiber or radio. Below this line, you do not care what the application meant. The line is a layer boundary, and each side of the line speaks a contract: "I will give you these guarantees; I do not care what you put inside."

Layering is the discipline of repeating that line several times, at well-chosen places, so that each layer can be implemented independently. The OSI model proposes seven such lines. The TCP/IP model collapses some of them and ends up with four. Either way, the value is the same: a programmer above the line does not need to know what is below it, and a programmer below the line does not need to know what is above it. This is the most important abstraction in networking. It is the reason your web app can run on copper, fiber, Wi-Fi, cellular, and Starlink without you changing a line of code.

#### 2.1.1 Encapsulation: The Headers Grow on the Way Down

Layers do not stack by magic. Each layer takes the data it gets from above, wraps it in a header (and sometimes a trailer) that contains the bookkeeping that layer needs, and hands the wrapped result to the layer below. The receiving stack does the reverse: each layer reads its header off the front, does whatever the header tells it to do, and hands the rest to the layer above.

So a single byte of application data, "A," might be wrapped in an HTTP request line, wrapped in a TLS record, wrapped in a TCP segment header, wrapped in an IP datagram header, wrapped in an Ethernet frame header, and pushed onto a fiber. By the time it reaches the wire, it looks like:
    
    
    [Ethernet header][IP header][TCP header][TLS record header][HTTP header]A[Ethernet trailer]
    

Receiving side: the Ethernet driver strips the Ethernet header and trailer, the IP stack strips the IP header, TCP strips the TCP header, TLS strips and decrypts, HTTP strips the HTTP header, the application sees "A."

Each layer adds between 8 and 60 bytes of overhead. On a 64-byte minimum-Ethernet packet, headers alone (14 Ethernet + 20 IPv4 + 20 TCP = 54 bytes) account for roughly 84% of the bytes — the application "payload" is at most ~10 bytes, the rest is padding. On a 1500-byte MTU packet, headers are about 4% — but the worst case is the small one. This is one of the costs of layering: protocol overhead. Layering is not free. But it is so cheap compared to the engineering complexity of monolithic stacks that the trade is uncontroversial.

#### 2.1.2 The Layer Contract Is Stronger Than the Layer Position

Here is a point that is easy to miss. The _position_ of a layer in the model is less important than the _contract_ it offers to the layer above. The contract is: "you give me a chunk of bytes shaped like this; I will deliver it to a peer with these guarantees." Whether that contract is layer 2, layer 3, layer 4, or layer 6 is, in some sense, a labeling question.

This will matter when we get to QUIC. QUIC offers a TCP-style reliable stream contract, but it sits where TCP would sit (layer 4 in the OSI numbering) while wrapping itself inside a UDP datagram (also layer 4) that travels in an IP packet (layer 3). The strict OSI position is ambiguous; the contract is clear. Modern protocols increasingly do not fit cleanly in a single layer slot, and this is fine. The slots are pedagogical, not normative.

### 2.2 The OSI 7-Layer Model

The seven layers, from bottom to top, are:

  1. **Physical** — bits on the wire (or in the air).
  2. **Data Link** — frames between adjacent nodes.
  3. **Network** — packets across multiple hops.
  4. **Transport** — end-to-end conversations.
  5. **Session** — managing dialogues (in OSI; nearly fictional in TCP/IP).
  6. **Presentation** — data format translation (in OSI; nearly fictional in TCP/IP).
  7. **Application** — what the user actually wanted.

There is a venerable mnemonic for remembering them: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away." That tells you Physical-Data-Network-Transport-Session-Presentation-Application bottom to top. Or, top to bottom: "All People Seem To Need Data Processing." Both are silly; both work.

Let us look at each layer with one canonical example, the contract it offers, and the chapter where we will go deep on it.

#### Layer 1: Physical

The physical layer turns bits into electrical signals (copper), light pulses (fiber), or radio waves (wireless), and turns them back. It defines voltage levels, pulse durations, modulation schemes, the shape of connectors, the impedance of cables.

Canonical examples: 1000BASE-T Ethernet over Cat6 copper. 1000BASE-LX over single-mode fiber. Wi-Fi 6E in the 6 GHz band. 5G NR over licensed cellular spectrum.

Contract offered upward: "you give me a sequence of bits; I will make them appear at the other end of the wire, with some bit-error rate."

This is the layer where physics dominates. Distance limits, signal attenuation, electromagnetic interference, the speed of light, all live here. We will visit physical-layer realities in Chapter 3, where we look at copper-vs-fiber-vs-radio properties, and Chapter 4, where we walk the modern Ethernet speed ladder up to 800 Gbps and meet DPUs.

#### Layer 2: Data Link

The data link layer organizes bits into _frames_ and exchanges them between _adjacent_ nodes (nodes connected by the same physical medium). It handles framing (where does a frame start and end), addressing on the local medium (MAC addresses), error detection on the local link (CRC), and contention for the shared medium (collision detection on classic Ethernet, CSMA/CA on Wi-Fi).

Canonical examples: Ethernet (IEEE 802.3). Wi-Fi (IEEE 802.11). PPP. ARP (technically straddles layer 2 and layer 3).

Contract offered upward: "you give me a packet for a peer on the same physical segment; I will deliver it (probably) with a frame check sequence, and I will tell you who is on the segment."

The phrase "same physical segment" is important. Data-link layers do not route across networks; they only deliver frames between directly attached nodes. To go further, you need the network layer above. Chapter 3 covers Ethernet, MAC addressing, and ARP. Chapter 4 covers modern variants and the DPU revolution that is moving more layer-2 work into specialized hardware.

#### Layer 3: Network

The network layer takes packets from a source and routes them across multiple hops to a destination, possibly on a different physical network. It introduces _logical addressing_ (IP addresses), routing decisions (which interface should this packet leave via?), fragmentation (when a packet is too big for the next link), and best-effort delivery.

Canonical examples: IP (both v4 and v6). ICMP (the network's own signaling, used by `ping`). The control-plane protocols that decide how IP packets are routed: OSPF, IS-IS, BGP.

Contract offered upward: "you give me a packet with a destination address; I will try to deliver it. I make no promise about reliability, ordering, or timing."

This is where the three constraints from Chapter 1 fully reveal themselves. The network layer is unreliable on purpose; the layer above (transport) is responsible for adding reliability if needed. Chapter 5 covers IPv4 and IPv6 addressing and headers. Chapter 6 covers intra-domain routing (OSPF, IS-IS). Chapter 7 covers BGP, the protocol that holds the entire inter-domain internet together. Chapter 8 covers NAT, which is technically a network-layer participant that bends the model.

#### Layer 4: Transport

The transport layer manages end-to-end conversations between a process on one machine and a process on another. It introduces _port numbers_ (which process on the destination should receive this?), and it can add reliability, ordering, and flow control on top of the unreliable network layer.

Canonical examples: TCP (reliable, ordered, byte-stream). UDP (unreliable, unordered, datagram, the thinnest layer-4 protocol possible). QUIC (reliable, ordered-per-stream, multiplexed, encrypted, built on top of UDP because the IETF could not evolve TCP fast enough).

Contract offered upward: depends entirely on which transport. TCP says "I give you a reliable, ordered byte stream." UDP says "I give you a datagram delivery; reliability and ordering are your problem." QUIC says "I give you many independent reliable ordered streams in one connection, with encryption built in."

We will spend Chapter 9 on TCP, Chapter 10 on UDP and QUIC, Chapter 11 on congestion control (which is technically part of TCP but deserves its own chapter), and Chapter 12 on the socket API by which applications use transport.

#### Layer 5: Session

The session layer manages dialogues between applications: opening and closing sessions, synchronizing checkpoints, managing dialogue tokens.

This is where the OSI model first parts company with reality. In the TCP/IP world, session management is folded into the application layer (HTTP has its own session concept, expressed via cookies, headers, or connection persistence) or into the transport layer (TCP connections themselves carry session state). There is no separate session-layer protocol on the modern internet that people commonly name.

You can pretend session functions live in TLS (handshake, session resumption with PSK), in HTTP cookies, in WebSocket connection state, or in application frameworks. None of these is layer 5 by any strict reading; all of them do something layer-5-ish. The honest answer is that OSI layer 5 is mostly empty in TCP/IP.

#### Layer 6: Presentation

The presentation layer translates between different data representations. The classic OSI example: one system stores integers in big-endian, another in little-endian; the presentation layer translates. Another example: ASCII to EBCDIC.

Again, mostly empty in TCP/IP. Presentation-layer functions are smeared across other layers: TLS encryption and decryption could be called presentation (it transforms data representations); HTTP content negotiation could be called presentation (the server picks JSON vs HTML based on Accept headers); MIME type handling sits in HTTP. But there is no protocol explicitly named "the presentation protocol." Layer 6 is a placeholder.

#### Layer 7: Application

The application layer is what the user actually wanted to do. Send email. Load a webpage. Stream a video. Synchronize a database. Place a phone call.

Canonical examples (so many it is easier to list categories): HTTP (web), SMTP/IMAP (email), DNS (naming, but everyone calls it application even though it is more like infrastructure), FTP (file transfer, mostly obsolete), SSH (remote shell), gRPC (RPC framework over HTTP/2), WebSocket (bidirectional messaging), MQTT (lightweight publish-subscribe), WebRTC (real-time audio/video).

Contract offered upward: whatever the application wants. Above layer 7 is the user.

In OSI you might say that "the application" is technically above layer 7 and that layer 7 is "application-supporting protocols." TCP/IP does not draw this distinction; layer 7 in common usage means whatever you would call the "topmost" protocol involved.

We will spend a lot of time at layer 7: Chapter 13 (DNS), Chapter 14 (HTTP semantics), Chapter 15 (HTTP/3 end-to-end), Chapter 16 (WebSocket, SSE, WebRTC, WebTransport).

#### 2.2.1 Putting It All Together: One HTTP GET on All Seven Layers

Let us trace the same operation, a browser's `GET /index.html` request, across all seven layers. This is the running example from Chapter 1, now annotated with the OSI slot map.

Layer | What is happening  
---|---  

6 Presentation | (Empty in TCP/IP, but conceptually: encoding the request in UTF-8 ASCII bytes.)  
5 Session | (Empty in TCP/IP, but conceptually: the TLS session keys make this request part of an authenticated dialogue.)  
4 Transport | TCP wraps the bytes in a segment with sequence number, port numbers, checksum.  
3 Network | IP wraps the segment in a datagram with source and destination IP addresses and TTL.  
2 Data Link | Ethernet wraps the datagram in a frame with source and destination MAC, CRC.  
1 Physical | The Ethernet driver pushes voltage transitions onto the copper, or light pulses onto the fiber.  
  
Reading the table from top to bottom gives you the path of a sent packet. Reading bottom to top gives you the path of a received packet. At every layer boundary, the data has a header added (going down) or stripped (going up). The application sees only what it sent or asked for; it does not see TCP segment headers, IP datagram headers, or MAC addresses.

The same `GET` over HTTP/3 would change three slots: HTTP/3 framing at layer 7, QUIC at the transport boundary (with TLS 1.3 integrated), and UDP rather than TCP underneath. The lower layers (IP, Ethernet, Physical) do not care.

#### Definition: OSI Layer

A named horizontal stratum of the OSI reference model. Each layer offers a service contract to the layer above and uses services from the layer below. The model has 7 such layers, numbered 1 (Physical) through 7 (Application).

In plain language, this means: a layer is a job description. The job is "take this kind of input, do this kind of work, hand off this kind of output." If a protocol does that job, it is in that layer. If a protocol does several jobs, it may straddle layers. If a protocol does no work, it can be skipped.

### 2.3 The Pragmatic TCP/IP 4-Layer Model

OSI is a reference model. It was specified by ISO (the same standards body that gives us A4 paper sizes), and its specifying documents stretch across many years and dozens of subsidiary documents. The protocols ISO actually built around the OSI model (X.25, X.400, OSI's own application protocols) lost to the TCP/IP family by the mid-1990s and are now historical curiosities.

What people actually deploy is TCP/IP. The TCP/IP model is leaner. It has four layers.

  1. **Link** (sometimes called "Network Interface") — the bottom; combines OSI layers 1 and 2.
  2. **Internet** — combines what OSI calls Network (layer 3).
  3. **Transport** — corresponds to OSI layer 4.
  4. **Application** — combines OSI layers 5, 6, and 7.

That is the entire model. Most modern texts describe protocols using this 4-layer model because it matches the actual protocol stack on every Linux, BSD, Windows, macOS, and embedded system in production.

#### 2.3.1 Mapping OSI to TCP/IP

OSI Layer | TCP/IP Layer | Example protocols  
---|---|---  
7 Application | Application | HTTP, DNS, SMTP, gRPC, WebSocket  
6 Presentation | Application | (TLS sits here-ish, though it is awkward)  
5 Session | Application | (Mostly empty; cookies, TLS resumption)  
4 Transport | Transport | TCP, UDP, QUIC  
3 Network | Internet | IP, ICMP, BGP, OSPF  
2 Data Link | Link | Ethernet, Wi-Fi, PPP  
1 Physical | Link | Cat6, fiber, RF  
  
The biggest collapses: OSI layers 5, 6, 7 all become TCP/IP "Application," and OSI layers 1 and 2 both become TCP/IP "Link." The TCP/IP model is admitting that real protocols do not cleanly split between Physical and Data Link (they are implemented together in NICs and drivers), and that real protocols do not have separate Session and Presentation layers (the Application protocol does whatever session and presentation it needs).

#### 2.3.2 Why We Still Teach OSI Despite TCP/IP Winning

OSI is mostly fictional. So why does every networking course in the world still teach it?

Three reasons.

_First_ , the seven-layer vocabulary is universal. Network engineers say "layer 4 load balancer" and "layer 7 proxy" and "this is a layer 2 problem" all day, every day. They mean OSI layer 4 (TCP/UDP), OSI layer 7 (HTTP), OSI layer 2 (Ethernet). If you do not know the OSI numbering, you do not understand the conversation. The TCP/IP model collapses some of these into "Application" or "Link," but no one says "layer 4 of TCP/IP," everyone says "layer 4" and means OSI's transport.

_Second_ , OSI's distinctions between session, presentation, and application, while not implemented as separate protocols, are useful as _concepts_. When a developer asks "where should I put my data-format translation?" the answer "that is a presentation concern" is useful even if there is no presentation-layer protocol. When a developer asks "how does my user session survive across multiple HTTP requests?" the answer "that is a session concern" points to specific patterns (cookies, JWT tokens, server-side session state) even though they are all implemented at OSI layer 7.

_Third_ , the OSI model is a useful _teaching tool_ because it forces a clean separation of concerns. Beginners who first learn OSI develop a sharp mental model of "this protocol is doing routing; that protocol is doing framing; they are not the same thing." Beginners who first learn TCP/IP often blur "Internet" and "Link" because they were taught as adjacent. The slight overspecification in OSI is pedagogically valuable.

So: teach OSI for the vocabulary, but build with TCP/IP for the implementation. Both are correct. Neither is fully right. The territory has moved on past both, and the only honest answer is to use whichever model best illuminates the problem you are solving.

### 2.4 Layer Violations and Why They Are Increasingly Common

Modern protocols routinely violate the clean OSI picture. This is not because the protocol designers were lazy; it is because the OSI model encodes assumptions that turned out to be wrong, and fixing the assumptions required straddling layers.

Let us look at four examples.

#### Example 1: TLS Straddles Layers 5, 6, 7

TLS does cryptography (which is presentation-ish, layer 6), session management with handshakes and session tickets (layer 5), and runs over TCP at the transport boundary. Where is TLS? Honestly, nowhere clean. People usually say "TLS sits between transport and application" or "TLS is in layer 6 in OSI but really runs as an application-layer library." The truth is TLS does its own thing, and the layer model bends around it. TLS is the protocol that taught a generation of engineers that the OSI model is a guideline, not a constitution.

#### Example 2: QUIC Absorbs the Transport and Crypto Layers

QUIC is one protocol that does TCP-style reliable streaming, TLS 1.3-style encryption, congestion control, and connection management, all together. It runs over UDP (because middleboxes ossified TCP and would not let new transports through), but it absorbs functions that traditionally lived in TCP, TLS, and parts of HTTP/2. Putting QUIC on the OSI slot map requires drawing the line between transport, presentation, and session three different ways. Better: just say "QUIC is a modern transport with crypto built in," and stop trying to place it precisely.

#### Example 3: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 Push State Up From the Transport

HTTP/1.1 was stateless above the connection. HTTP/2 introduced _streams_ : multiple independent logical conversations multiplexed over one TCP connection. The stream concept is transport-ish (it is about multiplexing), but it lives in HTTP. HTTP/3 inherited streams from HTTP/2 and now expresses them directly in QUIC. The whole stream concept moves up and down between layers depending on which version you are looking at.

#### Example 4: eBPF Operates Across Layers 2-7 Inside the Kernel

eBPF programs (which we will see in Chapter 25) can attach at XDP (very early in the receive path, near the NIC, conceptually layer 2/3) and at the socket layer (where applications touch the kernel, conceptually layer 4-7 boundary). The same technology operates across many layers depending on the hook point. This is fine, but it makes "what layer does eBPF live at?" a question without a single answer.

The general lesson: the OSI model worked well when protocols were monolithic and stayed in their slot. As protocols got more sophisticated, they spilled across slots. The model is still useful for naming things, but it is not predictive of where a modern protocol's complexity will live.

#### Common Misconception: A Protocol Must Live in Exactly One Layer

When learners first encounter layering, they often look for the "correct" layer for every protocol. They get confused when they realize that TLS, QUIC, BGP, and others do not fit cleanly. The misconception is that the model is normative.

It is not. The model is descriptive vocabulary. If a protocol does work at multiple layers, that is a fact about the protocol, not an error in the protocol. The model gives you words; it does not give you constraints. When you read about a new protocol, ask: "What contract does it offer? What does it consume?" Place it where its contracts naturally fall. If it straddles, name what it does at each layer. Do not waste effort forcing a single number onto a multi-function protocol.

### 2.5 Where Each Chapter Lives on the Map

This section is a forward index. As we add chapters to the book, you can return here to see where each one sits.

Chapter | Topic | OSI layer | TCP/IP layer  
---|---|---|---  
3 | Physical/link realities | 1, 2 | Link  
4 | Ethernet, Wi-Fi, DPUs | 1, 2 | Link  
5 | IPv4, IPv6 | 3 | Internet  
6 | Intra-domain routing (OSPF, IS-IS) | 3 (control plane) | Internet  
7 | BGP, RPKI | 3 (control plane) | Internet  
8 | NAT, firewalls | 3 (data plane bend) | Internet  
9 | TCP | 4 | Transport  
10 | UDP and QUIC | 4 (QUIC also bends 5, 6) | Transport  
11 | Congestion control (BBR, CUBIC) | 4 | Transport  
12 | Socket API | 4/7 boundary | Transport/Application boundary  
13 | DNS, DoH, DoT, DoQ | 7 | Application  
14 | HTTP semantics | 7 | Application  
15 | HTTP/3 and QUIC end-to-end | 4-7 | Transport/Application  
16 | WebSocket, SSE, WebRTC, WebTransport | 7 (some 5-ish session work) | Application  
17 | TLS 1.3, ECH, PQ hybrid | 6 (kind of), really 4-7 | Application (with transport bending)  
18 | Certificates, PKI, ACME | 7 (Application + Operational) | Application  
19 | WireGuard, Tailscale | 3-4 | Internet/Transport  
20 | Load balancers, service mesh | 4 (L4 LB), 7 (L7 LB) | Transport, Application  
21 | CDN architecture | 7 (mostly), 3 (anycast) | Application + Internet  
22 | Edge compute | 7 + compute | Application  
23 | DDoS at scale | All layers | All layers  
24 | Packet-level observability | All layers | All layers  
25 | eBPF | 2-7 | All layers  
26 | AI-generated network code | n/a | n/a  
27 | Synthesis | All layers | All layers  
  
Notice how many entries have "all layers" or "multiple layers" or "varies." This is the modern reality. The clean slot map is the floor, not the ceiling. Most interesting modern problems involve interactions across layers.

### 2.6 A First Look at "Hop-by-Hop" vs "End-to-End"

A concept that runs alongside the layer model is the distinction between _hop-by-hop_ operations (work that happens at each intermediate node) and _end-to-end_ operations (work that happens only at the two endpoints). This distinction is not part of the OSI model per se, but it intersects the layer model in important ways.

At layer 2 (data link), almost everything is hop-by-hop. Each Ethernet frame has a source and destination MAC, but those MAC addresses are only meaningful on the local segment. When the frame crosses a router, the router strips it off and constructs a new Ethernet frame with new MAC addresses for the next segment. The MAC address of the original sender is invisible by the time the packet reaches the destination.

At layer 3 (network), the source and destination IP addresses are end-to-end. They stay the same as the packet traverses many hops. Each router uses them only to decide where to forward; the addresses are not modified. (NAT is the famous exception, which we will see in Chapter 8.)

At layer 4 (transport), TCP sequence numbers, acknowledgements, and connection state are entirely end-to-end. No router in the middle knows or cares about TCP state. The two endpoints maintain the entire conversation between them.

This distinction will matter every time we ask "who can see what?" An ISP in the middle of an HTTPS connection can see hop-by-hop information (IP addresses, packet sizes, timing patterns) but cannot see most end-to-end information (the HTTP path, headers, and body), because TLS encrypts that. Note that until Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is universally deployed, the destination hostname is still visible in the TLS ClientHello's `server_name` extension on the very first handshake packet, so "the ISP sees nothing useful" is too strong — the ISP typically still learns _which site_ you visited, just not what you fetched there. Chapter 17 develops the ECH story.

### 2.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Name the seven OSI layers in order from bottom to top and state in one sentence what each layer adds that the layer below does not provide.

Hint

Each layer "introduces" something. Physical introduces signals; Data Link introduces frames and local addressing; Network introduces multi-hop routing; what comes next?

**Answer:** (1) Physical: turns bits into signals on a medium (and back). (2) Data Link: organizes bits into frames between adjacent nodes, with local addressing and error detection. (3) Network: routes packets across multiple hops between distant nodes, with logical addressing. (4) Transport: provides end-to-end conversation between processes, optionally with reliability, ordering, and flow control. (5) Session: manages dialogues, including establishment, synchronization, and teardown of sessions (mostly empty in TCP/IP). (6) Presentation: translates between data representations (mostly empty in TCP/IP). (7) Application: provides the actual service the user wants (web, email, chat, file transfer, RPC).

**Q2.** Map the seven OSI layers onto the four TCP/IP layers. Where are the collapses, and why?

Hint

The two collapses are at the bottom and at the top. What got combined where?

**Answer:** TCP/IP combines OSI layers 1 (Physical) and 2 (Data Link) into a single Link layer, because real implementations integrate the physical hardware and the framing software into one driver/NIC unit and they are rarely usefully separated. TCP/IP combines OSI layers 5 (Session), 6 (Presentation), and 7 (Application) into a single Application layer, because the TCP/IP-family protocols do not implement Session and Presentation as separate things: HTTP, SMTP, DNS, and the rest handle their own session state, content negotiation, and data encoding inside the application protocol. The middle two layers (Network and Transport) map directly, since IP is OSI's Network and TCP/UDP/QUIC are OSI's Transport.

**Q3.** A protocol designer wants to know "is TLS layer 6?" Why is the question ill-posed, and what would a better question be?

Hint

TLS does several things at once. Each thing has its natural layer. Pick a concrete TLS function and ask where that function belongs.

**Answer:** The question is ill-posed because TLS performs functions that span multiple OSI layers: key exchange and cryptographic transformation (which is most naturally Presentation, layer 6), session establishment and resumption (which is most naturally Session, layer 5), and operation directly on top of a transport (which makes it Application-layer-ish in TCP/IP terminology). A better question would be: "Which specific TLS function are we placing, and which layer does that function's contract live in?" For example, "the cryptographic transformation of application data into ciphertext is presentation-like (layer 6)," or "the TLS handshake messages are application-layer in the sense that they ride on top of TCP as ordinary payload." This reframing dissolves the confusion: TLS is not "in" one layer; it does work at several. The layer model is descriptive vocabulary, not a single-slot assignment.

**Q4.** Distinguish hop-by-hop from end-to-end fields in a packet's headers. Give one example of each.

Hint

MAC addresses and IP addresses behave differently as the packet traverses routers. Why?

**Answer:** A _hop-by-hop_ field is one that changes at every router on the path; only the next-hop relationship is meaningful, and the value is rewritten by each intermediate node. The MAC source/destination addresses in an Ethernet frame are hop-by-hop: when a router forwards a packet, it strips the incoming Ethernet frame and constructs a new one with the next hop's MAC addresses. An _end-to-end_ field is one that stays the same as the packet traverses many routers, meaningful to the two endpoints but not modified in transit. The source and destination IP addresses in an IP header are end-to-end: routers consult them to decide forwarding, but they do not rewrite them (with the exception of NAT, which is a deliberate model violation we will see in Chapter 8). TCP sequence numbers, acknowledgements, and TLS-encrypted payloads are also end-to-end.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Describe what each OSI layer does for a `ping` packet sent from a laptop in New York to a server in Sydney. Identify any layers that are essentially empty for this operation.

Hint

`ping` uses ICMP, which is an oddly placed protocol. Where does it sit?

**Answer:** Layer 1 (Physical) carries the packet as electrical or optical signals across the laptop's connector, across the local Wi-Fi or cable, across long-haul fiber, across undersea cables, and across the destination's local link. Layer 2 (Data Link) frames the packet at each hop: Wi-Fi 802.11 at the laptop, Ethernet inside the ISP, possibly SONET or OTN across the undersea path, Ethernet at the destination data center. Layer 3 (Network) sees an IP datagram with source and destination addresses and an ICMP Echo Request inside; ICMP technically rides on top of IP but is considered part of the network layer because it is the network's own diagnostic protocol. Layer 4 (Transport) is empty: ICMP does not use TCP or UDP, it sits directly on IP, and there are no port numbers. Layer 5 (Session) and Layer 6 (Presentation) are entirely empty for `ping`. Layer 7 (Application) is also essentially empty: the `ping` command-line tool is technically a user-level program, but there is no application-layer protocol beyond ICMP. So `ping` is one of the rare operations that exercises only layers 1, 2, and 3 in the strict reading. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM "what layer does `ping` work at?" and watch for the common error of placing ICMP at the transport layer because the LLM has seen "port" associated with `ping` in some contexts; the correct answer is layer 3, and there are no ports.

**Q2.** Trace an HTTP/3 request on a mobile phone to a CDN edge, naming the protocol at each TCP/IP layer (Link, Internet, Transport, Application) and noting where the application's bytes get encrypted.

Hint

HTTP/3 runs over QUIC, not TCP. QUIC integrates TLS 1.3. Where does that put the encryption boundary?

**Answer:** Link layer: depends on the radio environment, typically 5G NR or Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7 framing the bits over the air; once the packet enters the carrier's transport network it is reframed (often into Ethernet over fiber) at every backbone hop. Internet layer: IPv6 (or IPv4 with NAT64) datagram with source address from the carrier's CGNAT pool and destination address being the CDN's anycast address. Transport layer: UDP wrapping a QUIC packet. QUIC packets contain QUIC frames, including STREAM frames carrying HTTP/3 payload and CRYPTO frames carrying TLS 1.3 handshake data. Application layer: HTTP/3 frames (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS) carrying the HTTP request semantics. The encryption boundary is integrated into QUIC itself: from the very first QUIC packet after the Initial handshake, packet payloads are encrypted under keys derived from the TLS 1.3 key schedule. The HTTP/3 request line, headers, and body are all encrypted on the wire. Header compression (QPACK) operates on the plaintext side at both endpoints. Note that the QUIC connection ID and a small initial packet header are visible to the network for routing purposes; everything else is encrypted. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to write the HTTP/3 client; watch for Lie #3 (HTTP version confusion, assuming HTTP/2 server-push or HTTP/1.1 connection-keep-alive semantics that no longer apply) and Lie #4 (outdated TLS configuration; TLS 1.3 is mandatory for QUIC, but the LLM may pull in TLS 1.2 cipher suite lists).

**Q3.** A junior engineer is debugging an issue and reports: "It is a layer 2 problem." What concrete kinds of failure could "layer 2 problem" mean? Give at least four.

Hint

Layer 2 covers framing, local addressing, error detection, and medium access. Each can fail differently.

**Answer:** (1) _Framing error_ : a malformed Ethernet frame, perhaps due to a cable fault or a NIC driver bug, fails its CRC and is dropped at the receiving NIC. The reporting tool would show interface "RX errors" or "CRC errors" climbing. (2) _MAC address conflict_ : two hosts on the same segment configured with the same MAC address, causing intermittent reachability as ARP caches flip-flop. (3) _Wrong VLAN_ : the switch port is configured for the wrong VLAN, putting the host into a network where its IP address makes no sense. (4) _ARP failure_ : the host cannot resolve a peer's MAC address (perhaps because the peer is offline or because ARP traffic is being filtered), so even though the IP layer can route to the peer, the data-link layer cannot frame the packet for transmission. (5) _Switch loop / broadcast storm_ : a switching topology without proper Spanning Tree results in broadcast frames looping endlessly, saturating the segment. (6) _Wi-Fi link layer issue_ : weak signal causing 802.11 retransmissions and effective throughput collapse, or a captive portal intercepting at the L2 association level. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : have an LLM write the diagnosis script; watch for Lie #1 (mixing TCP and UDP semantics: the LLM may suggest a `ping` test as proof that L2 is fine, but `ping` only proves L3 reachability for ICMP, which can succeed even when most L2 frames are dropping due to CRC errors).

**Q4.** Design a layer 7 protocol from scratch for a new use case: small status updates from IoT sensors to a central server. Each sensor sends a 64-byte JSON payload every 30 seconds, with a maximum of 100,000 sensors. Specify what you would build below the application layer (transport, network, etc.) and what guarantees you want at each layer.

Hint

At 100,000 sensors × every 30 seconds × 64 bytes, total bandwidth is small but connection count is large. Choose protocols accordingly.

**Answer:** Aggregate bandwidth is 100,000 × 64 bytes / 30 seconds = roughly 1.7 Mbps to the server, trivial. Aggregate message rate is 100,000 / 30 = roughly 3,300 messages per second, manageable. The constraints are not bandwidth but connection state: 100,000 concurrent connections is expensive. _Transport choice_ : UDP, not TCP. The messages are independent, idempotent, and small; the cost of TCP connection state for 100,000 sensors is too high, and the cost of repeated connection setup if connections are not persistent is also too high. UDP datagrams are stateless on the server side. We will add reliability at the application layer with a sequence number, an acknowledgement, and a retry-with-jitter policy on the sensor. _Network layer_ : standard IPv4 or IPv6, no choices to make here. If the sensors are behind CGNAT, server-initiated communication is hard, but here only the sensor initiates. _Link layer_ : depends on the sensors; many will be on cellular, some on Wi-Fi, some on LoRa or other low-power radios that we treat as opaque. _Application layer_ : a simple binary or JSON format with a sensor ID, sequence number, timestamp, payload, and an HMAC for authenticity. Server sends a tiny ack with the sequence number. Sensor retries with exponential backoff if no ack arrives within a few RTTs. This is essentially what MQTT-SN (MQTT for sensor networks) does, and it works well. The big design lesson: when connection state is the bottleneck, push state out of the kernel (use UDP) and into application-layer idempotent messages. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : an LLM may suggest opening a fresh TCP connection per status update; this is Lie #5 (no connection pooling) and Lie #2 (missing idempotency reasoning, since retries without sequence numbers will double-record updates).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Argue (a) why the OSI 7-layer model survived even though no one implements it literally, (b) what would happen if the industry dropped the OSI vocabulary entirely tomorrow, (c) whether there is a better model that could replace both OSI and TCP/IP.

**Discussion:** (a) OSI survived because it gave the industry a shared vocabulary. Network engineers, vendors, and standards bodies needed a way to say "this is a layer 4 problem" or "this is a layer 7 device" without ambiguity. The vocabulary turned out to be more durable than the protocols, because the vocabulary is independent of which specific protocol implements which layer. When TCP/IP won the protocol war, the layer names stayed. Even today, a Cisco engineer and a Cloudflare engineer can have a productive conversation about "layer 7 load balancing" without reading the same RFC. (b) If we dropped OSI vocabulary, the industry would invent a near-identical vocabulary within months. Networks need a way to talk about "the thing that handles framing" vs "the thing that handles routing" vs "the thing that handles end-to-end conversations." Some words would have to fill those slots. Likely the TCP/IP "Link / Internet / Transport / Application" would expand into 6 or 7 words, because everyone needs to distinguish "physical media stuff" from "framing stuff" and "session stuff" from "content stuff." We would reinvent OSI's distinctions. (c) A better model would acknowledge that modern protocols cross-cut layers, and would let us talk about _contracts_ (reliability, ordering, congestion control, encryption, framing) as orthogonal axes rather than layered slots. You could classify QUIC as "transport-contract + crypto-contract + session-contract, riding on UDP-datagrams, riding on IP-routing, riding on Ethernet-framing, riding on physical-medium." The vocabulary would be N-dimensional rather than 7-layer. This is the direction modern protocol descriptions actually go (the IETF "what does this protocol guarantee?" descriptions are increasingly contract-oriented), but it has not produced a single named replacement model. We probably will not get one. The 7-layer model is wrong in interesting ways; the 4-layer model is wrong in convenient ways; everyone uses both.

**Q2.** Reflect on the layer model's role in the next decade. As more protocols absorb cross-layer functionality (HTTP/3 absorbing what was TLS+TCP+HTTP/2; eBPF operating at many layers in the kernel; DPUs offloading L2 through L4 in hardware), is the layer model becoming less useful or more useful? Defend your position.

**Discussion:** A defensible argument either way. _Becoming less useful_ : protocols that span layers, like QUIC and HTTP/3, are increasingly the load-bearing modern protocols, and the layer model fails to predict where their complexity will live. New engineers might learn faster from "protocol contracts" thinking than from "find the right layer" thinking. DPUs that implement layers 2 through 4 in silicon make the layer boundary less visible to software; the kernel may not even know which packet flows through hardware bypass. _Becoming more useful_ : precisely because so much complexity is cross-cutting, having a shared map for _where_ in the stack each piece of complexity lives becomes more important. When QUIC encrypts the connection-management headers that used to be visible at TCP, you need the layer model to say "this thing that ISPs used to see, they no longer see, because the function moved up the stack." When eBPF lets you attach a program at XDP (layer 2/3) or at the socket layer (layer 4-7 boundary), you need the layer model to describe what the program will and will not see. The model is becoming a vocabulary for talking about _change_ , not for predicting structure. Probably the right answer: less useful as a strict structural model, more useful as a shared vocabulary for discussing tradeoffs and changes. Teaching it remains valuable; building exclusively to it does not.

**Q3.** Consider the design of a future "internet" for interplanetary communication, where one-way latencies are tens of minutes (Earth to Mars varies between 4 and 24 minutes one way). Which assumptions in the current OSI/TCP-IP model break, and how would you restructure the layer model to make the new constraints visible?

**Discussion:** Almost every assumption above the network layer breaks. TCP's round-trip-based congestion control is meaningless when RTT is 20 minutes; flow control by acknowledgement is meaningless when you cannot wait for an ACK. HTTP's request/response model is impractical because no application can wait 40 minutes for a page to load. TLS's handshake takes 1 RTT in its fastest form, which is 40 minutes on this network. Even DNS lookup becomes catastrophically slow. The classic response from the Delay-Tolerant Networking community is to introduce a new layer, the _bundle layer_ , that sits between transport and application and handles long-delay, intermittent connectivity by storing data at intermediate nodes and forwarding when paths become available. This is essentially a "session" layer that was useful on Earth-internet and absolutely necessary on interplanetary internet. Other restructurings: route at the application layer (the application gets to decide what to send via the moon vs via deep-space network); replace request/response with one-way message passing with explicit identifiers; replace congestion control with strict scheduling against a finite set of well-known links. The layer model itself probably survives, but the relative weights of the layers shift: layer 4 (transport) becomes minimal because there is no continuous conversation to manage; layer 5 (session) becomes critical because storing partial conversations across days is the central concern; layer 7 (application) becomes responsible for things the transport used to do. The right answer is probably "the layer model is fine; the protocols at each layer change," which is the same answer that has applied to every previous internet upheaval.

### Chapter Summary

The OSI 7-layer model and the TCP/IP 4-layer model are not competing theories; they are complementary tools. OSI gives us the shared vocabulary the industry uses every day; TCP/IP gives us the shape of what actually runs. Use both. Insist on neither.

Each layer offers a _contract_ to the layer above and _consumes_ services from the layer below. The contract matters more than the layer position. When you encounter a new protocol, ask what contract it offers and what it requires from below; place it where its work naturally falls; do not force it into a single slot if it does work at several.

Modern protocols increasingly cross-cut layers. QUIC absorbs functions from TCP, TLS, and parts of HTTP. eBPF operates at many layers in the kernel. DPUs offload layers 2 through 4 into hardware. The layer model remains useful as vocabulary; it has become less useful as a strict structural predictor.

The running example (load a webpage) appeared in this chapter as a row in the seven-layer table. It will return in Chapter 9 viewed at TCP, in Chapter 14 viewed at HTTP, and in Chapter 27 viewed end-to-end with every byte annotated.

Chapter 3 takes us to the physical and data link layers, where bits become signals and frames become MAC addresses. The first real protocol we will dissect, Ethernet, lives at OSI layers 1 and 2.
