## Chapter 3: From Cable to Packet: Physical and Link Layer Realities

In Chapter 2 we placed every protocol on a layer map. In this chapter we descend to the bottom two layers: physical (where bits become signals) and data link (where bits become frames). This is where electricity and light and radio waves meet the abstractions that the rest of the book will lean on.

It is tempting to skip this layer if you write software. After all, you never deal with voltage levels in your day job; the kernel handles it; the NIC handles it. But the physical and link layers shape the upper layers in ways you cannot understand without seeing them at least once. Why is MTU 1500 on Ethernet, and what does that have to do with TCP performance? Why does Wi-Fi feel slow even when the speed test says it is fast? Why can you sometimes ping a host but not send it large packets? What is ARP, and why is it the protocol that sits in the seam between the layers? Every one of these questions has its answer in the bottom two layers, and the answer ripples up through TCP, HTTP, and your application.

The goals of this chapter:

  1. Build mental models for the three dominant physical media (copper twisted-pair, fiber, RF) and their failure modes.
  2. Read an Ethernet frame header.
  3. Explain MAC addressing and the forwarding-vs-routing distinction.
  4. Trace an ARP exchange and explain why ARP has to exist at all.

By the end you will be able to look at a `tcpdump -xx` output, point to bytes, and say "that is the destination MAC, that is the source MAC, that is the EtherType, that is the IP packet starting here." This is the lowest-level wire fluency that everything above depends on.

### 3.1 Three Physical Media: Copper, Fiber, Radio

Almost all bits on the modern internet travel through one of three physical media. Each has different failure modes, different distance limits, different costs, and different upper-layer implications.

#### 3.1.1 Copper Twisted-Pair Ethernet

The classic. Copper twisted-pair (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a, Cat7, Cat8) carries signals as differential voltage between pairs of wires. The "twist" is not decorative: twisting two wires together causes external electromagnetic noise to induce nearly the same voltage on both wires, which is then canceled out at the receiver because the receiver looks at the _difference_ between them, not the absolute level. This is differential signaling, and it is the reason copper Ethernet works in noisy environments at all.

A Cat6 cable supports 1 Gbps at 100 meters, or 10 Gbps at 55 meters. Cat6a supports 10 Gbps at 100 meters. Cat8 supports 40 Gbps at 30 meters but is uncommon outside data centers. The 100-meter limit is structural: at higher rates, signal attenuation across copper becomes too severe, and crosstalk between pairs in the same cable becomes hard to cancel.

Modulation has evolved with each speed. 10BASE-T used Manchester encoding (the simplest scheme). 100BASE-TX moved to MLT-3. 1000BASE-T uses PAM-5 across four pairs simultaneously, each pair carrying 250 Mbps. 10GBASE-T uses PAM-16. The trend is clear: more amplitude levels per symbol, more parallel pairs, more sophisticated coding to fight noise and intersymbol interference.

Failure modes of copper:

* _Attenuation_ : signal weakens with distance; past 100 meters, the receiver cannot distinguish the signal from background noise. Symptom: link does not come up, or comes up at a lower speed than expected.
* _Crosstalk_ : pairs in the same bundle interfere with each other (near-end crosstalk, far-end crosstalk). Symptom: high error rate, especially at the highest speeds.
* _Physical damage_ : a kinked or stretched cable. Symptom: intermittent link, errors that go away when you replace the cable.
* _Electromagnetic interference_ : running cable parallel to fluorescent lights or motor power cables couples noise. Symptom: rare errors at low speeds, common errors at high speeds.

Copper is cheap, easy to terminate (RJ45 connectors), and supports Power-over-Ethernet (PoE) to deliver electrical power along with the data signal, which is why most office IP phones, security cameras, and wireless access points use copper.

#### 3.1.2 Fiber Optic

Fiber carries data as light pulses through a glass strand thinner than a human hair. The light source is a laser (single-mode fiber, long distance, narrow beam) or an LED (multi-mode fiber, short distance, wider beam). The receiver is a photodiode that converts incoming light back into electrical signals.

Fiber has two key advantages over copper: distance and bandwidth. A single-mode fiber can carry 10 Gbps over 80 kilometers without amplification. With amplification, transoceanic fibers carry hundreds of terabits over thousands of kilometers. The bandwidth-distance product of fiber is roughly a million times that of copper.

Modulation on fiber has its own evolutionary path. Early 1 Gbps fiber used simple on-off keying (the laser is on for a 1, off for a 0). Modern 400 Gbps and 800 Gbps fiber uses PAM-4 (four amplitude levels), coherent detection with phase-shift keying, and wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) where many different colors of light share the same strand, each carrying its own data stream. A single modern fiber can carry over 100 Tbps using DWDM.

Failure modes of fiber:

* _Bend radius violation_ : bending fiber too sharply causes light to leak out at the bend. Symptom: signal loss, especially at longer paths or higher speeds.
* _Dirty connectors_ : a single speck of dust on a fiber endface scatters the laser. Cleaning fiber ends is a serious operational discipline. Symptom: high bit-error rate that comes and goes.
* _Cable cut_ : physical disruption (the backhoe scenario, or in the famous Asian internet outages, shark bites at undersea cable). Symptom: total link loss; usually obvious in the operations center within seconds via BGP withdrawals and routing reconvergence.
* _Wavelength drift_ : a laser's wavelength can drift with temperature; in DWDM systems where channels are 50 GHz apart, drift can collide with adjacent channels. Symptom: errors localized to one wavelength of a WDM system.

Fiber is the backbone medium of the modern internet. Every undersea cable, every long-haul terrestrial route, every data center interconnect, every metro fiber ring runs on glass. The first hundred feet of your ISP service might still be copper coax or copper twisted-pair, but the moment you leave the building, you are on fiber.

#### 3.1.3 Radio (Wireless Ethernet, Cellular, Satellite)

Radio carries data through space as modulated electromagnetic waves. The transmitter takes a digital signal, mixes it with a carrier frequency (anywhere from 30 MHz to 60 GHz depending on the technology), and broadcasts the result. The receiver tunes to that carrier, demodulates, and recovers the data.

The three modern wireless families on the consumer internet:

_Wi-Fi_ : short range (typically 10 to 50 meters indoors), licence-free spectrum (2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and starting in 2019 also 6 GHz). Modern variants: Wi-Fi 5 (802.11ac, 2014), Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax, 2019, adds OFDMA and MU-MIMO), Wi-Fi 6E (extends Wi-Fi 6 to 6 GHz), Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be, 2024, adds 320 MHz channels, multi-link operation, and 4096-QAM). Top theoretical speeds are now in the gigabits per second range, though real-world throughput is typically a fraction of theoretical due to shared medium contention.

_Cellular_ : long range (kilometers per tower), licensed spectrum (carrier-specific, usually below 6 GHz with millimeter-wave variants in the 24 to 40 GHz range for 5G). Generations: 3G (UMTS/HSPA), 4G (LTE), 5G (NR). 5G in particular splits into sub-6 (good range, moderate speed) and mmWave (very fast but very short range and easily blocked by walls). Network slicing in 5G allows the operator to provision different latency and bandwidth profiles for different traffic.

_Satellite_ : very long range (orbital). Two architectural families: geostationary satellites (about 36,000 km above Earth, fixed in the sky, RTT around 600 ms) and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) constellations (Starlink, around 550 km, fast-moving across the sky, RTT around 30 to 50 ms). LEO has displaced GEO for most non-broadcast use cases because the latency is dramatically lower.

Failure modes of radio:

* _Path loss_ : signal strength falls off with distance squared in free space, more sharply with obstacles. Symptom: slow throughput at the edge of the cell or far from the AP.
* _Multipath fading_ : the same signal arrives via multiple reflections at slightly different times, causing interference. MIMO antennas turn this into an advantage (by separating the paths and adding their information); single-antenna systems suffer from it.
* _Interference_ : another transmitter on the same frequency. In licenced bands (cellular, sat) the operator avoids interference by design; in unlicenced bands (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, the 2.4 GHz mess) interference is constant.
* _Bursty loss_ : physical obstacles, signal fades, and contention produce _clustered_ packet losses, not uniform Bernoulli losses. This breaks naive congestion control. Modern TCP variants (BBR, CUBIC) and QUIC's congestion control are increasingly tuned for bursty wireless loss.

The most important property of radio for upper-layer protocol design: _the loss pattern is bursty_. Wired networks lose individual packets at queues; wireless networks lose strings of packets when a fade or contention event hits. Protocols that assume Bernoulli loss (each packet independently dropped with some probability) get worse results on wireless than protocols that model bursty loss explicitly.

#### 3.1.4 The Same Frame Crosses Many Media

A single Ethernet frame leaving your laptop's Wi-Fi card might cross several physical media on its way to a server:

  1. Wi-Fi radio (your laptop to your access point).
  2. Cat6 copper (your access point to your home router).
  3. Coaxial cable (your home router to the cable plant).
  4. Fiber (the cable plant onward through the ISP).
  5. Long-haul fiber (across multiple ISPs, possibly across an undersea cable).
  6. Fiber (into the destination data center).
  7. Cat6 copper (the destination's top-of-rack switch to the server).

At every transition between media, a different transceiver converts the signal: the access point bridges Wi-Fi radio to copper Ethernet, the cable modem bridges coaxial to copper Ethernet, the optical transceiver in the ISP's router bridges fiber to copper inside the router. The data link layer above does not care which medium is in use; it only sees frames.

This is the point of the abstraction. The upper layers should not, in general, need to know whether the bits are crossing fiber or copper or radio. But the upper layer designers do need to know what failure modes can occur, because the failure modes inform protocol design. TCP's congestion control evolved to handle wireless loss patterns. HTTP/3 was designed in part to handle mobile network handoffs. The physical layer never goes entirely away.

### 3.2 The Data Link Layer and Ethernet Frames

Above the physical layer sits the data link layer. Its job is to take a stream of bits delivered by the physical layer and organize them into discrete _frames_ , each carrying one packet of higher-layer data, addressed to a specific peer on the local segment.

Ethernet is the dominant data link protocol on wired networks. Wi-Fi (802.11) is the dominant wireless variant. Both are members of the IEEE 802 family and share core concepts: a frame format with addresses and a checksum, MAC addresses for local identity, and a service contract of "deliver this frame to that peer on this segment, with reasonably high probability."

#### 3.2.1 The Ethernet Frame Format

The classic Ethernet II frame (the format used everywhere on the modern internet) looks like this:
    
    
    +--------------------+--------------------+----------+------------------+-----+
    | Destination MAC    | Source MAC         | EtherType| Payload (46-1500)| FCS |
    | 6 bytes            | 6 bytes            | 2 bytes  |                  | 4   |
    +--------------------+--------------------+----------+------------------+-----+
    

The fields:

* **Destination MAC** (6 bytes, 48 bits): the hardware address of the intended receiver on this segment. The all-ones address (`ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`) is the broadcast address, delivered to every host on the segment.
* **Source MAC** (6 bytes): the hardware address of the sender. Burned into the NIC at manufacture, though most modern NICs allow it to be overridden in software.
* **EtherType** (2 bytes): tells the receiver what kind of protocol is in the payload. Common values: `0x0800` for IPv4, `0x86DD` for IPv6, `0x0806` for ARP, `0x8100` for VLAN-tagged frames.
* **Payload** (46 to 1500 bytes): the actual packet from the layer above. The 1500-byte limit is the _Maximum Transmission Unit_ (MTU); the 46-byte minimum exists so the frame is long enough that collision detection on classic Ethernet could work (an artifact of half-duplex Ethernet that we keep for compatibility).
* **FCS** (4 bytes): Frame Check Sequence, a 32-bit CRC computed over the entire frame. If the FCS at the receiver does not match the computed CRC, the frame is dropped at the NIC; the upper layers are never notified.

Total frame size: 64 bytes minimum, 1518 bytes maximum (or 1522 with VLAN tag). Add 8 bytes of preamble (`10101010...` plus a start-of-frame delimiter) and a 12-byte inter-frame gap, and the minimum on-wire slot for one small frame is 84 bytes (12 IFG + 8 preamble + 64 frame). The inter-frame gap itself is 12 bytes; the 84-byte figure is the full slot, not the gap.

Why MTU 1500? Historically it was a compromise: large enough that the per-frame overhead (headers, CRC, gaps) was a small fraction of payload, small enough that a single frame's transmission time did not monopolize the shared medium. Today MTU 1500 is preserved primarily for compatibility, though many data centers run _jumbo frames_ (typically MTU 9000) for internal links where all hosts agree. The path-MTU-discovery mechanism we will see in Chapter 5 negotiates the smallest MTU along a route.

#### 3.2.2 MAC Addresses

A MAC address (Media Access Control address) is a 48-bit identifier for a network interface, written conventionally as six hex bytes separated by colons or dashes: `00:1a:2b:3c:4d:5e`. The first three bytes are the _OUI_ (Organizationally Unique Identifier), assigned by IEEE to a manufacturer; the last three bytes are assigned by the manufacturer to the individual NIC. In principle, every NIC on the planet has a unique MAC address.

In practice, MAC addresses can be programmatically changed; many modern phones rotate their MAC addresses for privacy reasons when scanning for Wi-Fi networks; virtual machines and containers get synthetic MAC addresses generated at startup. The "burned in" assumption is approximately true for physical hardware in fixed environments, and approximately false for everything else.

Two special MAC address types:

* **Broadcast** : `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`. All bits set. Delivered to every host on the segment.
* **Multicast** : any address with the least significant bit of the first byte set to 1 (e.g., `01:00:5e:...` for IPv4 multicast, `33:33:...` for IPv6 multicast). Delivered to hosts that have joined the multicast group.

MAC addresses are _local-only_. They have no meaning outside the segment on which they are used. When a packet crosses a router, the Ethernet frame is stripped off and a new frame is built with new MAC addresses for the next segment. This is the hop-by-hop nature of layer 2 addressing, contrasted with the end-to-end nature of layer 3 (IP) addresses.

#### Definition: MAC Address

A 48-bit hardware identifier assigned to a network interface, used by the data link layer to address frames to a specific peer on a local network segment. Globally unique by IEEE assignment, though programmable in software.

In plain language, this means: the MAC address is the name your NIC answers to on its local network. Other NICs on the same switch or Wi-Fi AP can send frames to it by name; NICs on the other side of a router cannot, because the router does not forward MAC-addressed frames.

#### Definition: Frame Check Sequence (FCS)

A 32-bit cyclic redundancy check appended to every Ethernet frame, computed over all preceding fields. The receiving NIC recomputes the CRC and discards the frame if it does not match.

In plain language, this means: every frame has a fingerprint, and frames that arrive with a corrupted fingerprint get thrown away silently. Higher layers must notice the missing frame and ask for a retransmission if they care.

### 3.3 The Forwarding-vs-Routing Distinction

A switch and a router both move packets from one interface to another, but they operate at different layers and make different decisions.

A _switch_ is a layer 2 device. It forwards Ethernet frames based on destination MAC addresses. When a frame arrives, the switch looks at the destination MAC, consults its MAC address table (which maps "MAC X is reachable via port Y"), and forwards the frame out of port Y. If the destination MAC is unknown, the switch _floods_ the frame out every port except the one it arrived on, on the bet that the destination will see it and respond. When the destination responds, the switch sees the response's source MAC arriving on a specific port, and it learns: "MAC Z is reachable via port W."

The MAC address table is built dynamically by this learning behavior. Entries age out after a few minutes if not refreshed. Switches do not run any routing protocol; they just observe what arrives where and remember.

A _router_ is a layer 3 device. It forwards IP packets based on destination IP addresses. When a packet arrives, the router strips off the incoming Ethernet frame (because the router was the destination of that frame, hop-by-hop), examines the IP header, consults its IP routing table (which maps "the network 10.1.0.0/24 is reachable via next-hop 10.1.1.1, out of interface eth2"), looks up the MAC address of that next-hop (using ARP, which we will see momentarily), constructs a new Ethernet frame with the next-hop's MAC as the destination, and sends it.

The routing table is built by routing protocols (OSPF, BGP, static configuration) which we will see in Chapters 6 and 7. The router runs explicit protocol state about which networks are reachable through which interfaces.

In summary:

Aspect | Switch (L2) | Router (L3)  
---|---|---  
Addresses used | MAC (48-bit, local) | IP (32 or 128-bit, global)  
Table is | Learned from observed traffic | Built by routing protocols  
Forwarding decision | One table lookup | Longest-prefix match, ARP lookup  
Frame action | Forward without modification (or VLAN tag) | Strip incoming, build new outgoing  
Crosses subnets | No | Yes  
  
Modern devices often combine both: a "switch with a router built in" or a "router with switching ports." These devices typically forward in switching mode when the destination is on the local subnet (fast path, hardware-accelerated) and in routing mode when crossing subnets (slower path, more sophisticated).

#### Common Misconception: A Switch Knows About IP

Pure layer 2 switches do not look at IP. They forward based on MAC addresses. If you configure a switch with VLANs, that is still all happening at layer 2; VLAN tags are an extension of the Ethernet header.

The misconception arises because most consumer "switches" sold today are actually layer 2 _and_ layer 3 devices (sometimes called L3 switches), and the device's web management interface lets you set IP addresses, configure VLAN routing, run DHCP, and so on. The L3 functions are routing, not switching, even though they happen in the same physical box. When you want to reason about a packet's path, ask which decision-making is happening: looking at MAC alone (switching) or looking at IP and consulting a routing table (routing).

### 3.4 ARP: The Glue Between IP and MAC

We have introduced IP (layer 3, end-to-end addresses) and MAC (layer 2, local addresses). Now ask: when you want to send an IP packet to `192.168.1.5`, and the packet is going to leave your NIC over Ethernet, what MAC address goes in the destination field of the Ethernet frame?

The answer is: the MAC of `192.168.1.5` (if it is on your local subnet), or the MAC of your default gateway (if it is not). Either way, you need to translate "IP address" into "MAC address" on the local segment. The protocol that does this translation is the _Address Resolution Protocol_ , or ARP.

ARP is one of the most interesting protocols in the stack because it straddles layers 2 and 3. It uses Ethernet frames (layer 2) to carry IP-related queries (layer 3 information) in order to populate a local cache that enables IP-over-Ethernet to work. The OSI model has no good slot for it; everyone agrees it is somewhere between layer 2 and layer 3.

#### 3.4.1 The ARP Exchange

Suppose your laptop has IP `192.168.1.10` and MAC `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01`, and it wants to send a packet to `192.168.1.5` on the same Wi-Fi network. Your laptop does not know the MAC of `192.168.1.5` yet. The exchange goes:

  1. Your laptop checks its _ARP cache_. The cache maps "IP X has MAC Y" entries learned recently. If `192.168.1.5` is in the cache, use the cached MAC. Done.
  2. If not in cache, your laptop sends an ARP request. The ARP request is an Ethernet frame addressed to the broadcast MAC `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, with EtherType `0x0806` (ARP), containing a payload that says: "Who has IP 192.168.1.5? Tell 192.168.1.10 (MAC aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:01)."
  3. Every host on the segment receives the broadcast. Most ignore it (the IP does not match theirs). The host with IP `192.168.1.5` (let us say MAC `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02`) responds.
  4. The response is a unicast ARP reply, addressed directly to your laptop's MAC, saying: "192.168.1.5 is at MAC aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02."
  5. Your laptop receives the reply, caches the mapping, and now sends the actual IP packet inside an Ethernet frame with destination MAC `aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02`.

Once the cache entry exists, subsequent packets to `192.168.1.5` go directly without further ARP traffic. Cache entries time out (typically after 5 to 20 minutes) and are refreshed by another ARP exchange when needed.

#### 3.4.2 The ARP Request and Reply Wire Format

An ARP packet has its own format inside the Ethernet payload:
    
    
    +----------------+----------------+--------------+--------------+
    | Hardware type  | Protocol type  | Hardware len | Protocol len |
    | 2 bytes        | 2 bytes        | 1 byte       | 1 byte       |
    +----------------+----------------+--------------+--------------+
    | Operation                                                     |
    | 2 bytes                                                       |
    +---------------------------------------------------------------+
    | Sender hardware address (6 bytes for Ethernet MAC)            |
    +---------------------------------------------------------------+
    | Sender protocol address (4 bytes for IPv4)                    |
    +---------------------------------------------------------------+
    | Target hardware address (6 bytes for Ethernet MAC)            |
    +---------------------------------------------------------------+
    | Target protocol address (4 bytes for IPv4)                    |
    +---------------------------------------------------------------+
    

For a typical IPv4-over-Ethernet ARP request:

* Hardware type = 1 (Ethernet)
* Protocol type = 0x0800 (IPv4)
* Hardware length = 6 (MAC bytes)
* Protocol length = 4 (IPv4 bytes)
* Operation = 1 (request) or 2 (reply)

In the request, the target hardware address is all zeros (the requester does not know it yet). In the reply, all four fields are filled in.

#### 3.4.3 IPv6 Replaces ARP with NDP

ARP is IPv4-only. IPv6 replaces it with _Neighbor Discovery Protocol_ (NDP), which is built on ICMPv6 and serves a similar role but with extensions: not just address resolution, but also router discovery (find your default gateway), prefix advertisement (learn the local network's prefix), and duplicate address detection. We will see NDP in passing in Chapter 5.

For now, just internalize: ARP for IPv4, NDP for IPv6, same conceptual role.

#### Common Misconception: ARP Is a Routing Protocol

ARP does not route. It does not forward packets. It does not maintain knowledge of distant networks. ARP only resolves local-subnet IP addresses to MAC addresses. The moment a packet needs to cross a router, ARP's role ends; the router uses its own routing table, and then ARPs for the _next hop's_ MAC inside its own subnet.

The confusion arises because ARP is necessary for IP to function on Ethernet, and the routing decision (send to this gateway) precedes the ARP query (what MAC is the gateway?). They are related but distinct: the routing decision picks the next-hop IP; ARP translates that IP into a MAC for framing.

#### 3.4.4 The Wire-Level Artifact: ARP from tcpdump

Here is what a real ARP exchange looks like in `tcpdump`:
    
    
    14:23:01.123456 ARP, Request who-has 192.168.1.5 tell 192.168.1.10, length 28
    14:23:01.124789 ARP, Reply 192.168.1.5 is-at aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02, length 28
    

With `-xx` to show the bytes:
    
    
    14:23:01.123456 ARP, Request who-has 192.168.1.5 tell 192.168.1.10, length 28
            0x0000:  ffff ffff ffff aabb ccdd ee01 0806 0001
            0x0010:  0800 0604 0001 aabb ccdd ee01 c0a8 010a
            0x0020:  0000 0000 0000 c0a8 0105
    

Decoded:

* `ffff ffff ffff` — destination MAC (broadcast)
* `aabb ccdd ee01` — source MAC (the requester)
* `0806` — EtherType (ARP)
* `0001` — Hardware type (Ethernet)
* `0800` — Protocol type (IPv4)
* `06` — Hardware length (6)
* `04` — Protocol length (4)
* `0001` — Operation (request)
* `aabb ccdd ee01` — Sender hardware address (the requester's MAC)
* `c0a8 010a` — Sender protocol address (192.168.1.10 in hex)
* `0000 0000 0000` — Target hardware address (unknown, all zeros)
* `c0a8 0105` — Target protocol address (192.168.1.5 in hex)

You can capture and inspect this on any Linux or macOS machine with `sudo tcpdump -xx -nn arp`. Watching this exchange the first time is one of the most clarifying moments in learning networking. The whole conversation, the entire dance between IP and MAC, fits in 28 bytes of ARP payload — though on a real wire each frame will also carry an Ethernet header (14 bytes) and be padded to the 60-byte minimum payload (so an actual `-xx` dump shows 18 trailing pad bytes after the 28 ARP bytes; the FCS is normally stripped by the NIC before `tcpdump` sees it). It is the first wire-level artifact of the book, and we will see many more.

### 3.5 What Else Happens at Layer 2: VLANs, Spanning Tree, Auto-Negotiation

Three more concepts deserve at least passing introduction.

#### 3.5.1 VLANs

A _VLAN_ (Virtual LAN) is a way to logically partition a physical Ethernet network into multiple isolated segments. Two hosts on the same physical switch but different VLANs cannot reach each other at layer 2; they need a router (or a VLAN-aware switch acting as one) to talk.

VLANs are implemented by inserting a 4-byte tag into the Ethernet frame, between the source MAC and the EtherType. The tag includes a 12-bit VLAN ID (so up to 4096 VLANs per network) and a 3-bit priority. The EtherType for tagged frames is `0x8100`, and the original EtherType is moved two positions later.

VLANs let one physical infrastructure carry multiple logical networks with traffic isolation. Most enterprises and data centers use them heavily.

#### 3.5.2 Spanning Tree

If you connect switches in a cycle (switch A to switch B, switch B to switch C, switch C back to switch A), a broadcast frame can loop forever, growing the loop traffic exponentially. This is called a _broadcast storm_ , and it can take down an entire network in seconds.

The _Spanning Tree Protocol_ (STP) prevents this by detecting the cyclic topology and disabling some links to make the network a tree (no cycles). When a link fails, STP can re-enable a previously disabled link to restore connectivity. Modern variants (RSTP, MSTP) are faster, but the core idea is the same: keep the topology a tree at any moment.

#### 3.5.3 Auto-Negotiation

When two Ethernet devices connect, they negotiate the highest speed and duplex mode they both support. This is auto-negotiation, defined in 802.3u. The two devices exchange "I can do X" messages until they find the common-best setting. If auto-negotiation fails, you can end up with a _duplex mismatch_ (one side full duplex, the other half), which produces a high error rate and slow throughput that is famously hard to diagnose without inspecting the interface counters.

Auto-negotiation almost always works in 2026. When it does not, you have a broken cable, broken transceiver, or one device with auto-negotiation forced off and the other forced to a different speed.

### 3.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Differentiate the three physical media (copper, fiber, radio) by their dominant failure mode. Give one upper-layer protocol implication for each.

Hint

Copper fails locally and physically; fiber fails catastrophically when a cable is cut; radio fails statistically and burstily.

**Answer:** _Copper_ fails most often by attenuation (signal weakens past 100 meters) and electromagnetic interference (noise coupling). Upper-layer implication: copper links have well-defined bandwidth and reasonably stable latency, so TCP's congestion control finds a comfortable operating point; copper failures are typically link-down rather than intermittent. _Fiber_ fails most often by physical cable cuts and connector contamination. Upper-layer implication: fiber failures are usually total and binary; BGP routing reconvergence handles them within seconds via withdrawal of routes; in between cuts, fiber loss is negligible, so TCP runs at high efficiency. _Radio_ fails most often by path loss, multipath fading, and interference, producing bursty packet loss. Upper-layer implication: TCP congestion control must distinguish wireless loss (does not indicate congestion) from queue-based loss (does indicate congestion); algorithms like BBR specifically address this; HTTP/3 with connection migration explicitly handles the wireless handoff case.

**Q2.** Walk the Ethernet frame format field by field. For each field, state its size, its purpose, and what happens if it is corrupted in transit.

Hint

Six fields including preamble. Where does the CRC catch corruption, and what is silently allowed through?

**Answer:** _Preamble + SFD_ (8 bytes): a synchronization pattern (`10101010...10101011`) that signals to the receiver "a frame is about to start." If corrupted, the receiver may miss the start of the frame entirely; this is rare on healthy links. _Destination MAC_ (6 bytes): the target NIC's address. If corrupted, the frame arrives at the wrong NIC (which will drop it because it does not match) or no NIC accepts it, but the FCS will likely catch the corruption first. _Source MAC_ (6 bytes): the sender's address. Corruption here causes the receiver to learn an incorrect MAC-to-port mapping in switches, which can cause forwarding loops or blackholes for return traffic. _EtherType_ (2 bytes): identifies the payload protocol. Corruption causes the receiving stack to hand the payload to the wrong upper-layer protocol (e.g., IPv4 stack receives ARP bytes and misinterprets them); usually quickly detected. _Payload_ (46 to 1500 bytes): the upper-layer packet. Corruption is exactly what upper-layer checksums (IP, TCP) would also catch, layered on top. _FCS_ (4 bytes): the frame check sequence. If any earlier field is corrupted, the receiver's recomputed CRC will not match the FCS field, and the frame is dropped silently at the NIC. If the FCS itself is corrupted, the frame is also dropped. The 32-bit CRC catches all single-bit errors and burst errors up to 32 bits long; longer bursts have a roughly 2−322^{-32}2−32 chance of slipping through, which is why upper-layer protocols also use their own checksums.

**Q3.** Define MAC address. Explain why MAC addresses are described as "local-only" and why this is different from IP addresses.

Hint

What happens to the MAC fields when a packet crosses a router?

**Answer:** A MAC address is a 48-bit hardware identifier for a network interface, used by the data link layer to address frames on a local network segment. It is conventionally globally unique by IEEE allocation but is programmable in software. MAC addresses are "local-only" because they are meaningful only within a single Ethernet broadcast domain (one or more switches connected without intervening routers). When a packet crosses a router, the router strips the incoming Ethernet frame entirely (including both MAC addresses), examines the IP header to decide forwarding, performs an ARP lookup to find the MAC of the next hop, and constructs a new Ethernet frame with new source and destination MACs for the next segment. The IP addresses inside the packet do not change as the packet crosses routers (with the exception of NAT, which we will see in Chapter 8); the MAC addresses change at every hop. This makes MAC hop-by-hop and IP end-to-end. A consequence: the destination server has no idea what MAC the original sender used; it only knows the MAC of the last-hop router that delivered the final frame.

**Q4.** State why ARP exists. What problem does it solve, and what is the alternative if you somehow disabled ARP?

Hint

The IP header has the destination IP. The Ethernet frame has the destination MAC. How does the sending host derive the second from the first?

**Answer:** ARP exists because IP packets specify destination addresses in IP-address form (32 bits for IPv4), but the Ethernet data link layer requires destination addresses in MAC-address form (48 bits). To send an IP packet over an Ethernet segment, the sender must construct an Ethernet frame around it, and the destination MAC field of that frame must be filled in. ARP is the protocol that translates "destination IP X on my local subnet" into "destination MAC Y," which can then be used to construct the frame. If ARP were disabled, you would have to manually configure the MAC of every host you wanted to talk to in your local ARP table (this is supported via static ARP entries: `arp -s 192.168.1.5 aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:02`). This is unworkable at scale; ARP automates the discovery. In IPv6, ARP is replaced by NDP (Neighbor Discovery Protocol), which serves the same role over ICMPv6 with additional features for router and prefix discovery. The deeper architectural reason is that IP layer (3) and Ethernet layer (2) use different address spaces by design, and the layered model requires a translation step between them.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** On a typical residential Wi-Fi network, a user's phone gets IP `192.168.1.42` and the home router (also the default gateway) has IP `192.168.1.1`. The phone wants to load a webpage from a server at `203.0.113.50`. Walk through the layer 2 addresses used at each step.

Hint

The destination IP is not on the local subnet, so the destination MAC at layer 2 is _not_ the destination server's MAC.

**Answer:** The phone determines that `203.0.113.50` is not in its local subnet (`192.168.1.0/24`). So the packet needs to be routed, and the next hop is the default gateway, `192.168.1.1`. The phone does not yet know the gateway's MAC, so it sends an ARP request asking "who has 192.168.1.1?" The home router replies with its MAC, say `bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:01`. The phone now constructs an Ethernet frame: source MAC = phone's MAC (`aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:42`), destination MAC = router's MAC (`bb:cc:dd:ee:ff:01`), EtherType = `0x0800` (IPv4), payload = the IP packet with source IP `192.168.1.42` and destination IP `203.0.113.50`. The frame travels over Wi-Fi from the phone to the access point, and over Ethernet (probably) from the AP to the router. The router receives the frame, sees that the destination MAC is itself, strips the Ethernet frame, looks at the IP destination, consults its routing table, determines that `203.0.113.50` is reachable via its ISP-facing interface. The router does its own ARP (or, more likely, looks up its cache) for the ISP's gateway MAC, builds a new Ethernet (or PPPoE, or DOCSIS-encapsulated) frame for that next hop, and forwards. At every hop along the way, the MAC addresses change to reflect the local segment's neighbors; the IP source and destination remain unchanged (assuming no NAT, which the home router likely will perform on the source IP, replacing `192.168.1.42` with the public WAN IP, but the destination remains `203.0.113.50`). _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to write a packet-construction routine; watch for Lie #1 (TCP/UDP semantics mixed up: the LLM may try to set TCP-related fields on an ICMP echo and get confused) and a related layer-confusion error of treating MAC and IP as interchangeable.

**Q2.** A new piece of WiFi-connected office equipment is being commissioned. After connecting it to the network, it can reach hosts in the same subnet but cannot reach the internet. The user tries `ping 8.8.8.8` and gets no response. Walk through the troubleshooting from layer 1 upward, naming concrete tools.

Hint

Layer 1 problems show as no link. Layer 2 problems show as ARP failures. Layer 3 problems show as routing or DHCP-config issues.

**Answer:** _Layer 1_ : confirm physical/wireless link is up. `ip link show` on Linux reports interface state; `ifconfig` or `networksetup` on macOS; the OS GUI on Windows. If link is down, check the cable, the switch port, or the Wi-Fi association status. Since the user can reach local hosts, layer 1 is fine. _Layer 2_ : confirm the device is on the right segment. Check `arp -a` to see if the default gateway's MAC has been learned. If the gateway is in the ARP table, layer 2 to the gateway is working. If not, attempt to ARP the gateway: `ping 192.168.1.1` should trigger an ARP exchange; if the ARP fails, there is a layer 2 problem (wrong VLAN, MAC filtering, or the gateway is offline). _Layer 3_ : confirm IP configuration. `ip addr` on Linux, `ifconfig` on macOS, `ipconfig` on Windows should show an IP address from the expected subnet, a netmask, and a default gateway. `ip route` (or `route -n`) should show a default route via the gateway. If any of these is missing, DHCP did not succeed: check the DHCP server, the device's DHCP client logs, or static configuration. _Layer 3 reachability_ : `ping 192.168.1.1` (the gateway) should work; if not, layer 3 connectivity to the gateway is broken. `traceroute 8.8.8.8` shows where the packet stops; if it stops at the gateway, the gateway cannot reach further (ISP or upstream firewall issue); if it stops further out, the problem is upstream. _Layer 4-7_ : probably not the issue here, since basic `ping` (ICMP, layer 3) is failing, but if `ping` works and DNS lookups fail, you have a DNS configuration problem (no resolver, or resolver unreachable). _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : an LLM may suggest skipping ahead to test DNS or HTTP without first verifying layer 3 reachability; this is the classic layer-confusion bug (jumping to the top before validating the bottom).

**Q3.** A network engineer notices that her datacenter is mysteriously dropping 0.1% of all packets, but only on Tuesdays between 2pm and 3pm. Form three hypotheses about what could be happening, and design a measurement plan to discriminate among them.

Hint

0.1% is much higher than fiber bit-error rates would produce. What changes periodically in a datacenter?

**Answer:** Three hypotheses: (1) _Scheduled job causing congestion_ : a backup or batch job runs Tuesdays 2-3pm, saturating a particular link, causing queue drops on that link. (2) _Crosstalk from external EMF source_ : a building HVAC system or other equipment that runs on a Tuesday afternoon schedule produces electromagnetic interference affecting cables in a specific run. (3) _Routine maintenance window_ : a router reload or BGP convergence event during the Tuesday-afternoon maintenance window briefly drops traffic. _Measurement plan_ : First, capture per-link counters every minute via SNMP or streaming telemetry, looking for the link with elevated drops at 2-3pm Tuesdays. If one specific link shows queue-tail drops (FIFO drop counter incrementing) during the window, hypothesis 1 is supported; correlate with bandwidth utilization on the link, which should also peak at the same time. If the elevated drops are CRC errors (FCS failures) rather than queue drops, hypothesis 2 is supported; physically inspect cable routing in the affected area for proximity to building infrastructure. If the drops correlate with router-CPU spikes, control-plane churn, or BGP route flapping, hypothesis 3 is supported; check change-management logs for that window. Cross-correlate `tcpdump` captures during the affected window with the upper-layer drops the application is seeing; bursty packet loss (clustered) suggests medium-level interference, while uniform drops suggest queue saturation. The discrimination is concrete and at-the-counter, not by guesswork. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to write a diagnostic script; watch for it suggesting protocol-level captures without first checking interface counters (the bottom layer is almost always where you should start).

**Q4.** A developer is writing a tool that needs to construct raw Ethernet frames in user space (perhaps for testing, perhaps for a custom layer 2 protocol). What four fields must the developer get right for the frame to be accepted by a switch, and what happens if each one is wrong?

Hint

The CRC is computed by the NIC, usually. The minimum frame size is important. What else?

**Answer:** _Destination MAC_ : must be valid (unicast on the segment, the broadcast address, or a multicast group). If it is a unicast address that no host on the segment has, the frame is forwarded into the void by the switch and silently dropped. If it is a broadcast or multicast, all hosts receive it. _Source MAC_ : should be the sender's MAC (or a deliberately spoofed value if testing). If it is a value that conflicts with another host on the segment, the switch's MAC table will flip between ports, causing forwarding chaos. _EtherType_ : must indicate a payload protocol the receiver knows. If it is `0x0800` (IPv4) and the payload is gibberish, the receiver's IP stack will try to parse it as an IPv4 packet and reject it; if it is `0x0000` or some other unrecognized value, most NICs will deliver the frame to user space if the receiver has set up a raw socket, otherwise drop it. _Frame size_ : must be between 64 bytes (minimum, including FCS) and 1518 bytes (maximum without VLAN tag) on standard Ethernet. Frames smaller than 64 bytes are called _runts_ and are dropped at the receiving NIC; frames larger than 1518 bytes are called _giants_ and are dropped unless jumbo frames are enabled. The FCS is usually computed by the NIC automatically in hardware when transmitting a raw frame, so the developer typically does not need to compute it manually; the NIC also strips and validates the FCS on receive. If the developer is using a tool like AF_PACKET on Linux to send raw frames, the kernel may take care of inserting valid Ethernet headers and the FCS, leaving the developer responsible for only the payload. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to write a raw-Ethernet-frame sender; watch for Lie #2 (no error handling for kernel-rejected frames: the LLM may write `send()` without checking the return value, and frames that fail validation are silently dropped, leaving the developer puzzled).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Reflect on whether the strict layering of MAC (local) and IP (end-to-end) was the right design. What would happen if every host had only one address that was both globally unique and used for local switching? List at least three concrete consequences.

**Discussion:** This is essentially the design question that led to the modern split. Consequences: (1) _Forwarding table size explodes_ : every switch would need to know about every host in the world, because there is no aggregation by network. With MAC-only addressing, the switch table is bounded by hosts on the local segment (typically thousands); with IP aggregation, internet routers carry routes to _networks_ , summarized to roughly one million entries today. A flat global namespace would require routers to carry billions of entries. (2) _Mobility becomes catastrophic_ : when a host moves from one segment to another (laptop unplugs from Ethernet, reconnects to a different network), its globally unique address would need to be re-advertised everywhere. Today, IP addresses are usually assigned per-network and change when the host moves, but the locally unique MAC stays. A flat global addressing would conflate these two roles. (3) _Privacy and reassignment become harder_ : a globally unique address tied to a specific NIC is a permanent identifier that follows the user; you cannot rotate it for privacy without breaking forwarding. The current split allows IP addresses (which appear in traffic logs) to be reassigned regularly via DHCP, while MAC stays semi-stable for local switching. (4) _Failure isolation suffers_ : a misbehaving host in one network broadcasting bad traffic would, with a flat namespace, affect routing globally. With hierarchical routing, the blast radius is contained. The hierarchy of "MAC for local, IP for end-to-end" turns out to be the right trade because it matches the hierarchy of administrative control: each network operates its own switching independently, while the global IP routing is a different concern. Some experimental architectures (IPv6 with link-local prefixes; Identifier-Locator Network Protocol) re-examine this split, but the durability of the current scheme suggests the original designers got it right.

**Q2.** Argue (a) why the 1500-byte MTU has survived from 1980 to 2026, (b) what would change if the entire internet moved to a 9000-byte MTU tomorrow, (c) what we can predict about MTU in 2036.

**Discussion:** (a) MTU 1500 survived because of compatibility lock-in. Every router, switch, host, and protocol implementation assumed MTU 1500 on Ethernet for decades. Path-MTU-discovery exists but is fragile (ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" messages are often blocked by misconfigured firewalls, causing PMTUD blackholes). The cost of changing MTU is path-wide coordination, which the internet cannot do without a flag day. (b) If everyone moved to MTU 9000 (jumbo frames) overnight: TCP throughput would increase substantially for large transfers because per-packet overhead becomes a smaller fraction of payload (about 0.7% rather than 4%); CPU usage on hosts would drop because there are fewer packets to process for the same byte count; TCP congestion control would slightly favor jumbo frames during slow-start because each segment is larger. But: middleboxes that hard-code 1500 would silently drop the larger frames; older wireless and some satellite links cannot handle 9000 bytes; tunneling protocols (VXLAN, GRE) that add headers would fragment again. The flag day is technically infeasible without years of careful coordination. (c) In 2036, expect MTU 1500 to remain dominant on the public internet, but most data center east-west traffic, cloud-VPC traffic, and CDN-to-origin traffic to run at MTU 9000 in controlled environments where path-MTU is known. The split between "internet-facing" (MTU 1500) and "internal" (MTU 9000 or higher) will continue. We may see protocols that gracefully handle variable MTU by working in larger logical blocks (QUIC's connection-management can negotiate larger packetization), but the 1500-byte default is likely to remain because of pure inertia.

**Q3.** Consider the scenario in which all wired networks are eventually replaced by some new physical medium (perhaps photonic on-chip, perhaps wireless mesh). How much of the current layer 2 architecture (Ethernet frames, MAC addresses, ARP) would survive, and what would change?

**Discussion:** Surprisingly little of the wire-specific stuff would have to change. The Ethernet frame format (destination, source, EtherType, payload, FCS) is a useful abstraction regardless of medium; new media would likely tunnel "Ethernet frames" over their native framing for compatibility, as Wi-Fi already does (Wi-Fi frames carry Ethernet-style payloads with a slightly different header layout). MAC addresses are independent of medium and would survive directly; their 48-bit space might grow to 64 or 128 bits if the device population needed it. ARP would survive in IPv4 contexts as long as IPv4 exists, but the world is increasingly IPv6-first, and NDP (ICMPv6-based neighbor discovery) is already the modern equivalent. The thing that would change is the lower-half (physical signaling, error rates, contention models). A photonic chip would have different signaling than copper; wireless mesh would have different contention models than today's CSMA/CD. The data link layer abstraction would absorb these changes; the protocols above would not notice. This is exactly the point of layering: the bottom can change while the middle and top stay stable. The lesson for designers is that the well-chosen abstraction (Ethernet frame + MAC address + frame check sequence) is durable across enormous physical-layer change. The OSI model's separation between layer 1 and layer 2 turns out to be one of its most valuable contributions.

### Chapter Summary

The bottom two layers of the network stack are where bits become signals and signals become frames. Three physical media dominate: copper twisted-pair for short-range last-mile links, fiber for long-range and high-bandwidth backbones, and radio for mobile and wireless access. Each has its own failure modes that ripple up into how the upper-layer protocols are designed.

The data link layer organizes bits into frames addressed by MAC addresses. Ethernet's frame format (destination, source, EtherType, payload, FCS) is the dominant wired format; Wi-Fi 802.11 uses a related but more complex format with additional control fields. MAC addresses are local-only: they apply on a single segment and are rewritten at every router hop.

The forwarding-vs-routing distinction is fundamental. Switches forward Ethernet frames based on MAC; routers route IP packets based on IP address; modern devices combine both. ARP is the protocol that translates IP addresses to MAC addresses on a local segment, sitting awkwardly between layers 2 and 3, and replaced in IPv6 by NDP.

The wire-level artifact of this chapter, a captured ARP exchange, will be referenced repeatedly. The 28-byte ARP packet contains the entire dance between IP and MAC. If you can read it, you have crossed the first wire-fluency threshold.

In Chapter 4 we walk up the Ethernet speed ladder to 800 Gbps, introduce Wi-Fi 6 and 7 at literacy, and meet DPUs: the 2026 reality in which the NIC is itself a Linux box and the data link layer is moving into specialized silicon.

## Chapter 4: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, and the DPU Revolution

The previous chapter introduced classical Ethernet, classical MAC addressing, and the ARP exchange. Those concepts are durable, but the speeds, the topologies, and the silicon underneath them have transformed since the 1990s. A data center in 2026 looks almost nothing like a data center in 2006. Your home Wi-Fi router today negotiates protocols and antenna arrangements that did not exist five years ago. And the NIC in your server is no longer a passive frame-mover; it is a small Linux computer with its own CPUs, its own memory, and its own operating system.

This chapter walks the modern data-link landscape: the Ethernet speed ladder up to 800 Gbps, Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7 at literacy level, and the DPU revolution that is moving large fractions of the network stack into specialized silicon. By the end of the chapter you will be able to look at a 2026 server bill-of-materials and explain what each NIC is doing, why it costs 3,000 USD instead of 30 USD, and what fraction of the kernel networking stack it has absorbed.

### 4.1 The Ethernet Speed Ladder

The IEEE 802.3 working group has been delivering new Ethernet speeds at roughly 5-year cadence since 1983, when 10 Mbps Ethernet was standardized over thick coaxial cable. The progression has been an order of magnitude every ten or fifteen years, sometimes faster.

Standard | Speed | Year | Typical medium | Reach  
---|---|---|---|---  
10BASE-T | 10 Mbps | 1990 | Cat3 copper | 100 m  
100BASE-TX | 100 Mbps | 1995 | Cat5 copper | 100 m  
1000BASE-T | 1 Gbps | 1999 | Cat5e/Cat6 copper | 100 m  
10GBASE-T | 10 Gbps | 2006 | Cat6a copper | 100 m  
10GBASE-SR | 10 Gbps | 2002 | multi-mode fiber | 300 m  
25GBASE-SR | 25 Gbps | 2016 | multi-mode fiber | 100 m  
40GBASE-SR4 | 40 Gbps | 2010 | multi-mode fiber, 4 lanes | 100 m  
100GBASE-SR4 | 100 Gbps | 2014 | multi-mode fiber, 4 lanes | 100 m  
400GBASE-SR8 | 400 Gbps | 2017 | multi-mode fiber, 8 lanes | 100 m  
800GBASE-DR8 | 800 Gbps | 2022 | single-mode fiber, 8 lanes | 500 m  
1.6 Tbps (planned) | 1.6 Tbps | ~2026 | single-mode fiber | TBD  
  
The current state of the art in deployed equipment is 400 Gbps per interface, with 800 Gbps shipping in late 2024 and into 2025 in hyperscaler data centers. 1.6 Tbps is in the late-standardization phase; first deployments expected by 2026 or 2027.

Two patterns dominate the climb:

_Pattern 1: Parallel lanes_. Past about 25 Gbps per single optical lane, increasing the per-lane rate hits physics limits (laser modulation speed, signal integrity). The solution is parallel lanes: 100GBASE-SR4 is four parallel 25 Gbps optical channels; 400GBASE-SR8 is eight parallel 50 Gbps channels; 800GBASE-DR8 is eight parallel 100 Gbps channels. The optical transceiver does all the parallelization; the host sees one logical interface.

_Pattern 2: More bits per symbol_. Older Ethernet used simple on-off keying (NRZ): the laser is on for a 1, off for a 0. Modern Ethernet uses PAM-4: four amplitude levels per symbol carrying 2 bits. This doubles throughput at the same symbol rate. Future generations may use PAM-6 or PAM-8, or coherent optical modulation (phase-shift keying with multiple amplitude levels), which is the approach used in long-haul DWDM.

The result of these two patterns is that the per-lane speed has climbed at modest rates (NRZ at 1 Gbps in 1999, PAM-4 at 100 Gbps in 2024 is about 100x in 25 years), but per-interface speed has climbed much faster because of parallelization (1 Gbps in 1999, 800 Gbps in 2024 is 800x).

#### 4.1.1 SFP, QSFP, OSFP: The Modular Optical Form Factors

Modern Ethernet switches and NICs do not include the optical transceiver in the device itself. The transceiver is a pluggable module, allowing the same switch to be configured for short-range multi-mode fiber, long-range single-mode fiber, copper direct-attach cables, or active-optical cables depending on the deployment.

The form factors:

* **SFP / SFP+ / SFP28** : a small form-factor pluggable, supports 1 / 10 / 25 Gbps respectively. The dominant single-lane transceiver since the early 2000s.
* **QSFP / QSFP+ / QSFP28 / QSFP56** : Quad SFP, four lanes in one transceiver, supports 4x10 = 40, 4x25 = 100, 4x50 = 200 Gbps.
* **QSFP-DD / OSFP** : dual-density or octal small form-factor, eight lanes, supports 400 Gbps and 800 Gbps.

A typical 2026 hyperscaler top-of-rack switch has 32 or 64 ports of QSFP-DD, each running 400 or 800 Gbps. The switching ASIC behind those ports forwards 12.8 Tbps to 51.2 Tbps of aggregate bandwidth. A single rack of servers might consume one of these switches at full bandwidth.

#### 4.1.2 Copper Direct Attach and Active Optical Cables

Inside a rack, fiber transceivers are overkill: the distances are short, and a passive copper cable with terminations soldered directly to QSFP connectors works fine for distances up to about 5 meters. These are _direct-attach copper_ (DAC) cables, and they cost a fraction of what fiber transceivers cost.

For distances between 5 and 100 meters within a data center, _active optical cables_ (AOC) are common: a fiber strand with permanently attached transceivers on both ends, factory-built to a specific length. Cheaper than swappable transceivers because the transceivers can be optimized for known fixed conditions.

Past 100 meters, swappable transceivers and standalone fiber become the norm.

#### 4.1.3 What These Speeds Mean for Applications

At 400 Gbps, the time to transmit a 1500-byte frame is roughly 30 nanoseconds. The frame is on the wire for _less time than a single CPU cache miss_ (typically 50-100 ns on modern hardware). Per-frame the CPU has at most a few hundred nanoseconds to look up routing state, run filters, and forward — far less than the kernel's traditional network path consumes. The CPU cannot drive a 400 Gbps NIC at line rate using traditional kernel networking; there is not enough CPU per byte to make decisions about every packet.

This is the fundamental driver of every modern networking innovation: kernel bypass, DPDK, AF_XDP, RDMA, DPU offload. The traditional model of "the kernel handles every packet" simply does not scale to terabit speeds. We will see each of these mechanisms in detail later in the book; for now, internalize that 400 Gbps is _the regime where the kernel cannot keep up_ , and applications and infrastructure that operate at those speeds have moved most of their per-packet work out of the kernel.

### 4.2 Modern Wi-Fi: 6, 6E, and 7

Wi-Fi is the dominant wireless data-link layer in homes and offices. Its evolution since Wi-Fi 5 has been dramatic, and the marketing names (Wi-Fi 4, 5, 6, 6E, 7) hide a lot of substance.

#### 4.2.1 Wi-Fi 6 (802.11ax, 2019)

The big additions over Wi-Fi 5:

* **OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access)** : Wi-Fi 5 transmitted one frame at a time on a channel; Wi-Fi 6 can divide the channel into smaller resource units and transmit to multiple devices simultaneously in the same time slot. This is huge for environments with many low-bandwidth devices (a coffee shop with 50 phones; an office with 200 IoT sensors).
* **MU-MIMO uplink** : multi-user MIMO was downlink-only in Wi-Fi 5; Wi-Fi 6 adds uplink. Now multiple devices can transmit to the AP simultaneously.
* **1024-QAM** : each symbol carries 10 bits, up from 256-QAM (8 bits) in Wi-Fi 5. About 25% throughput improvement at close range.
* **Target Wake Time (TWT)** : devices can negotiate scheduled wake-up windows with the AP, allowing radios to sleep between scheduled exchanges. This is critical for IoT battery life.
* **Spatial reuse (BSS coloring)** : a 6-bit "color" tag on each transmission lets the radio quickly decide whether a detected transmission is from a co-channel neighbor (could potentially be ignored) or its own AP (must defer). This raises spectral efficiency in dense deployments.

#### 4.2.2 Wi-Fi 6E (2020)

The same Wi-Fi 6 protocol, extended to operate in the 6 GHz band (5.925 to 7.125 GHz). This added 1.2 GHz of new spectrum, increasing the available channels from a few (in 2.4 GHz) and a couple of dozen (in 5 GHz) to up to seven non-overlapping 160-MHz channels in 6 GHz. Crucial for high-density deployments where the older bands are already congested.

#### 4.2.3 Wi-Fi 7 (802.11be, ratified 2024)

The big additions over Wi-Fi 6E:

* **320 MHz channels** : twice the bandwidth of Wi-Fi 6's 160 MHz channels. Doubles theoretical peak throughput.
* **4096-QAM** : 12 bits per symbol, up from 1024-QAM's 10 bits. About 20% throughput improvement at close range.
* **Multi-Link Operation (MLO)** : a device can use two or more bands simultaneously (e.g., 5 GHz and 6 GHz at the same time), aggregating their bandwidth or using them for redundancy. This is the headline feature.
* **Restricted TWT** : tighter scheduling than Wi-Fi 6 TWT, allowing latency-sensitive devices (VR headsets, gaming consoles) to reserve specific time slots.

Theoretical peak per-stream throughput in Wi-Fi 7: roughly 5.8 Gbps on a single 320 MHz channel. Real-world throughput is typically 30 to 60 percent of theoretical, and even that drops sharply with distance, interference, and the number of contending stations.

#### 4.2.4 Wi-Fi Versus Cellular for Modern Mobile

The line between Wi-Fi and cellular has blurred. Modern smartphones seamlessly hand off between Wi-Fi and 5G; applications often do not know which is in use. But the performance and reliability differ:

* _Wi-Fi_ : limited range (10 to 50 meters typically), unlicensed spectrum (subject to interference from neighbors), higher peak throughput, lower latency in good conditions, free to operate.
* _5G_ : licensed spectrum (no interference, much more reliable), wider range (kilometers per tower), lower peak throughput but more consistent, requires carrier subscription.

For most users in most situations, Wi-Fi is the home/office choice and 5G is the on-the-go choice. Modern protocols (HTTP/3 with QUIC connection migration, Multipath TCP, certain VPN protocols) are designed to handle the transition between them without dropping connections, which we will see in Chapters 10, 15, and 19.

### 4.3 The DPU Revolution

A DPU (Data Processing Unit) is a programmable computer attached to a network interface, with its own CPUs (typically ARM cores), its own memory (typically 16 to 64 GB of DDR4 or DDR5), its own storage, and its own operating system (typically a stripped-down Linux). It plugs into a server's PCIe slot like a regular NIC would, but it is not a regular NIC. It is a parallel computer that the server's main CPU can offload network and storage work to.

The DPU concept is not new; SmartNICs have existed for years. What is new in 2026 is the convergence: the major hyperscalers (AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta) and the merchant DPU vendors (NVIDIA BlueField, AMD Pensando, Marvell Octeon, Intel IPU) have all settled on a similar architecture and a similar usage pattern. DPUs are mainstream in 2026 in a way they were not in 2020.

#### 4.3.1 What a DPU Does

A modern DPU typically handles, in hardware or in its own ARM cores:

* **Network virtualization** : VXLAN encapsulation/decapsulation, GENEVE tunneling, the entire data plane of a software-defined network. Inside an AWS or Azure data center, every server has a DPU (in AWS, it is called Nitro) that implements the VPC abstraction by encapsulating customer traffic into tunnels that traverse the underlying physical network.
* **TLS termination** : handshaking, key derivation, and bulk encryption can run on dedicated crypto cores in the DPU, freeing the host CPU.
* **Storage offload** : NVMe-over-Fabrics, where remote storage appears as a local NVMe drive but is actually accessed over RDMA across the network. The DPU implements the NVMe-oF target side.
* **Firewall and security** : stateful packet inspection, connection tracking, DDoS mitigation. The DPU can drop attack traffic at line rate without burdening the host CPU.
* **Service mesh data plane** : in some architectures, the Envoy or Cilium proxy that traditionally runs as a sidecar container can be offloaded to the DPU.
* **Telemetry** : the DPU can sample packets, build flow records, generate eBPF-style metrics, and push them to a collector, all without the host CPU touching individual packets.
* **Cryptographic operations** : TLS, IPsec, MACsec, and various proprietary VPN protocols can all run on dedicated crypto engines.

The host CPU sees a simpler interface: it submits application-level requests (read this block from storage, send this stream of bytes to that endpoint) and the DPU translates those into wire-level operations. The host CPU does not see individual packets at line rate.

#### 4.3.2 Three Modern DPUs

_NVIDIA BlueField-3_ : announced in 2022, shipping in volume by 2023. 16 ARM Cortex-A78 cores, up to 32 GB DDR5, two 400 Gbps Ethernet ports, dedicated crypto engines, and an accelerator for cryptographic offload. Targeted at hyperscaler and enterprise data centers. Runs DOCA (NVIDIA's DPU software framework) on top of Ubuntu.

_AMD Pensando DSC_ : AMD acquired Pensando in 2022. The DSC line has 16 ARM cores, programmable P4 data plane, and 200/400 Gbps networking. Heavily used by Oracle Cloud and others.

_AWS Nitro_ : AWS's internal DPU, not sold externally. Every AWS EC2 instance from late 2017 onward has a Nitro card handling the network, storage, and security plane. Nitro is the architectural foundation of EC2's scaling: by moving the hypervisor's network and storage logic into a separate hardware-isolated card, AWS could provide bare-metal instances (just the CPU and DRAM exposed to the customer) and could replace the hypervisor with a much smaller one running on the main CPU. This is widely credited with enabling AWS to pull ahead of Azure and GCP in raw instance performance during the late 2010s.

#### 4.3.3 The Kernel-Bypass Story

DPUs are one expression of a broader trend: moving network processing out of the kernel and onto specialized hardware (or onto carefully-optimized user-space frameworks). The trend has three main embodiments:

_DPDK (Data Plane Development Kit)_ : a user-space packet I/O framework originally started at Intel and now governed under the Linux Foundation (since 2017). Applications using DPDK take ownership of a NIC entirely, bypassing the kernel network stack, and process packets in user space with hand-tuned code. Achieves 10x or more throughput improvements over kernel networking. Standard in NFV (Network Function Virtualization) deployments.

_AF_XDP_ : a Linux kernel feature that exposes a fast-path socket interface to user space, where packets can be received and transmitted with minimal kernel processing. Half the benefit of full DPDK without quite the complexity. Increasingly used in cloud-native networking.

_RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access)_ : a wholly different approach where one machine's NIC writes directly into another machine's memory across the network, with no CPU involvement on either side. Originally InfiniBand only; now also available over Ethernet (RoCE, RoCE v2). Used heavily in HPC clusters, machine learning training clusters (where it is essential for parameter synchronization), and high-frequency trading.

_DPUs_ : the most extreme version, moving entire subsystems (network, storage, security, telemetry) onto dedicated hardware adjacent to but separate from the main CPU.

The cumulative effect: in 2026, a high-performance server's "network stack" is split across the host CPU's user space, the host CPU's kernel, the DPU's ARM cores, the DPU's hardware accelerators, and the NIC's data plane. The traditional 7-layer model still applies to the _protocols_ , but the _implementation_ of each layer can live in many different physical places.

#### 4.3.4 Wire-Level Artifact: An Ethernet Frame with DPU Offload Path

Let us trace a single Ethernet frame on a DPU-equipped server, annotating where each layer's processing happens.
    
    
    +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
    | Frame field               | Processed by                      |
    +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
    | Preamble + SFD            | NIC ASIC (DPU's network port)     |
    | Destination MAC           | NIC ASIC (filter; forward to DPU) |
    | Source MAC                | NIC ASIC                          |
    | VLAN tag (if present)     | DPU P4 data plane                 |
    | EtherType (0x0800 IPv4)   | DPU P4 data plane                 |
    | IP header                 | DPU P4 data plane                 |
    | - VXLAN decap, if tunnel  | DPU hardware accelerator          |
    | - Connection tracking     | DPU's flow table (HW + ARM cores) |
    | TCP header                | DPU (offload) or kernel (fallback)|
    | TLS record header         | DPU crypto engine                 |
    | Application payload       | Host CPU (after decryption)       |
    +---------------------------+-----------------------------------+
    

The host CPU's network stack never sees the Ethernet, IP, or even TCP headers in this typical case. The host sees a stream of plaintext bytes arriving on a socket; the DPU handled everything below. This is the offload model.

When something goes wrong, you have to debug across both worlds. The DPU is a Linux box you can SSH into; you can run `tcpdump` on its network ports, look at its kernel logs, examine its eBPF programs. The host CPU is the other Linux box; you can do the same there. The challenge is correlating events between them, which is its own observability discipline.

### 4.4 What Wi-Fi Brings to the DPU Story

DPUs are mostly a data-center phenomenon. But the data-link-layer-in-silicon trend extends to consumer-side devices too. A modern Wi-Fi 7 router has dedicated radio silicon for the new modulation schemes, dedicated hardware for OFDMA scheduling, sometimes dedicated security processors for WPA3 cryptography. The "router" is no longer a single CPU running Linux on top of a passive radio; it is a small SoC with multiple specialized accelerators, where the radio data plane runs largely independently of the CPU.

This matters when you reason about home network performance. The throughput you observe on a Wi-Fi 7 router is not bottlenecked by the CPU; it is bottlenecked by the radio, the medium, and the contention with neighbors. The CPU is, increasingly, just the configuration interface.

### 4.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Why has the per-interface speed of Ethernet climbed from 1 Gbps in 1999 to 800 Gbps in 2024, while the per-optical-lane speed has only climbed about 100x in the same period? What architectural choice closed the gap?

Hint

Look at the lane count of modern transceivers.

**Answer:** Per-lane speed climbed slower because of physical limits: as you push more bits per second through a single optical lane, you hit limits on laser modulation speed, signal integrity, and dispersion. Past about 100 Gbps per lane (using PAM-4 modulation), you cannot easily push more bits down a single optical channel. The architectural choice that closed the gap is parallelization: 800GBASE-DR8 is eight parallel 100 Gbps optical lanes in one transceiver, multiplexed onto eight fiber strands or onto eight wavelengths in one strand. The transceiver presents one logical 800 Gbps interface to the host but is internally eight parallel lanes. This is the same idea as PCIe Gen 5 x16 (16 parallel lanes inside the PCIe slot) or DDR5 with its multi-channel architecture: when serial speeds are physics-limited, go parallel.

**Q2.** Distinguish OFDMA from MU-MIMO. Both are Wi-Fi 6 features that improve dense-deployment performance, but they work differently.

Hint

OFDMA divides the channel in frequency; MU-MIMO divides it in spatial streams.

**Answer:** OFDMA (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiple Access) divides a single channel's frequency space into smaller resource units called subcarriers, and assigns subsets of these subcarriers to different devices simultaneously. So if you have 20 MHz of channel bandwidth, OFDMA can split it into many 2-MHz allocations, each going to a different device at the same time. The total throughput is the same, but the channel is divided in frequency. MU-MIMO (Multi-User Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) uses spatially separated antenna patterns to transmit to (or receive from) multiple devices simultaneously on the _same_ frequency. The AP transmits a beam-formed signal to device A and a different beam-formed signal to device B at the same time, on the same channel; each device receives mostly its own signal because the beams are spatially distinct. OFDMA is best for many devices with small payloads (IoT sensors, IM-style traffic) because it efficiently shares the channel without contention. MU-MIMO is best for few devices with larger payloads (a 4K video stream to one device while another large file uploads from a second device) because it lets the full per-stream throughput go to each. Wi-Fi 6 combines both.

**Q3.** Name three classes of work that a DPU offloads from the host CPU. For each, explain what the host CPU would otherwise have to do.

Hint

Network virtualization, cryptographic operations, and storage are all common offload targets.

**Answer:** (1) _Network virtualization (VXLAN, GENEVE)_ : the DPU encapsulates outgoing packets into virtual-network tunnels and decapsulates incoming packets back to their original form. Without offload, the host CPU's network stack would parse the tunnel headers on every packet, copy data through extra buffers, and consume CPU cycles per packet that scale linearly with packet rate; on a 400 Gbps link at small packet sizes, this can consume 4 to 8 CPU cores. (2) _TLS termination_ : the DPU performs the TLS handshake and bulk symmetric encryption/decryption of TLS records. Without offload, the host CPU's kernel TLS or user-space TLS library handles all the cryptographic operations, using AES-NI hardware extensions but still consuming significant cycles, especially at higher cipher strengths and connection rates. (3) _NVMe-over-Fabrics storage_ : the DPU exposes remote storage as a local NVMe device, handling RDMA-based transport to the storage server. Without offload, the host CPU would manage the RDMA queues, handle storage protocol state, and deal with re-transmission and failover, again consuming cores per gigabit of storage throughput. (4) _Stateful firewall and connection tracking_ : the DPU maintains flow state for millions of concurrent connections and applies firewall rules per-packet. Without offload, the host's kernel `nftables` or `conntrack` does this in software, with significant per-packet overhead at scale.

**Q4.** Why does kernel networking become inadequate at 400 Gbps, and what are three alternative approaches?

Hint

At 400 Gbps with small packets, packet arrival rate is in the hundreds of millions per second.

**Answer:** At 400 Gbps with 64-byte packets (the worst case for packet rate), the arrival rate is around 600 million packets per second. A modern x86 CPU can execute roughly 1 to 3 billion instructions per second per core. Allowing only a few hundred instructions per packet (which is what kernel networking takes for a full RX-to-deliver path) means a single core can handle maybe 5 to 10 million packets per second of kernel networking. To process 600 million packets per second through the kernel would require 60 to 120 cores, which is far beyond what is reasonable to dedicate to packet processing on a typical server. Three alternative approaches: (1) _DPDK_ : bypass the kernel entirely; have a user-space application take ownership of the NIC; use polling rather than interrupts; eliminate context switches and copies. Achieves 100x or more performance over the kernel. (2) _AF_XDP_ : use the kernel's XDP fast path to deliver packets directly to a user-space socket via shared memory, with minimal kernel processing. Roughly half the benefit of full DPDK with much less complexity. (3) _DPU offload_ : move the packet processing entirely to a separate piece of silicon (the DPU). The host CPU sees only the application-level data, not individual packets. The DPU itself uses some combination of hardware acceleration and its own ARM cores running optimized data-plane code.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A data center is upgrading from 100 Gbps Ethernet (QSFP28) to 400 Gbps Ethernet (QSFP-DD). List the components that need to change, and identify what backwards compatibility considerations apply.

Hint

Switch ports, transceivers, cables, NICs all matter. The physical form factor differs.

**Answer:** Components that need to change: _Switches_ : the top-of-rack and spine switches must have QSFP-DD ports (or OSFP), which physically accept the larger transceiver. Existing 100 Gbps switches with QSFP28 cannot accept QSFP-DD; full replacement is needed. _Transceivers_ : 400 Gbps transceivers (400GBASE-SR4 for short-range multi-mode fiber, 400GBASE-DR4 for medium-range single-mode, etc.) are required at each end. _Cables_ : QSFP28 100 Gbps used four 25 Gbps lanes on multi-mode fiber; QSFP-DD 400 Gbps uses eight 50 Gbps lanes. The fiber infrastructure may need to be upgraded if the existing cabling does not support enough parallel lanes or if the modal bandwidth is insufficient. _NICs_ : the server-side NICs (or DPUs) must be 400 Gbps capable, with QSFP-DD ports and the necessary PCIe Gen 5 bandwidth (a single PCIe Gen 5 x16 slot can deliver about 63 GB/s after 128b/130b encoding, or roughly 500 Gbps, just enough headroom for a 400 Gbps NIC). Backwards compatibility: QSFP-DD ports are mechanically backward-compatible with QSFP28 modules (you can plug an older 100 Gbps transceiver into a QSFP-DD port and the port will negotiate down), but not the other way around. Mixed-speed networks are common during transition periods, with the switch auto-negotiating per port. The breakdown is purely physical; no application changes are needed because the upper layers see only "an Ethernet link with X Gbps" and adapt. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM about 400G migration; watch for Lie #4 (outdated configuration suggestions referencing older 40G or 100G standards as if they were current) and a related risk of suggesting QSFP+ (40G) instead of QSFP28 (100G) when discussing the previous generation.

**Q2.** A startup is deciding between using a standard NIC with kernel networking, a DPDK-based user-space stack on a standard NIC, or a DPU for their high-frequency-trading market data feed. The feed runs at 25 Gbps with 100-byte packets. Walk through the analysis.

Hint

Compute packet rate. Estimate CPU cores per million packets per second for each option.

**Answer:** Packet rate at 25 Gbps with 100-byte packets: roughly 30 million packets per second (Mpps). Standard kernel networking handles maybe 5 to 10 Mpps per core, so we would need 3 to 6 cores dedicated to RX, plus more for the application logic. Total: 5 to 8 cores. Latency per packet is dominated by the kernel path: typically 5 to 20 microseconds, with significant jitter due to interrupt timing and context switching. For HFT, this latency is unacceptable. DPDK with user-space polling: handles 30 to 50 Mpps on a single core, so a single core can handle the entire packet stream. Latency drops to 1 to 5 microseconds with much lower jitter because the application polls the NIC directly without interrupts or context switches. The application code must be DPDK-aware (using DPDK's APIs for packet allocation, free, and processing), which is a development cost. DPU: the DPU handles all packet ingress, runs filtering and parsing logic on the DPU itself, and delivers parsed market data updates to the host as application-level messages. Host CPU never sees individual packets. Latency depends on the DPU's pipeline; modern DPUs can match DPDK's latency for hot-path operations but at higher hardware cost. Recommendation for HFT: DPDK is the standard answer because the latency profile is tightly controlled, the development model is well-understood, and the cost is just CPU cores plus development time. DPUs are appealing if the firm wants to centralize filtering logic across many feeds, but the DPU's added complexity (separate OS to manage, separate observability) often is not worth it for a single feed.
