## Chapter 6: Intra-domain Routing: OSPF and IS-IS at Literacy

In the previous chapter we put addresses on packets. Now we ask: given that a packet has a destination IP address, how does each router on the path decide which interface to forward it out of?

The answer is _routing_. A router consults its routing table, which is built by routing protocols that exchange reachability information between routers. There are two broad classes of routing protocol: _intra-domain_ (within a single autonomous system, run by one administrative entity) and _inter-domain_ (between autonomous systems, run cooperatively across organizational boundaries). This chapter covers intra-domain; Chapter 7 covers inter-domain (BGP).

The two dominant intra-domain protocols are OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) and IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System). Both are link-state protocols; both compute shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm; both have nearly identical capabilities; both have entrenched user bases that have little reason to switch. We will see both, contrast them, and develop the underlying conceptual machinery (link state, area design, ECMP, convergence) that applies regardless of which protocol is in use.

The chapter's level is "literacy": enough to understand what a network engineer is doing when they say "I am bringing up an OSPF adjacency on this link," not enough to design a global IS-IS deployment from scratch. We are setting up the BGP story in Chapter 7; intra-domain routing is the foundation BGP rides on.

### 6.1 Why Routing Protocols Exist

A router has multiple interfaces. Each interface is connected to a different network. When a packet arrives, the router needs a rule that says "for packets destined to network X, forward out interface Y."

The rules are stored in a _routing table_ (also called a _Forwarding Information Base_ , FIB, when stored in hardware data structures optimized for fast lookup). Routes can be installed by:

  1. **Direct attachment** : the router knows that any address in network X is directly reachable on interface Y because Y is configured with an address in X.
  2. **Static configuration** : an administrator manually writes "for network X, send to next-hop Z out of interface Y." Useful for simple networks, brittle for complex ones.
  3. **Dynamic routing protocols** : routers exchange information about which networks they know about and through which interfaces. The protocols compute optimal paths, install routes automatically, and react to topology changes.

For any network beyond a few routers, dynamic routing is essential. Routing protocols exchange information continuously, react to link failures within seconds, and produce consistent forwarding decisions across all routers in the network.

#### 6.1.1 Two Families: Distance-Vector vs Link-State

Routing protocols come in two algorithmic families.

_Distance-Vector_ : each router tells its neighbors "I can reach network X at distance D." The neighbors don't know what the topology looks like; they only know their neighbors' claims. Each router picks the best (shortest) claim it has heard and uses that path. Old examples: RIP (Routing Information Protocol). Modern relevance: BGP is technically a distance-vector protocol with extra attributes.

_Link-State_ : each router floods a complete description of its own links to every other router in the network. Every router thus learns the complete topology. Each router then runs Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm on the full graph to compute the path from itself to every destination. OSPF and IS-IS are link-state protocols.

The trade: distance-vector is simpler (less state per router) but slower to converge and prone to routing loops. Link-state is more complex (every router has full topology) but converges fast and has no loops (because shortest-path is well-defined on a connected graph).

For intra-domain routing, link-state has won. Modern enterprise networks and ISPs run OSPF or IS-IS. For inter-domain (BGP), distance-vector-with-policy is essential because the topology is too large for any one entity to know completely, and policy matters more than physics.

#### Definition: Routing Table

A data structure maintained by a router, mapping destination network prefixes to next-hop information (outgoing interface, next-hop IP address, metric). Built by routing protocols and manual configuration; consulted on every packet to decide forwarding.

In plain language, this means: "if the packet is for network X, send it to interface Y toward host Z." For every prefix the router knows about, it has one or more such entries; the router picks the one with the longest matching prefix (most specific) for each packet.

#### Definition: Link-State Protocol

A routing protocol in which every router floods a description of its directly attached links to every other router in the routing domain. Each router uses the received descriptions to build a complete topology graph and then computes shortest paths using Dijkstra's algorithm.

In plain language, this means: every router learns the whole map, then everyone independently computes the best paths. Because all routers see the same map and use the same algorithm, they all reach the same forwarding decisions.

### 6.2 OSPF (Open Shortest Path First)

OSPF is the IETF-standardized link-state protocol. It is widely deployed in enterprise networks and within smaller-to-medium ISPs. Two versions matter:

* **OSPFv2** : IPv4 only. Runs directly on IP (protocol number 89). RFC 2328 (1998).
* **OSPFv3** : IPv6 (and can also carry IPv4 with a slight extension). Runs over IPv6. RFC 5340.

The big similarity: both versions use the same algorithm. The big differences are in addressing and in how addresses are advertised. We will focus on OSPFv2 for concreteness; OSPFv3 differs in details that matter operationally but not conceptually.

#### 6.2.1 The OSPF Packet Types

OSPF uses five packet types:

  1. **Hello** : sent periodically (every 10 seconds by default) to discover and maintain neighbor relationships.
  2. **Database Description (DBD)** : sent during adjacency formation to exchange link-state database information.
  3. **Link-State Request (LSR)** : sent to ask a neighbor for the full content of specific LSAs (link-state advertisements) we know we are missing.
  4. **Link-State Update (LSU)** : contains one or more LSAs, sent in response to LSR or proactively when topology changes.
  5. **Link-State Acknowledgement (LSAck)** : acknowledges receipt of LSAs to ensure reliable flooding.

#### 6.2.2 The LSA Types

OSPF defines several LSA types; the important ones for literacy:

* **Type 1 (Router LSA)** : produced by every router, describes that router's links and their costs.
* **Type 2 (Network LSA)** : produced by the _Designated Router_ on a multi-access network, describes the set of routers attached to that network.
* **Type 3 (Summary LSA)** : produced by area border routers, summarizes routes from one area into another.
* **Type 4 (ASBR Summary LSA)** : produced by area border routers, tells routers in other areas how to reach an ASBR. Pairs with Type 5: a router in Area 1 needs Type 4 to find the ASBR before it can use the Type 5's next-hop information.
* **Type 5 (External LSA)** : produced by _Autonomous System Boundary Routers_ (ASBRs), describes routes learned from outside OSPF (typically from BGP or static).

#### 6.2.3 OSPF Areas

OSPF supports a hierarchical structure: the routing domain is divided into _areas_ , with all areas connecting to a special _backbone area_ (Area 0).

Why areas? Because flooding LSAs to every router in a large network is expensive: a 1000-router network with every router flooding its LSAs to every other router produces a lot of LSA traffic and a lot of Dijkstra computation. Areas localize the flooding: LSAs within an area are flooded only within that area. Inter-area routes are summarized at area borders, so each router only sees full topology details for its own area, plus summary routes for other areas.

The rules:

* Every area connects to Area 0 (the backbone). Inter-area routing always goes through Area 0.
* Area Border Routers (ABRs) live in two or more areas, including Area 0.
* LSAs flooded within a non-backbone area are not flooded into Area 0 directly; they are summarized into Type 3 LSAs by the ABR.

This is similar in spirit to how the internet aggregates routes via CIDR: at each abstraction boundary, detailed information is summarized to keep the state manageable.

A typical enterprise OSPF design: one Area 0 connecting major sites; per-site areas (Area 1, 2, 3, ...) for local routing; ABRs at each site boundary connecting their local area to the backbone.

#### 6.2.4 Metric: Cost

OSPF assigns a _cost_ to each link, typically computed as `reference_bandwidth / link_bandwidth` where `reference_bandwidth` is 100 Mbps in the original spec (and modernly often configured as 100 Gbps or higher to allow distinction among very fast links). Lower cost is preferred.

The shortest path is computed as the sum of link costs along the path, in the standard Dijkstra sense.

#### 6.2.5 Adjacency States

Two OSPF neighbors progress through a series of states as they form an adjacency:

  1. **Down** : no Hellos received yet.
  2. **Init** : Hello received from neighbor, but neighbor has not yet acknowledged our Hello.
  3. **2-Way** : bidirectional Hello exchange; both routers acknowledge each other.
  4. **ExStart** : beginning of database exchange.
  5. **Exchange** : exchanging Database Description packets.
  6. **Loading** : requesting and receiving LSAs to fill gaps.
  7. **Full** : adjacency fully established; both routers have synchronized LSDB.

The state machine is one of the most diagnosed things in OSPF operations. When something is wrong, the state stuck at 2-Way or ExStart or Exchange tells you precisely where to look.

#### 6.2.6 An OSPF Link-State Advertisement on the Wire

The Router LSA (Type 1) carries the meat of OSPF's link-state information. Its format includes:

* Router ID (the originating router's identifier).
* Number of links described.
* For each link: link ID, link type (point-to-point, transit, stub, virtual), metric, link data.

A small example: a router with two links to neighbors and one stub network.
    
    
    LSA Header:
      LS Age: 200
      Options: 0x22
      LS Type: 1 (Router LSA)
      Link State ID: 10.0.0.1 (this router's ID)
      Advertising Router: 10.0.0.1
      LS Sequence Number: 0x80000005
      LS Checksum: 0xa5b3
      Length: 60
    
    Router LSA:
      Flags: 0x00
      Number of Links: 3
    
      Link 1:
        Link ID: 10.0.0.2 (neighbor router ID)
        Link Data: 10.0.1.1 (my IP on this link)
        Type: 1 (point-to-point)
        Metric: 10
    
      Link 2:
        Link ID: 10.0.0.3
        Link Data: 10.0.2.1
        Type: 1
        Metric: 15
    
      Link 3:
        Link ID: 10.0.3.0 (network address)
        Link Data: 255.255.255.0 (subnet mask)
        Type: 3 (stub)
        Metric: 5
    

Reading this LSA: router `10.0.0.1` describes itself as having two point-to-point links to neighbors `10.0.0.2` (metric 10) and `10.0.0.3` (metric 15), and one stub network `10.0.3.0/24` (metric 5). When every router in the area floods its Router LSA, every router can assemble the full topology.

### 6.3 IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System)

IS-IS is the alternative link-state protocol. It originated in the 1980s as part of the OSI protocol stack (where "Intermediate System" was OSI-speak for "router") and was later adapted for IP routing.

The key differences from OSPF:

  1. **Runs directly on the data link layer** , not on IP. IS-IS packets are encapsulated in Ethernet (or other L2) frames with a specific protocol identifier; they do not have IP headers. This makes IS-IS protocol-agnostic: the same IS-IS process can carry routes for both IPv4 and IPv6 in a single instance.

  2. **Two levels** instead of areas: L1 (intra-area) and L2 (backbone). L1 routers communicate within their area; L2 routers communicate across areas; L1/L2 routers do both. The L1/L2 distinction is similar to OSPF's area-0 backbone, but with two-level routing rather than full hierarchy.

  3. **Different metric semantics** : IS-IS originally had a small metric range (0 to 63); the modern "wide metrics" extension uses 24-bit or 32-bit costs.

  4. **Different naming** : IS-IS uses NSAP-style addresses for router identifiers, which look strange to people only familiar with IP.

Despite these differences, IS-IS does the same thing OSPF does: each router floods a description of its links, every router runs Dijkstra, every router has a consistent forwarding decision.

#### 6.3.1 Why ISPs Use IS-IS

Large ISPs (especially Tier 1s) tend to use IS-IS for several reasons:

* **Protocol independence** : a single IS-IS process can carry IPv4 and IPv6 routes in parallel, simplifying multi-protocol deployments. OSPF requires two separate instances (v2 and v3).
* **Faster timers** : IS-IS uses Hello intervals of 3 to 10 seconds and LSP refresh of 15 minutes by default, faster than OSPF's typical 10-second Hellos and 30-minute LSA refresh, though both can be tuned.
* **No "magical packet type 5"** or other complexity: IS-IS's LSPs are uniform in type; you flood your LSP and that is it. OSPF has multiple LSA types with subtly different flooding rules.
* **History** : many ISP backbones were built when the IS-IS-vs-OSPF debate was active, and the protocols carry forward.

#### 6.3.2 Why Enterprises Use OSPF

Enterprises tend to use OSPF for:

* **Better tooling** : every routing-vendor's enterprise management GUI is OSPF-aware; IS-IS is more niche and less consumer-friendly.
* **Vendor support** : OSPF is universally supported; some vendors implement only OSPF for entry-level enterprise products.
* **Documentation** : more tutorial material, more StackOverflow answers, more familiar concepts for engineers trained on OSPF.

The split is mostly historical: both protocols work; both can scale; both have similar feature sets. Picking one is a matter of organizational preference and existing skill base.

### 6.4 ECMP and Why It Matters

So far we have implied that the routing protocol computes "the" shortest path to each destination. In practice, networks often have multiple paths of equal cost; the routing protocol should use all of them.

_Equal-Cost Multi-Path_ (ECMP) is the discipline of installing multiple equal-cost routes and distributing traffic across them. The forwarding decision is per-flow (so packets of one TCP connection stay on the same path, preserving order at the receiver) or per-packet (which can reorder, generally avoided unless the receiver is tolerant).

The per-flow load balancing is typically done by hashing some combination of fields from the packet (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol; sometimes called the "5-tuple") to pick a path. Same 5-tuple always picks the same path, so the same TCP connection stays on the same physical path through the network. Different connections may go on different paths.

#### 6.4.1 ECMP in Modern Data Centers

In modern data center fabrics (especially leaf-spine and Clos topologies), ECMP is the dominant load-balancing mechanism. A single 400 Gbps server might connect to multiple top-of-rack switches; each top-of-rack switch connects to multiple spine switches; the spine layer has many parallel paths. ECMP lets the network use all of them.

A typical 2026 hyperscale Clos fabric might have 16 to 64 spine switches and 32 to 128 leaves, with one link from each leaf to each spine. From any given leaf, that yields 16-64 equal-cost paths up to the spine; ECMP across this fabric provides aggregate bandwidth far beyond any single path.

#### 6.4.2 The Failure Modes of ECMP

ECMP is elegant when the paths are equal-cost and well-behaved. Failure modes:

* **Hash polarization** : if every router in the path hashes the same way, the same flows get pushed to the same paths at every layer, leading to uneven utilization. The fix is "hash randomization" at each layer: each router uses a slightly different hash function.

* **Asymmetric paths under ECMP** : the forward and reverse paths may take different physical routes, even though both are equal-cost. This is fine for most traffic but breaks tools that assume symmetry (some passive measurement tools, some firewalls).

* **Mid-flow reordering** : if a topology change causes ECMP to remap a flow to a different path, packets in flight on the old path may arrive after packets on the new path, causing reordering. TCP and QUIC can recover from this but not for free.

* **Flowlet-based ECMP** : some modern fabrics break flows into "flowlets" (consecutive packets with no inter-packet gaps) and rebalance per-flowlet, allowing finer granularity. Microsoft has published on flowlet-based ECMP in their Azure fabric.

### 6.5 Convergence and Why It Matters

When the topology changes (a link goes down, a router reboots, a new prefix is added), the routing protocol must propagate the change so all routers update their forwarding decisions. The time to do this is _convergence time_.

Slow convergence means traffic blackholes: packets are forwarded to a route that no longer exists, get dropped, and the sender thinks the destination is unreachable for the duration of the convergence window.

OSPF and IS-IS can typically converge in 1 to 5 seconds for a single-link failure with default timers. With tuned timers (sub-second Hellos, fast SPF computation), convergence can be reduced to 200 to 500 milliseconds. Modern ISPs run with tuned timers for fast convergence.

Even faster mechanisms exist:

* **Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)** : a separate lightweight protocol that detects link failures within 50 to 100 milliseconds and triggers the routing protocol to re-converge immediately. Standard in modern ISP backbones.
* **IP Fast Reroute (FRR) / Loop-Free Alternates (LFA)** : precompute backup paths at the routing layer so a failure causes an immediate failover to a precomputed alternative, without waiting for full re-convergence. Some ISPs achieve 50 millisecond failover.
* **Segment Routing** : a newer paradigm that encodes paths into the packet header itself, enabling rapid traffic-engineering-driven failover. We will not go deep into segment routing in this book, but it is increasingly deployed in large ISP backbones.

#### Common Misconception: OSPF or IS-IS Is the Right Tool for Inter-AS Routing

OSPF and IS-IS scale to thousands of routers within an AS. They do not scale to the entire internet (millions of routers across hundreds of thousands of ASes), nor do they handle the _policy_ dimension that inter-AS routing requires (transit vs. peering, business relationships, route filtering for security). For inter-AS routing, BGP is the only practical choice. We will see why in Chapter 7.

### 6.6 The Wire-Level Artifact: An OSPF LSA Captured

A typical OSPF lab setup: two routers (R1 and R2) connected on a point-to-point link, each with a loopback interface in some subnet, OSPF Area 0 configured on the link and on the loopbacks.

After OSPF converges, `tcpdump -i eth1 ip proto 89` on either router captures OSPF packets:
    
    
    14:00:00.000123 IP 10.0.1.1 > 224.0.0.5: OSPFv2, Hello, length 48
    14:00:10.000456 IP 10.0.1.1 > 224.0.0.5: OSPFv2, Hello, length 48
    14:00:15.123789 IP 10.0.1.1 > 224.0.0.5: OSPFv2, LS-Update, length 96
    14:00:15.124023 IP 10.0.1.2 > 224.0.0.5: OSPFv2, LS-Ack, length 64
    

The Hello packets are sent every 10 seconds. The LS-Update was triggered by a topology change (perhaps R1's loopback came back up). The LS-Ack acknowledges receipt.

With more verbose flags (`-v` or `-vvv`), tcpdump decodes the LSA contents inside the LS-Update, showing the same kind of structure we sketched earlier: router ID, link descriptions, metrics.

Reading these captures is the first hands-on activity in operating OSPF. Every network engineer learning OSPF should spend an afternoon watching adjacency formation on a lab; the state transitions (Down → Init → 2-Way → ExStart → Exchange → Loading → Full) become tangible.

### 6.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Distinguish link-state from distance-vector routing protocols. Give one concrete consequence of each design choice.

Hint

What does each router know about the network?

**Answer:** _Link-state protocols_ (OSPF, IS-IS) work by having each router flood a description of its own links to every other router in the routing domain; each router then assembles the full topology and runs Dijkstra's algorithm independently. Every router has identical knowledge of the network. _Distance-vector protocols_ (RIP historically, BGP today) work by having each router tell its neighbors "I can reach destination X at distance D"; each router knows only what its neighbors claim, not the underlying topology. Consequences: link-state converges quickly because every router can compute the new shortest path as soon as the link-state database updates, and link-state is loop-free because Dijkstra produces a tree. Distance-vector can suffer from routing loops if a topology change is propagated inconsistently (the famous "count-to-infinity" problem of old RIP), and convergence can be slower because each router has to wait for its neighbors to update before it can compute its own routes. Link-state's cost is per-router CPU and memory (full topology graph); distance-vector's cost is propagation delay and loop risk. For intra-domain routing, the link-state trade is the right one. For inter-domain (BGP), the topology is too large for any one router to hold completely, and policy considerations matter more than physics, so the distance-vector-with-policy approach is preferred.

**Q2.** What is an OSPF area, and why does OSPF support areas?

Hint

Why would you not want every router in a large network to receive every LSA from every other router?

**Answer:** An OSPF area is a logical subdivision of the routing domain. All routers in an area maintain a synchronized link-state database for that area only; they do not see the link-state databases of other areas. Area Border Routers (ABRs) summarize routes from their areas into a special backbone area (Area 0), and the backbone area connects all the others. OSPF supports areas because flooding LSAs across a large network is expensive: a 1000-router network with every router flooding to every other router would produce a million LSA flooding events per topology change, and every router would need to store the full database. Areas localize the flooding to within an area, reducing LSA volume and database size. Inter-area routing is then handled by ABRs summarizing routes between areas; routers in non-backbone areas see summaries rather than detailed topology of other areas. The cost is loss of fine-grained traffic engineering across areas (the ABR's summary may not reveal which specific path through the area is best); the benefit is the protocol scales to thousands of routers. Most enterprise OSPF deployments have a single area for small networks and a hierarchy of areas for large ones.

**Q3.** What is ECMP, and why is hash-based per-flow ECMP preferred over per-packet round-robin?

Hint

What property of TCP would per-packet round-robin disturb?

**Answer:** ECMP (Equal-Cost Multi-Path) is the discipline of installing multiple equal-cost routes to the same destination and distributing traffic across them. _Per-flow_ ECMP hashes a tuple of packet fields (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol) to select a path, so packets of the same flow (same TCP/UDP connection) always take the same path. _Per-packet_ round-robin distributes consecutive packets across paths regardless of which flow they belong to. Per-flow is preferred because it preserves packet order within a flow. TCP and most other transport protocols assume packets in a flow arrive in roughly order; out-of-order delivery triggers TCP's fast-retransmit machinery and degrades throughput. Per-packet round-robin can deliver packets of a single TCP connection over different paths with different latencies, causing reordering. Modern variants (flowlet-based ECMP) split flows at natural gap boundaries to enable finer load balancing without disturbing TCP ordering within each flowlet. The choice of hashing function matters; using only the 3-tuple (source IP, destination IP, protocol) gives less granularity (large flows would map to the same hash bucket) than the 5-tuple, but the 5-tuple is the standard in modern routers and switches.

**Q4.** Explain "convergence time" in a routing protocol and name two mechanisms used in modern networks to reduce it.

Hint

Failure detection plus precomputed backup paths.

**Answer:** Convergence time is the duration between a topology change (link failure, router reboot, new prefix advertised) and the moment all routers in the network have updated their forwarding tables to reflect the change. During this period, traffic may be black-holed (dropped at a router that still thinks the old route is good) or loop (if different routers disagree about the new best path). With default timers, OSPF and IS-IS converge in 1 to 5 seconds for a single-link failure; with tuned timers, this can drop to 200 to 500 milliseconds. Modern networks use additional mechanisms to reduce convergence: (1) _Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD)_ : a lightweight protocol that detects link failures within 50 to 100 milliseconds by exchanging heartbeats between routers; faster than waiting for the routing protocol's own Hello timer to expire. (2) _IP Fast Reroute (FRR) / Loop-Free Alternates (LFA)_ : precompute backup paths during normal operation; on link failure, immediately switch to the precomputed backup without waiting for full re-convergence. Some ISPs achieve 50 millisecond failover this way. (3) _Segment Routing_ : encodes paths into packet headers, enabling immediate traffic-engineering-driven failover. (4) _Modern OSPF/IS-IS tuning_ : sub-second Hello timers and faster SPF computation. The cumulative effect: in a well-tuned modern ISP backbone, single-link failures cause sub-second user-visible service disruption; multi-failure scenarios (rare but possible) may still cause longer disruption.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** An enterprise has 50 routers in 5 sites. Design an OSPF area structure. Justify the choice.

Hint

Every area must connect to Area 0.

**Answer:** Reasonable design: each of the 5 sites is its own non-backbone area (Areas 1, 2, 3, 4, 5), and a backbone Area 0 connects them. Each site has 10 routers; each site has at least one Area Border Router (ABR) that participates in both the site's area and Area 0. The Area 0 backbone consists of the ABRs plus any dedicated backbone-only routers (such as core routers at the headquarters). The reasons: (1) localizing LSA flooding within each site keeps the database size small per router (each site router has 10 LSAs in its local area plus summary information for the 4 other sites); (2) topology changes within a site do not flood across the entire network; (3) the area boundaries match the physical site boundaries, which matches both the network engineering and the IT operations structure. Alternative designs to avoid: a single Area 0 covering everything (works but does not scale beyond 100 routers); a deep area hierarchy with many small areas (unnecessary at this scale); using stub or totally-stubby areas to limit inter-area routing (overkill for 5 sites). _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the OSPF structure; watch for Lie #4 (suggesting deprecated area types like NSSA without explaining their special use case; the LLM may produce a needlessly complex design with stubs, totally-stub, and NSSA areas all mixed in for a network that needs no such complexity).

**Q2.** A network engineer at a Tier 1 ISP needs to run a single routing protocol for both IPv4 and IPv6 across the backbone. Argue for IS-IS over OSPF in this scenario.

Hint

What is fundamentally different about how OSPF and IS-IS carry address-family information?

**Answer:** IS-IS runs directly on the data-link layer (not inside an IP packet), and it can carry routes for any network protocol as part of its LSP (Link State Protocol Data Unit) format using TLVs (Type-Length-Value extensions). A single IS-IS process can simultaneously carry IPv4 reachability TLVs and IPv6 reachability TLVs in the same protocol exchange, with one set of timers, one neighbor table, and one synchronized LSP database. OSPF works differently: OSPFv2 is IPv4-only; OSPFv3 is IPv6 (with extensions to also carry IPv4). Running OSPF for both protocols requires two parallel OSPF instances, two sets of timers and adjacencies, two databases. For a Tier 1 ISP that runs a dual-stack backbone, this means doubled state and doubled operational complexity in OSPF, vs. unified single-protocol operation in IS-IS. Other reasons for IS-IS: (1) faster default timers and lower per-LSP overhead in well-tuned deployments; (2) the LSP format is more extensible (TLVs); (3) longstanding deployment in major ISP backbones and a strong cultural fit for ISP operations engineers. The case for OSPF in enterprises (better tooling, broader vendor support, more familiar to engineers trained on enterprise) is real but less relevant at Tier 1 ISP scale. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to recommend a protocol; watch for Lie #4 (recommending OSPFv3 alone for a dual-stack network without realizing v4 support requires extensions that not all vendors implement consistently).

**Q3.** A datacenter Clos fabric has 16 spine switches. A new server is added with two 100 Gbps uplinks to two different top-of-rack switches. How will ECMP distribute traffic from this server to a destination elsewhere in the fabric? List the hashing inputs that matter and the failure modes to watch for.

Hint

The server has two NIC ports; each ToR has up to 16 paths to the spine; what does that multiply to?

**Answer:** Distribution: from the server, the OS (or the NIC driver) chooses which uplink to use for each outgoing flow, typically by hashing the destination IP plus port (or via the kernel's connection-based load balancer). From the first ToR, ECMP picks one of the 16 spine switches by hashing the 5-tuple (source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol); the same flow always picks the same spine because the hash is deterministic. From the spine, traffic descends to the destination ToR via a single path (the spine has only one connection to each leaf ToR). From the destination ToR, the packet is delivered to the destination server's NIC port. So the server has 2×16=322 \times 16 = 322×16=32 possible paths for each flow (2 server uplinks times 16 spine choices); within a flow, the path is consistent. Hashing inputs to watch: (1) 5-tuple hashing is standard; if hashing only the 3-tuple is configured, large bidirectional flows (e.g., source picks port 5000 for everything) will collide on hash and concentrate on one path. (2) Hash function consistency across layers: if every layer uses the same hash function (poor randomization), the same flows get pushed to the same paths everywhere, causing "polarization" where some paths are saturated and others idle; the fix is hash randomization at each layer. (3) Flow size distribution: ECMP balances flow count, not bytes. A handful of "elephant flows" (large, long-lived flows like backups or streaming) can imbalance bandwidth even with perfect flow distribution. Solutions include flowlet-based ECMP, explicit flow scheduling, or letting the application use multiple concurrent connections to spread the load. Failure modes: link flap on a server uplink redistributes flows but interrupts the in-flight ones briefly; spine failure removes one of the 16 spine choices, causing the ECMP fabric to reconverge and pushing the remaining flows onto the other 15 spines (15/16 of capacity remains). _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the data flow; watch for Lie #5 (assuming long-lived connection pools will always distribute well, without considering elephant flow concentration).

**Q4.** An ISP is configuring BFD between two backbone routers to achieve sub-second failover when a link fails. What does BFD do, what timers should be chosen, and what is the failure mode if BFD timers are too aggressive?

Hint

BFD is a heartbeat protocol; what is being heartbeated, and what happens if the heartbeat is missed?

**Answer:** BFD (RFC 5880, Bidirectional Forwarding Detection) is a lightweight protocol that runs between two adjacent routers to detect link failures faster than the routing protocol's own Hello timer. Each end sends BFD packets at a configured interval; if a configurable number of consecutive BFD packets are missed, BFD declares the link failed and notifies the routing protocol (OSPF, IS-IS, BGP), which then triggers convergence. Typical configuration: BFD interval of 50 to 300 milliseconds, with a multiplier of 3 (so failure is declared after 150 to 900 milliseconds without a packet). Aggressive ISP configurations use 50 ms intervals with multiplier 3, declaring failure in 150 ms. The chosen timers should be: (1) short enough to detect link failures within the SLA; (2) long enough to avoid false positives from temporary congestion or BFD packet loss; (3) supported by both ends (some equipment cannot generate BFD at sub-100 ms intervals). Failure mode if timers are too aggressive: BFD declares the link failed when in fact the link is fine but congested, causing unnecessary route reconvergence and traffic disruption. False positives cascade: BFD declares the link down, routing reconverges, traffic shifts to alternate paths, congestion on alternate paths triggers more BFD events, and the network oscillates. The standard tuning starts at 300 ms intervals with multiplier 3 (failure in 900 ms) and tightens only after observing stability. A mature ISP backbone with high-quality fiber may run BFD at 50 ms; an enterprise on best-effort networking might stick with 300 ms or default to no BFD. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to configure BFD; watch for Lie #6 (no jitter awareness: setting BFD timers without considering measurement variance, which leads to oscillation under load).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Reflect on whether the future of intra-domain routing is centralized (an SDN controller computing paths and pushing them to switches) or distributed (each router computing independently like OSPF/IS-IS). What are the trade-offs, and where is the industry heading?

**Discussion:** Both models have merits, and the industry is moving toward hybrids. The classic distributed model (OSPF, IS-IS) has been the workhorse of the internet for 30 years; its strengths are local failure resilience, no single point of failure, autonomous operation. Its weaknesses are limited global optimization (each router does its own thing based on local information) and the difficulty of expressing complex policies (traffic engineering is a hack on top of metric manipulation). The centralized SDN model (with a controller computing optimal paths and installing them via OpenFlow or NETCONF) has been deployed in some hyperscaler networks (Google's B4 WAN is the classic example) and offers fine-grained global optimization but requires a reliable controller plane and is vulnerable to controller failure. The 2026 reality is hybrid: the data plane runs distributed forwarding (often with segment routing for the path-encoding); the control plane has a centralized component (a network controller for traffic engineering and fault response) running alongside the distributed routing protocols. Examples: Cisco's Application Centric Infrastructure (ACI), Juniper's Apstra, the Microsoft Azure backbone. The deeper trend: SDN never fully replaced distributed routing, but it added a programmable layer on top. By 2030 expect most large networks to have a centralized controller managing high-level policy and traffic engineering, with distributed routing protocols providing local resilience and forwarding. Pure distributed (no controller) will persist in small enterprises and Tier 2 ISPs; pure centralized (no distributed protocol) will remain rare because of resilience concerns. The optimal architecture is hybrid: centralized policy with distributed execution.

**Q2.** Argue for or against the proposition that the distinction between intra-domain and inter-domain routing protocols is becoming obsolete. Large networks now span multiple administrative regions; CDNs have hundreds of POPs; AS boundaries are increasingly internal to a single company.

**Discussion:** The proposition is partly right and partly wrong. _Right_ : large hyperscalers (Google, Facebook, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare) operate networks that span dozens of physical locations and hundreds of thousands of routers; the line between "one AS" and "many ASes" becomes architectural choice rather than a fundamental given. Many hyperscalers run their entire backbone as a single AS internally, with the AS boundary at the customer edge. In these cases, the entire backbone is intra-domain. _Wrong_ : BGP remains essential for routing between hyperscalers and the rest of the internet; the protocol of inter-AS routing has not gone away; it has just been pushed to the edges of these massive single-AS networks. Hyperscalers still must speak BGP to their peers, customers, and transit providers. And the policy dimension (which BGP encodes via attributes, communities, local-pref) is more important than ever, because hyperscalers want fine control over how their traffic flows to and from the rest of the world. So the trend is: the geographic extent of one AS has grown (a single AS used to be one ISP in one city; now an AS can be a planet-scale network); but the AS boundary still exists and BGP still runs across it. The intra-vs-inter distinction is therefore less about size and more about _administrative trust_ : within an AS, all routers trust each other; across ASes, they must filter and police. This trust boundary is the lasting reason to separate the two domains. Probably correct prediction: by 2035, OSPF and IS-IS still dominate intra-domain (especially in hyperscalers' single-AS giants), BGP still dominates inter-domain. Segment routing absorbs some of the traffic-engineering work that used to live in BGP communities, simplifying both worlds. The 30-year-old protocol family is durable.

**Q3.** Imagine intra-domain routing in a network with 100,000 routers (a hypothetical hyperscaler scale). Would OSPF or IS-IS scale? What would have to change in the protocol design?

**Discussion:** Standard OSPF and IS-IS hit scaling limits well before 100,000 routers. The bottleneck is full-mesh LSA flooding within an area, which produces O(n2)O(n^2)O(n2) flooding traffic on topology changes. With 100,000 routers in one area, that is 10 billion LSA flooding events per change, far beyond what is practical. Possible scaling approaches: (1) _Hierarchical areas at much deeper levels_ : instead of OSPF's 2-level (area + backbone), use 3 or 4 levels of hierarchy. IS-IS already supports L1/L2; extending to L3/L4 would push the scale. (2) _Use a different routing protocol_ : BGP can be used as an internal routing protocol (iBGP) at very large scale because its distance-vector-with-policy model scales differently than link-state. Some hyperscalers do this. (3) _Centralized control plane_ : replace the distributed routing protocol with a centralized SDN controller that pushes forwarding state to each router; the routers run a minimal protocol (perhaps just BGP for keepalives) and trust the controller for path information. Microsoft's Azure backbone is reportedly close to this. (4) _Segment routing with computed paths_ : encode paths into packet headers and let the controller compute paths for all flows; the routers just forward based on the segment in the header, with no link-state database needed. (5) _Federate at the topology level_ : break the 100,000-router network into many smaller routing domains and route between them via BGP. In practice, most hyperscalers do option 5 plus pieces of options 3 and 4. They run a federated topology (each region or each fabric is its own IS-IS or OSPF instance, with BGP between them) and a centralized controller for policy. Pure protocol scaling to 100,000 routers in one routing instance is not solved; the answer is to structure the network so no one routing instance has to deal with that scale.

### Chapter Summary

Intra-domain routing builds the forwarding tables that move packets within a single autonomous system. OSPF and IS-IS are the two dominant link-state protocols; both flood link descriptions, build a topology graph, and compute shortest paths via Dijkstra. OSPF is more common in enterprises; IS-IS is more common in large ISPs because of its multi-protocol carrying ability and its ISP-friendly history.

Both protocols support hierarchical structuring (OSPF areas, IS-IS levels) to keep the per-router state manageable. ECMP distributes traffic across equal-cost paths, with per-flow hashing being the standard to preserve TCP ordering. Convergence time is the duration between topology change and forwarding-table update; modern networks reduce it via BFD, IP Fast Reroute, and tuned timers.

The wire-level artifact (an OSPF LSA captured on a lab link) is the entry point for hands-on learning. A few hours watching OSPF adjacency formation cements concepts that no diagram can convey.

The themes from this chapter set up Chapter 7's BGP coverage: scale, policy, convergence, and the difference between knowing a topology and managing a policy. OSPF/IS-IS work because all routers in the domain trust each other and care about physics (shortest paths, fast failover). BGP works because all ASes in the world _cannot_ trust each other and must manage policy first, physics second. The transition between these mental models is the central conceptual climb of the next chapter.
