## Chapter 10: UDP and the QUIC Story

TCP earned the previous chapter's depth because it is the workhorse of the internet. This chapter is about its more minimal sibling (UDP) and its modern descendant (QUIC). UDP is the smallest possible transport protocol on IP: it adds ports and a checksum and nothing else. QUIC is the maximum: it absorbs TCP, TLS, and parts of HTTP/2 into one unified protocol that runs over UDP because the IETF could not change TCP fast enough.

Together UDP and QUIC tell two complementary stories. UDP tells the story of "what if we just don't bother with reliability and ordering, and let the application decide." QUIC tells the story of "what if we keep reliability and ordering, but rebuild them in user space with modern crypto and modern multiplexing, all wrapped in encryption so middleboxes cannot ossify us again."

This chapter covers UDP's minimalism, QUIC's design (connection IDs, streams, 0-RTT, connection migration), the 0-RTT replay-safety problem, and Jin Park's QUIC migration from his TCP/CGNAT pain in Chapter 5. The wire-level artifact is a QUIC handshake compared to TLS-over-TCP, with the latency budget side by side.

By the end you should be able to read a UDP header in your sleep, articulate exactly why QUIC exists, explain how connection migration works, and reason about when 0-RTT is safe and when it is dangerous.

### 10.1 UDP: The Minimalism Thesis

UDP (User Datagram Protocol, RFC 768) is the simplest possible transport on IP. The header is 8 bytes:
    
    
    +--------+--------+--------+--------+
    |     Source      |   Destination   |
    |      Port       |      Port       |
    +--------+--------+--------+--------+
    |     Length      |    Checksum     |
    +--------+--------+--------+--------+
    |         Data...                   |
    +-----------------------------------+
    

Four fields:

* **Source Port** (16 bits): the sender's port.
* **Destination Port** (16 bits): the receiver's port.
* **Length** (16 bits): total length (header + data) in bytes.
* **Checksum** (16 bits): a 16-bit one's complement checksum over the UDP header, the data, and a pseudo-header (IP source, IP dest, protocol number, UDP length). In IPv6, the checksum is mandatory; in IPv4 it is optional (but almost always set).

That is all. No handshake. No sequence numbers. No acknowledgements. No flow control. No congestion control. No connection state. The receiver gets a packet and processes it; if the packet was lost in transit, the sender does not know, and the receiver does not know there should have been one.

#### 10.1.1 What UDP Buys You

UDP buys: (1) _lower latency_ (no handshake before the first packet of data); (2) _no head-of-line blocking_ (each packet is independent); (3) _no congestion-control overhead_ (which can be a feature or a problem depending on your view); (4) _broadcast and multicast support_ (TCP does not support these); (5) _connectionless semantics_ (the server does not need per-client state, scales to many clients).

UDP costs: (1) the application must handle reliability if it wants it; (2) the application must handle ordering; (3) the application must implement flow control and congestion control or risk being a bad citizen on the network; (4) most middleboxes treat UDP with more suspicion than TCP (some corporate firewalls block all UDP by default).

#### 10.1.2 What Uses UDP

A short tour of UDP applications:

* **DNS** : lookup queries are typically a few hundred bytes, fit in one UDP datagram, and the cost of TCP setup would dwarf the lookup itself. DNS over UDP is the default; DNS over TCP is the fallback for large responses (Chapter 13).
* **NTP** (Network Time Protocol): same reasoning, plus the protocol is designed to handle occasional loss.
* **DHCP** : lookup-style protocol; uses broadcast UDP for initial discovery.
* **SNMP, syslog** : small, frequent, lossy-OK.
* **Voice and video over RTP** : latency matters more than reliability for real-time media; lost packets are dropped rather than retransmitted.
* **Online gaming** : similar reasoning: fast, frequent, small updates; retransmitting stale game state is worse than missing it entirely.
* **QUIC** : covered below; uses UDP as its substrate because IPv4/IPv6 routers happily forward UDP but new protocols on raw IP are blocked by middleboxes.
* **WireGuard, Tailscale, IPsec ESP** : VPN protocols that benefit from UDP's statelessness and that wrap their own reliability inside.

#### 10.1.3 Why "No Congestion Control" Became a Problem

When UDP was designed in 1980, the internet was small, and "be a good citizen" was a social agreement among the operators. When UDP applications proliferated (especially streaming video, gaming, BitTorrent) and started moving billions of packets per second, the lack of built-in congestion control became a problem: a UDP-based application could send as fast as the link allowed, starving TCP flows on the same link.

The community's response: (1) IETF guidance for any new UDP-based protocol to include congestion control (RFC 8085: UDP Usage Guidelines); (2) some operating systems and routers limit UDP throughput in various ways; (3) protocols like QUIC explicitly include TCP-equivalent congestion control.

A modern UDP application that does not implement congestion control is bad citizenship and may be throttled by various network elements. Browsers' QUIC implementations and most production UDP protocols include their own congestion control to be good network citizens.

### 10.2 Why QUIC Exists

To understand QUIC's design, you have to understand what failed about TCP.

#### 10.2.1 TCP's Problems on Modern Networks

Three categories of TCP problems motivated QUIC:

**Latency** : TCP's 3-way handshake takes 1 RTT before any data flows. TLS handshake on top takes 1 to 2 more RTTs. Total: 2 to 3 RTT before the first byte of application data. On a 100ms RTT link, that is 200 to 300ms of pure setup before the user sees anything. In 2010s mobile networks where RTTs commonly exceeded 100ms, this was painful for every short web request.

**Head-of-line blocking** : TCP delivers a single ordered byte stream. HTTP/2 introduced multiplexing of multiple requests over one TCP connection, but TCP's byte stream constraint meant a single dropped packet stalled all multiplexed streams until the retransmission arrived. The very feature that made HTTP/2 fast (multiplexing) was undermined by TCP's ordering guarantee.

**Middlebox ossification** : NATs, firewalls, and load balancers all hard-coded assumptions about TCP. Adding new TCP options or new features got harder over time because some middlebox somewhere would drop the packets. The IETF tried to evolve TCP (TCP Fast Open, Multipath TCP, ECN); each evolution took 5 to 10 years to deploy because of middlebox ossification.

The IETF concluded around 2013: we cannot evolve TCP at the speed the modern internet needs. We need a new transport that we control end-to-end, that middleboxes cannot inspect or modify, that runs on top of UDP (which middleboxes do forward), and that integrates everything (handshake, encryption, multiplexing, congestion control) into one unified design.

That protocol became QUIC.

#### 10.2.2 QUIC's Core Properties

QUIC (RFC 9000, 9001, 9002) is:

* **Built on UDP** : avoids the new-protocol-on-IP middlebox problem.
* **Encrypted end-to-end** : almost every byte after the initial handshake is encrypted; middleboxes cannot inspect or modify QUIC content. This deliberately prevents future ossification.
* **0-RTT to 1-RTT handshake** : 1 RTT for new connections; 0 RTT for repeat connections (under replay-safety constraints).
* **Connection-ID-based** : a variable-length connection ID (0-20 bytes per RFC 9000 §5.1; 8 bytes is the common deployment choice) identifies the connection, not the IP+port tuple. This enables connection migration (the client's IP can change without breaking the connection).
* **Multi-streamed** : multiple independent ordered streams per connection, each with its own flow control. A drop in one stream does not block others (no head-of-line blocking across streams).
* **TLS 1.3 integrated** : QUIC's handshake is essentially TLS 1.3, with the transport-layer parameters negotiated alongside cryptographic parameters.

The implementation is in user space (initially in Chromium, now in Linux kernels for some servers, and in many independent libraries). User-space implementation makes evolution fast: a new QUIC feature can ship with a new browser release, no kernel upgrade needed.

### 10.3 The QUIC Handshake

A new QUIC connection's handshake:
    
    
    Client                                Server
      |                                    |
      |  Initial (CRYPTO frame: ClientHello)
      |  -------------------------------->|
      |                                    |
      |    Initial (ACK + ServerHello)     |
      |    Handshake (Cert, Finished)      |
      |  <--------------------------------|
      |                                    |
      |  Handshake (Finished)              |
      |  + 1-RTT data (Application data)   |
      |  -------------------------------->|
      |                                    |
      |    1-RTT (Application data)        |
      |  <--------------------------------|
    

In one RTT (the time for the first packet to reach the server and the response to come back), the client has:

  1. Sent its ClientHello with TLS 1.3 key shares.
  2. Received the server's response (ServerHello, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished).
  3. Sent its Finished plus application data.

The application data in step 3 is encrypted with the handshake-derived keys. The first 1-RTT data from the server arrives in step 4. Compared to TCP+TLS 1.3 which takes 2 RTTs minimum (TCP handshake + TLS handshake), QUIC saves a full RTT for new connections.

#### 10.3.1 0-RTT Resumption

For repeat connections (the client has connected to this server before and has a pre-shared key, PSK, from the previous session), QUIC can send application data with the very first packet:
    
    
    Client                                Server
      |                                    |
      |  Initial (CRYPTO frame: PSK)       |
      |  0-RTT (Application data)          |
      |  -------------------------------->|
      |                                    |
      |    1-RTT (Application data)        |
      |  <--------------------------------|
    

The client sends its application data alongside the initial handshake message, encrypted with keys derived from the PSK. The server, if it accepts the PSK, processes the data immediately. The user's request reaches the server in 0.5 RTT (half of one round trip). The server's response arrives in 1 RTT.

This is the "0-RTT" advantage. For a typical HTTPS request, 0-RTT means the user sees content roughly twice as fast as on TCP+TLS.

#### 10.3.2 0-RTT Replay Safety

The big caveat: 0-RTT data can be replayed. An attacker who captures the 0-RTT request can resend it later, and the server will accept it (because the PSK is still valid). This means 0-RTT must only be used for _idempotent_ requests: GETs, not POSTs that change state.

In TLS 1.3 and QUIC, 0-RTT is opt-in: the client and server agree on which operations are 0-RTT eligible. HTTP/3 mandates that 0-RTT can only be used for GET, HEAD, OPTIONS (idempotent methods), not POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH. Implementations enforce this.

The replay-safety problem is the canonical 0-RTT gotcha. It is one of the recurring stories of QUIC adoption: developers want the latency benefit but forget the idempotency constraint, leading to subtle bugs.

### 10.4 Connection IDs and Migration

In TCP, a connection is identified by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). If any of these changes (the client moves networks, gets a new IP), the TCP connection dies because the kernel cannot match incoming packets to the right socket.

QUIC introduces _connection IDs_ (CIDs): variable-length identifiers (0–20 bytes per RFC 9000 §5.1; 8 bytes is the common deployment choice) that appear in every long-header QUIC packet and in short-header packets after the handshake (in cleartext, so middleboxes can route). The connection ID is what identifies the connection, not the 4-tuple. Each endpoint chooses the CIDs it wants peers to send to it; both sides may rotate CIDs over the connection's lifetime, both for migration and for linkability resistance.

When a client's IP changes (it migrates from Wi-Fi to cellular, for instance):

  1. The first QUIC packet from the new IP carries the same connection ID.
  2. The server sees a packet with a known connection ID arriving from a different IP+port.
  3. The server validates the new path (sends a small probe to confirm reachability and prevent address spoofing).
  4. Once validated, the server updates its mapping and continues the connection.

The application sees no disruption. The TCP-and-TLS-handshake-and-redownload-everything that mobile users experience when they hand off between networks is eliminated.

#### 10.4.1 Path Validation

QUIC's path validation prevents abuse: an attacker could send a connection-ID with a forged source IP, trying to redirect the server's responses to a victim (a "reflection" attack). The server's path validation requires the new IP to respond to a challenge, ensuring the path is genuine.

#### 10.4.2 Server-Initiated Migration

QUIC supports the server changing its IP too, useful for load balancing or maintenance. The server signals the change via a frame; the client updates its mapping. Less commonly used than client migration but architecturally clean.

### 10.5 Streams: Multiplexing Without Head-of-Line Blocking

QUIC supports many independent streams per connection. Each stream is a byte stream with its own flow control. A drop in one stream's traffic does not block other streams.

This solves HTTP/2's head-of-line blocking problem. In HTTP/2 over TCP, multiplexing multiple requests on one connection meant that a single packet drop stalled all of them until retransmission completed. In HTTP/3 over QUIC, each request is its own stream; a drop only affects its own stream.

#### 10.5.1 Stream Types

QUIC streams are bidirectional or unidirectional, client-initiated or server-initiated. Stream IDs encode this:

* IDs ending in `00`: client-initiated, bidirectional.
* IDs ending in `01`: server-initiated, bidirectional.
* IDs ending in `10`: client-initiated, unidirectional.
* IDs ending in `11`: server-initiated, unidirectional.

HTTP/3 uses bidirectional streams for request/response, plus unidirectional streams for protocol control (settings, push promises).

#### 10.5.2 Flow Control: Per-Stream and Per-Connection

QUIC implements flow control at two levels:

* **Per-stream** : each stream has its own receive window. The receiver can throttle one stream without affecting others.
* **Per-connection** : the connection has an aggregate receive window across all streams.

This dual-level flow control is essential: an application can prioritize one stream over another, and a slow consumer on one stream cannot starve the entire connection.

### 10.6 Jin Park's QUIC Migration

Recall from Chapter 5: Jin Park's app at the Korean fintech kept dropping sessions on a carrier's CGNAT. The TCP keep-alive hotfix shipped within a day; the real solution was migrating the app to QUIC/HTTP/3.

Jin's migration plan:

  1. **Server-side** : deploy QUIC support. The backend is Go-based gRPC; gRPC over HTTP/3 is supported via the `grpc-go` library with QUIC integration. Update the server to listen on UDP/443 alongside TCP/443.

  2. **Client-side** : update the mobile app to use QUIC. iOS supports QUIC since iOS 15 via URLSession; Android via Cronet. The client library is updated to prefer HTTP/3.

  3. **DNS** : publish HTTPS resource records (RFC 9460) indicating QUIC support. Modern browsers and OS clients use these records to discover QUIC availability without an initial TCP fallback.

  4. **Fallback** : if QUIC is blocked (some corporate firewalls block UDP/443), the client falls back to HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP. The application code is transport-agnostic at the gRPC layer.

  5. **Validation** : monitor metrics. Specifically: connection establishment time (should drop from 200-400ms to 100-200ms), connection drop rate on CGNAT carriers (should approach zero), CPU and bandwidth costs (QUIC is more CPU-intensive than TCP+TLS because of user-space crypto, but acceptable on modern phones).

The migration takes 3 months from server-side deployment to majority of clients on QUIC. The connection drop problem disappears: QUIC's connection migration handles CGNAT mapping changes natively, so even when the CGNAT box swaps a port mapping, the QUIC connection survives.

Jin's metrics post-migration: median connection establishment time roughly a third faster (mostly from the 0-RTT path on warm connections); the p99 tail dropped roughly in half on lossy cellular paths; CGNAT-related session drops effectively eliminated by QUIC's connection-ID-driven migration; server-side CPU cost up a small but visible amount (mid-teens percent) from user-space crypto vs in-kernel TCP. The migration is judged a success. (These ranges are illustrative; expect 20-40% / 40-70% improvements on the two latency metrics in typical deployments, with the wins largest on mobile-heavy traffic.)

### 10.7 The Wire-Level Artifact: QUIC vs TLS-over-TCP

Let us compare the connection setup of QUIC and TLS-over-TCP side by side, on a network with 80ms RTT.

**TLS 1.3 over TCP** :
    
    
    Time   Packet
    0ms    Client → Server: TCP SYN
    80ms   Server → Client: TCP SYN-ACK
    80ms   Client → Server: TCP ACK + TLS ClientHello
    160ms  Server → Client: TLS ServerHello + Certificate + Finished
    160ms  Client → Server: TLS Finished + HTTP Request
    240ms  Server → Client: HTTP Response (first bytes)
    

Total time to first response byte: 240ms. Three round trips.

**QUIC 1-RTT (new connection)** :
    
    
    Time   Packet
    0ms    Client → Server: Initial (ClientHello)
    80ms   Server → Client: Initial + Handshake (ServerHello, Cert, Finished)
    80ms   Client → Server: Handshake (Finished) + 1-RTT (HTTP Request)
    160ms  Server → Client: 1-RTT (HTTP Response)
    

Total time to first response byte: 160ms. Two round trips.

**QUIC 0-RTT (repeat connection)** :
    
    
    Time   Packet
    0ms    Client → Server: Initial (PSK) + 0-RTT (HTTP Request)
    80ms   Server → Client: 1-RTT (HTTP Response)
    

Total time to first response byte: 80ms. One round trip.

On 80ms RTT, QUIC 1-RTT saves 80ms (33%) over TLS+TCP; QUIC 0-RTT saves 160ms (67%). For mobile networks with 100ms+ RTTs, the savings are larger. This is why QUIC adoption took off for HTTP traffic: the latency wins are real and visible to users.

qlog and qvis are the standard observability formats for QUIC. A QUIC connection emits a qlog file (JSON-formatted) detailing every packet, every frame, every key derivation. qvis visualizes this. Reading qlog traces is the QUIC equivalent of reading tcpdump for TCP: essential operational skill.

### 10.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is UDP, and what minimal functions does it add over IP?

Hint

The UDP header has four fields.

**Answer:** UDP (User Datagram Protocol, RFC 768) is the minimum transport-layer protocol on IP. The UDP header is 8 bytes and contains four fields: source port (16 bits), destination port (16 bits), length (16 bits), and checksum (16 bits). The functions UDP adds over raw IP are: (1) _Port multiplexing_ : source and destination ports allow multiple applications on the same IP to share the protocol layer; the OS demultiplexes incoming packets to the right process based on destination port. (2) _Integrity check_ : the checksum (with a pseudo-header including IP source/dest) catches in-transit corruption; in IPv6 the checksum is mandatory, in IPv4 optional but almost always set. (3) _Length field_ : explicitly indicates the size of the datagram, allowing the receiver to distinguish data from any padding. UDP does NOT add: reliability (the receiver may not receive what was sent), ordering (datagrams may arrive in any order), flow control (the receiver cannot throttle), congestion control (the sender has no awareness of network state), or connection state (no handshake, no teardown). Applications using UDP must handle these themselves if they need them.

**Q2.** Why does QUIC run on top of UDP rather than directly on IP?

Hint

What can routers and middleboxes do with packets they don't recognize?

**Answer:** QUIC runs on UDP because adding a new protocol on raw IP would require routers and middleboxes (NAT gateways, firewalls, load balancers) to handle a previously-unknown IP protocol number. In practice, middleboxes are configured to either drop packets with unknown IP protocols or to "fail closed" by routing them through slow paths. Deploying a new IP protocol globally would require updating millions of middleboxes, a coordination problem that is operationally infeasible. UDP, on the other hand, is handled by every middlebox in existence: routers forward UDP packets normally, NATs translate UDP source ports (with their state-table semantics), firewalls have well-understood rules for UDP. By running QUIC inside UDP datagrams, the QUIC protocol can deploy globally without requiring any middlebox upgrades: any path that supports any UDP application supports QUIC. This is the "deploy on top of what works" pragmatic decision that enabled QUIC's rapid adoption. The cost is the 8-byte UDP header on every QUIC packet (small overhead), and that QUIC reuses UDP port 443 by convention (which some restrictive firewalls block, requiring HTTP/2 fallback).

**Q3.** What is connection migration in QUIC, and why does it matter for mobile users?

Hint

What happens to a TCP connection when the client's IP address changes?

**Answer:** Connection migration is QUIC's ability to continue a connection across changes to the client's IP address. The mechanism: every QUIC long-header packet (and every short-header packet after the handshake) carries a connection ID — variable-length 0-20 bytes per RFC 9000, typically 8 bytes in deployment — in cleartext so middleboxes can route on it. The connection is identified by this ID, not by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port) as in TCP. When a client's IP changes (it migrates from Wi-Fi to cellular, or moves between cells, or its NAT mapping resets due to CGNAT timeout), the next QUIC packet from the new IP carries the same connection ID. The server sees a known connection ID from a new IP, performs a path validation challenge to ensure the new IP is genuine (to prevent reflection attacks), and updates its routing. The application sees no disruption. This matters for mobile users because mobile networks change paths constantly: handoffs between cellular towers, transitions between Wi-Fi and cellular, NAT-table churn at carrier CGNAT. In TCP, every such change requires a fresh connection (full handshake plus TLS resumption plus application-layer state recovery), which can take 200ms to 1 second. In QUIC, the connection survives the change transparently. For real-time applications (video calls, live games, streaming), this is a major user experience improvement. Jin Park's CGNAT problem from Chapter 5 is exactly this: TCP cannot survive CGNAT mapping changes; QUIC can.

**Q4.** What is the 0-RTT replay-safety problem, and how is it mitigated?

Hint

What can an attacker do with a captured 0-RTT request?

**Answer:** In QUIC and TLS 1.3, 0-RTT lets a returning client send application data with the very first packet, encrypted under a pre-shared key derived from a previous session. The replay-safety problem: an attacker who captures a 0-RTT packet can resend it later. The server, finding the same PSK valid, will accept the replayed packet and process the application data. If the data triggers a state-changing operation (e.g., a POST that transfers money, or a DELETE that removes a resource), the operation can be duplicated. Mitigations: (1) Application-level idempotency: only allow 0-RTT for idempotent operations (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS in HTTP). The application or HTTP library refuses 0-RTT for POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH. This is what HTTP/3 mandates and what Chromium/Firefox/Safari enforce. (2) Server-side replay window: the server tracks recent 0-RTT requests by a time-bound deduplication mechanism (each PSK can only be used once for 0-RTT, or only within a short time window). This makes replay attacks impractical even if the application has non-idempotent operations. (3) Server can configure whether 0-RTT is allowed for specific HTTP methods or URL patterns. (4) Single-use tickets: TLS session tickets that include 0-RTT permission can be single-use, so a captured ticket cannot be replayed. Despite these mitigations, 0-RTT is a deliberate trade: latency saved at the cost of replay risk. The protocol design says: enable 0-RTT only where the application's risk model can tolerate replay.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Compare UDP and TCP for a real-time multiplayer game's traffic. The game sends 60 small (50-byte) state updates per second between client and server. Which protocol is more appropriate, and what application-layer mechanisms are needed?

Hint

Reliability matters less than timeliness; stale updates are useless.

**Answer:** UDP is more appropriate. Game state updates have these properties: (1) Small payloads (50 bytes), so per-packet overhead matters more than throughput. (2) High frequency (60/sec), so any per-packet handshake or retransmission overhead is wasteful. (3) Stale updates are useless: if update #45 is lost, the client does not want it retransmitted at update #50's arrival time; it wants update #50 and to skip #45 entirely. TCP's reliability is the wrong tool: TCP would retransmit lost updates, blocking subsequent updates until they arrive (head-of-line blocking), which is the opposite of what a game wants. Application-layer mechanisms needed: (1) _Sequence numbers in the application protocol_ : every state update has a number so the client can detect lost ones and decide what to do with them. (2) _Server-authoritative state_ : the server has the canonical state; if the client missed update #45, it just receives the corrected state in #50. (3) _Application-level congestion adaptation_ : if many UDP packets are being lost, the application should reduce send rate (to be a good citizen and to avoid further loss); some games skip updates rather than reduce update rate. (4) _Encryption at the application layer_ : DTLS (Datagram Transport Layer Security) is the UDP equivalent of TLS, providing encryption without ordering guarantees. (5) _Optional reliability_ : critical events (player health change, score update) can be sent reliably via an application-level retransmission mechanism while routine state updates are unreliable. The architecture is more complex than just "use TCP," but it produces dramatically better latency and responsiveness for the game. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the game protocol; watch for Lie #1 (using TCP semantics for a real-time game and adding application-layer "fast retransmit" hacks instead of using UDP from the start; this is the classic TCP-for-everything pitfall).

**Q2.** A web application is migrating from HTTP/2 over TLS to HTTP/3 over QUIC. List the concrete operational changes needed, and identify the biggest deployment risk.

Hint

DNS, firewall, load balancer, monitoring.

**Answer:** _Operational changes_ : (1) _Server-side_ : deploy a QUIC-capable server. Nginx (with the OpenSSL +QUIC patch or via BoringSSL), HAProxy 2.6+, Envoy, Cloudflare's quiche library, AWS CloudFront support QUIC. The server now listens on UDP/443 in addition to TCP/443. (2) _Load balancer_ : must be QUIC-aware. L4 load balancers can hash on connection ID (cleartext in the QUIC header) for session affinity. L7 load balancers (Envoy) can terminate QUIC and re-originate as HTTP/2 to backends. (3) _Firewall_ : UDP/443 must be allowed, both inbound and outbound. Many enterprise firewalls block UDP/443 by default. (4) _DNS_ : publish HTTPS resource records (RFC 9460) advertising QUIC support, so clients can preemptively try QUIC without an HTTP/2 fallback round-trip. The alt-svc header is the older mechanism (returned in HTTP responses), still useful but less efficient. (5) _Monitoring_ : add qlog generation to the server, and qvis or similar tooling for inspection. Standard HTTP metrics still apply but new QUIC-specific metrics matter (connection migration events, 0-RTT acceptance rate, retry rate). (6) _Client-side_ *: most modern clients (Chrome, Firefox, Safari, recent iOS/Android URLSession/Cronet) support QUIC; the application doesn't need to change. Older clients fall back to HTTP/2. _Biggest deployment risk_ : UDP being blocked by some networks. Corporate firewalls, some public Wi-Fi, some carriers in certain regions actively block or rate-limit UDP. If a meaningful percentage of users are on such networks, QUIC fails to establish, and the client falls back to HTTP/2 over TCP after a delay. The fallback works but adds 200-500ms of wasted time. Mitigation: aggressive race-and-fallback logic in the client (try QUIC, but if no response in 100ms, try HTTP/2 in parallel); careful telemetry on QUIC vs HTTP/2 share by region; education of network operators on UDP/443 being legitimate. The 2026 reality is that 70-85% of traffic to QUIC-enabled sites is HTTP/3; the remainder falls back. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to plan the migration; watch for Lie #3 (assuming HTTP/2-style server-push will work in HTTP/3 the same way: Chrome removed HTTP/2 server-push support in 2022, HTTP/3 server-push exists in RFC 9114 but is effectively unused in deployment, and the modern replacement is `103 Early Hints` plus resource hints — not "server-initiated streams") and Lie #4 (suggesting TLS 1.2 configurations for QUIC: QUIC requires TLS 1.3, not negotiable).

**Q3.** Jin Park's QUIC migration: design the validation phase. What metrics should he track to confirm the migration is successful?

Hint

Compare TCP vs QUIC paths on several dimensions.

**Answer:** _Metrics to track during the validation phase_ : (1) _Connection establishment time_ : time from "client wants to connect" to "first byte of application data sent." TCP+TLS 1.3 baseline is typically 2 RTT; QUIC 1-RTT should reach 1 RTT; QUIC 0-RTT on returning users should reach 0.5 RTT. Plot per-user CDFs. (2) _Time to first byte (TTFB)_ : the user-perceived latency of getting the first bytes of a response. This includes connection setup and request-processing time. Lower is better; the QUIC benefit is mostly in the connection-setup portion. (3) _Connection failure rate_ : how often does a connection attempt fail to complete? With QUIC, failures should be lower (no SYN-ACK race conditions, no TLS handshake stalls). On UDP-blocked networks, failures should be tracked separately and counted as QUIC-blocked, not application-level errors. (4) _Connection migration events_ : how often does the client's IP change mid-connection, and how often does QUIC successfully migrate without disruption? On Korean mobile networks with frequent cell handoffs and CGNAT churn, this should be high (one or more migrations per hour of active app usage). (5) _0-RTT acceptance rate_ : of clients with prior sessions, what fraction can use 0-RTT? The PSK should be cached for some hours; users who return within that window should get 0-RTT. Track the fraction of HTTP requests that complete via 0-RTT. (6) _Session drop rate_ : critically, the metric from the original incident: how often does a long-lived connection drop in a way that requires re-authentication? With QUIC, this should approach zero. (7) _Server CPU and memory cost_ : QUIC is more CPU-intensive than TCP+TLS (user-space crypto, no TCP segmentation offload on the kernel). The cost should be acceptable, perhaps 10-20% higher, but not 5x. (8) _Server bandwidth cost_ : 1 to 2% higher for QUIC due to slightly larger headers; negligible. (9) _Per-region or per-carrier metrics_ : split all of the above by region (Korea vs other Asian markets) and by carrier (each carrier's CGNAT behavior is different). The migration is judged successful if metrics (1)-(6) improve substantially and metrics (7)-(8) stay within acceptable ranges. The validation phase typically lasts 4-8 weeks of phased rollout. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the metrics; watch for Lie #2 (missing observability dimensions: monitoring only connection success rate without per-region or per-carrier breakdown, which hides the worst cases).

**Q4.** A new microservice in a data center wants to use QUIC for internal traffic between services. Argue whether this is a good idea, given the alternative of using HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP or pure gRPC over HTTP/2.

Hint

What are the differences between data-center networks and the public internet?

**Answer:** _Probably not a good idea for typical internal traffic_. Reasons: (1) Data-center networks are not the use case QUIC was designed for. The motivations for QUIC (variable RTT, mobile network churn, middlebox ossification) are largely absent inside a data center. The RTT between two services in the same DC is sub-millisecond; the path is stable; there are no middleboxes blocking new TCP options. (2) The latency win from QUIC's 1-RTT handshake is negligible when RTT is 1 ms anyway. (3) QUIC is more CPU-intensive than TCP+TLS because it does crypto in user space without kernel TLS offload (kTLS) and without TCP segmentation offload (TSO). This matters when both endpoints are CPU-constrained (high-rate microservices). (4) Existing tooling (load balancers, observability, mesh services) is much more mature for HTTP/2 over TCP than for HTTP/3. (5) Connection migration (a major QUIC feature) is not useful inside a stable DC. (6) Head-of-line blocking is partly addressed by HTTP/2 multiplexing, and within a DC with low loss, HOL blocking is rare. _Why use QUIC inside a DC_ : (i) experimental: testing QUIC at scale, learning operational characteristics; (ii) some metrics: HTTP/3 client libraries are increasingly the default, so using HTTP/3 throughout simplifies the dependency tree; (iii) future-proofing: as HTTP/3 becomes universal, internal services should support it too. _Recommended choice_ : stay on HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP for internal traffic; use QUIC at the edge (where the network is messy and the QUIC benefits matter); if a strong reason emerges to use QUIC internally, measure the CPU cost carefully. For pure-RPC internal traffic, gRPC over HTTP/2 over TCP is still the production norm in 2026. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the internal communication; watch for Lie #4 (recommending HTTP/3 everywhere because "it's the latest" without measuring the actual gain in the data-center context; cargo-cult adoption).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Argue (a) why QUIC's encryption-everything design is good for evolution, (b) what was lost compared to TCP's middlebox-friendly model, (c) whether this tradeoff is sustainable.

**Discussion:** (a) QUIC encrypts almost every byte after the initial handshake, including most of the transport-layer headers (offsets, ACK ranges, flow-control values, connection IDs at certain layers). The only cleartext bits are the QUIC version, connection ID for routing, and a few other necessary fields. The benefit for evolution: middleboxes cannot inspect or modify the protocol's behavior. New QUIC features can ship as software updates to client and server without breaking any middlebox. TCP's evolution had been blocked by middleboxes that dropped packets with unknown options or that interfered with new behavior; QUIC's design makes this impossible. (b) What was lost: (i) deep packet inspection for security: some security tools rely on parsing transport-layer headers to detect anomalies; with QUIC, they cannot. (ii) traffic management: some QoS systems modify ECN bits or adjust TCP behavior; with QUIC, they cannot. (iii) operational debugging: tcpdump on a QUIC stream shows mostly encrypted bytes; debugging requires qlog from one of the endpoints. (iv) network research: studying internet behavior used to involve passive observation of TCP/IP headers; with QUIC, much of this becomes impossible. (c) Sustainable? Yes, with caveats. The argument for sustainability: the previous era of "middleboxes can see everything" was used to ossify the protocol, and the cost (slow evolution) exceeded the benefit (slightly easier operations). The argument against: as QUIC becomes the dominant transport, security tools and operations will adapt to it (more endpoint-based observability, more cooperation between endpoints and security tools), and a steady-state will emerge where the tradeoff is fine. The downside: QUIC makes it harder for legitimate network management (regulatory compliance, lawful intercept, DDoS detection) to operate, and these pressures may push for compromises (e.g., transport-layer fields that are encrypted but accessible to specific authorized parties). The 2026 reality: QUIC is winning at the public-internet edge; in regulated environments (banking, healthcare, government) the question of how to operate QUIC alongside compliance requirements is still being worked out. The deeper insight: encryption-by-default is a defensive design choice that prioritizes long-term protocol health over short-term operations convenience, and that bet has been mostly correct.

**Q2.** Make an argument for whether the IETF should have spent the QUIC effort on a TCP extension instead. Could TCP have been made to do what QUIC does, with less protocol-replacement disruption?

**Discussion:** No, probably not, for two complementary reasons. (a) _Middlebox ossification_ : even simple TCP extensions (TCP Fast Open for 0-RTT, Multipath TCP for multi-homing, ECN for explicit congestion notification) took 10+ years to deploy because middleboxes dropped or interfered with the packets. Any "TCP 2.0" effort would have run into the same problem multiplied many times over: NATs would not pass packets with new fields; load balancers would not handle new flag combinations; firewalls would drop packets with unexpected options. The fundamental problem is that TCP has been a stable protocol for 40 years, and every middlebox in existence assumes it stays that way. (b) _Per-stream multiplexing requires breaking byte stream semantics_ : TCP's contract is "one ordered byte stream"; you cannot retrofit per-stream HOL-blocking-free semantics without changing this contract. Once you change the contract, applications must be updated to use the new semantics anyway, which is most of the work of switching to QUIC. (c) _Crypto integration is awkward in TCP_ : TCP and TLS are layered (TCP first, TLS on top), which means the TCP handshake happens before TLS knows anything. Tighter integration (handshake combining transport and crypto) requires breaking the layering, which is essentially what QUIC does. Could it have been done on top of TCP? Maybe, but the result would have been almost as different from "current TCP" as QUIC is. The pragmatic conclusion: QUIC is the right design, and starting fresh on UDP was the right choice. The alternative (TCP 2.0) would have failed in the field, taking much longer. The cost (protocol replacement) is real but is being paid down: by 2030, QUIC will dominate the public web; HTTP/3 will be the default; the transition period will be largely over.

**Q3.** Reflect on the future of UDP as a substrate. If QUIC becomes the dominant transport, will UDP remain visible as a separate concept, or will it become an implementation detail of QUIC?

**Discussion:** UDP will remain visible because: (1) Many applications use UDP directly without QUIC: DNS, NTP, online games, WebRTC's media flows, IoT protocols. None of these need QUIC's full feature set. (2) The cleartext UDP layer remains the network's view of the traffic; firewalls, NATs, and load balancers all see UDP packets and apply their rules. (3) Operational tools (tcpdump, Wireshark) parse UDP regardless of what is inside. From the network's perspective, QUIC traffic looks like UDP traffic. (4) New protocols may emerge that use UDP differently than QUIC: MASQUE (running TCP inside QUIC for some VPN use cases) is an example. The MoQ (Media over QUIC) protocol stack uses QUIC plus its own framing; the underlying UDP packets remain visible. _The pragmatic view_ : UDP is the "thin waist" of the modern transport story, the substrate on which various reliable and unreliable protocols are built. UDP itself is barely a protocol (just ports and a checksum), but its role as the unifying substrate has grown more important with QUIC. By 2030 expect: UDP for short, low-overhead exchanges (DNS, gaming, real-time media); QUIC for reliable transport (HTTP/3, gRPC); QUIC-on-UDP for VPNs (MASQUE, WireGuard's modern variants); TCP for legacy and intra-DC applications. The architecture is layered: UDP is the substrate; QUIC is one notable consumer; other UDP-based protocols continue to exist. Operationally, every network engineer needs to understand UDP, even if most user-visible traffic is QUIC. The deeper insight: in protocol design, the substrate often outlives the specific protocols built on top. UDP is now in the position TCP was: the durable lower-layer that everything else builds on.

### Chapter Summary

UDP is the minimum transport on IP: 8 bytes of header carrying ports, length, and a checksum. It adds nothing else: no reliability, no ordering, no flow or congestion control. Applications using UDP must handle these themselves. UDP is the substrate for DNS, NTP, real-time media, gaming, VPNs, and QUIC.

QUIC is the modern transport that absorbed TCP, TLS 1.3, and HTTP/2 multiplexing into a single protocol running on UDP. Its key features: 1-RTT handshake (down to 0-RTT for repeat connections), per-stream multiplexing eliminating head-of-line blocking, connection IDs enabling migration across IP changes, encryption everywhere, fast evolution because middleboxes cannot ossify it.

The 0-RTT replay-safety constraint is QUIC's canonical gotcha: 0-RTT data can be replayed by attackers, so it must only be used for idempotent operations. HTTP/3 mandates this; libraries enforce it.

Jin Park's QUIC migration from his TCP/CGNAT pain shows the protocol's real-world impact: connection migration handles CGNAT mapping changes natively, eliminating the session-drop class of bugs. Mobile users on lossy or churning networks benefit substantially.

The wire-level artifact (QUIC handshake vs TLS-over-TCP, side by side) shows the latency improvement concretely: 1 RTT saved on new connections, 2 RTTs saved on repeat connections. For typical mobile RTTs of 100ms+, this is 100-200ms of user-visible improvement per page load.

In Chapter 11 we cover congestion control in depth: CUBIC, BBR, BBRv3, and the modern fairness debate. Congestion control is where most of TCP/QUIC's intelligence lives; understanding it is essential for reasoning about performance.

## Chapter 11: Congestion Control: BBR, CUBIC, and the Modern Default

Congestion control is the part of TCP/QUIC that decides how fast to send. It is the protocol's response to a question with no easy answer: given that we cannot see other flows on the network, given that routers do not tell us their queue depths, given that loss can mean congestion or wireless interference or both, how fast should we send?

For 35 years the answer was "react to loss." When packets are lost, slow down; when ACKs flow back smoothly, speed up. This is the basic loop of TCP Reno and its descendants. CUBIC, which became the Linux default around 2008, refined the curve; CTCP (Compound TCP, briefly the Windows default) added a delay-based component; many variants tinkered with the constants. All worked with the same fundamental model: loss is the signal.

In 2016, Google researchers shipped BBR (Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time). BBR rejected the premise: it ignores loss as a congestion signal, measures the actual bottleneck bandwidth and minimum RTT, and sets the sending rate accordingly. The results were striking: on lossy wireless links, BBR could be 100x faster than CUBIC. On clean wired links, BBR delivered comparable throughput with better fairness.

This chapter develops the congestion-control story from Reno through CUBIC to BBRv3. We cover the fairness debate, bufferbloat, ECN as a hint, and the wire-level artifact of BBR vs CUBIC on a lossy link. By the end you should be able to read a congestion-control algorithm's behavior, predict its performance on a given network, and pick the right one for a given workload.

### 11.1 The Setup: Why Congestion Control Is Hard

A sender wants to send as fast as possible. The network has finite capacity. Multiple senders share the network. Each sender's behavior affects the others. None of the senders can directly observe the network's state.

The sender knows two things: (1) which packets the receiver has acknowledged, and how quickly, (2) which packets appear to have been lost or delayed. From these signals, the sender must infer the network's state and pick a sending rate. This inference problem is the heart of congestion control.

#### 11.1.1 What Congestion Control Aims For

A good congestion control algorithm should:

* **Use available capacity** : do not leave the network idle.
* **Avoid overload** : do not push the network into deep queueing or loss.
* **Be fair** : when multiple flows share a bottleneck, each should get a roughly equal share.
* **Be responsive** : react quickly to changes in network conditions.
* **Be stable** : not oscillate wildly.
* **Be deployable** : work without requiring router changes; coexist with other algorithms on the same network.

These goals trade off against each other. Aggressive use of capacity tends to push the network into queueing, hurting other flows. Conservative behavior wastes capacity. Algorithms balance these on a spectrum.

#### 11.1.2 The Bandwidth-Delay Product Revisited

We met BDP in Chapter 9: `bandwidth × RTT`. It is the amount of data "in flight" at full utilization. For a 100 Mbps link with 100 ms RTT, BDP is 1.25 MB. To use the link at full speed, the sender must have ~1.25 MB unACKed at any moment.

If the sender's window is smaller than BDP, the link is underutilized. If larger, the excess data fills router queues, increasing latency without increasing throughput. The optimum is `window = BDP`.

But the BDP is not constant. The bottleneck bandwidth varies with cross traffic. The RTT varies with queue depth at the bottleneck. The sender must track these continuously to set the right window.

### 11.2 Reno and Its Descendants

The original congestion control is TCP Tahoe (1988); the standard reference is TCP Reno (1990). The basic idea: cwnd grows on each ACK, shrinks on loss. Specifically:

**Slow start** : cwnd doubles each RTT (covered in Chapter 9). Continues until `cwnd = ssthresh` or a loss is detected.

**Congestion avoidance** : cwnd grows by 1 MSS per RTT (additive increase). Continues until loss.

**On loss (3 duplicate ACKs)** : `ssthresh = cwnd / 2`; `cwnd = ssthresh` (or some variation); enter fast recovery.

**On loss (timeout)** : `ssthresh = cwnd / 2`; `cwnd = 1 MSS`; restart slow start.

The fundamental rule is _additive increase, multiplicative decrease_ (AIMD): grow slowly, cut aggressively. This gives long-term fairness across flows sharing a bottleneck: each flow probes for capacity, retreats on contention, and the aggregate behavior is steady.

Reno works. It is conservative. It assumes loss is congestion, which is true on wired backbones and increasingly false on wireless edges.

#### 11.2.1 NewReno

NewReno (RFC 3782) fixes a Reno bug: after a fast retransmit, Reno would exit fast recovery as soon as the retransmitted packet was ACKed, but if there were multiple losses in the same window, only one would be retransmitted, leading to slow recovery. NewReno stays in fast recovery until all losses in the window are recovered.

NewReno was the standard for years and is still the textbook congestion control. Most modern variants are extensions or replacements.

#### 11.2.2 CUBIC

CUBIC, introduced by Ha, Rhee, and Xu in 2008, was designed for high-bandwidth long-RTT links where Reno is too slow to ramp back up after loss. Instead of linear growth in congestion avoidance, CUBIC grows the window as a _cubic_ function of time since the last loss:
    
    
    W(t) = C * (t - K)^3 + W_max
    

where `W_max` is the window before the last loss, `K = (W_max * (1-beta) / C)^(1/3)`, `beta = 0.7` (the multiplicative decrease factor), and `C = 0.4` is a constant.

The cubic shape: when far from the last loss point (small `t`), the function rises slowly (concave). When near `W_max`, it rises fast. Beyond `W_max`, it accelerates (convex). The intuition is that CUBIC probes carefully around the previous "good" window, then aggressively probes higher if nothing breaks.

CUBIC has been the Linux default since around 2008. On wired networks with moderate loss, it works well: faster recovery than Reno, similar fairness, RTT-fairness (flows with different RTTs get similar throughput, which Reno does not provide).

CUBIC's weakness: like Reno, it uses loss as the congestion signal. On wireless links with intrinsic loss (Wi-Fi fading, cellular radio events), CUBIC interprets random loss as congestion and backs off, wasting capacity.

### 11.3 BBR: A Different Model

BBR, developed by Cardwell, Yeganeh, Jacobson, and colleagues at Google in 2016, takes a different approach: ignore loss entirely as a congestion signal. Instead, measure two things:

* **BtlBw** (bottleneck bandwidth): the maximum rate at which the network is delivering ACKs, observed over a recent window.
* **RTprop** (minimum RTT): the minimum round-trip time observed, taken as the network's intrinsic propagation delay.

The optimal sending rate, by BBR's model, is `BtlBw` packets per second. The optimal congestion window is `BtlBw × RTprop` (the BDP). BBR sets cwnd to this value.

When the network's behavior changes (bandwidth drops, RTT shifts), BBR re-measures and adapts.

#### 11.3.1 The State Machine

BBR cycles through states:

* **Startup** : Like slow start, ramp cwnd quickly. Continue until BtlBw stops increasing.
* **Drain** : Briefly reduce cwnd to drain any queue built up during startup.
* **ProbeBW** : The steady state. cwnd is roughly BDP; cycle the pacing rate above and below BtlBw to probe for additional bandwidth.
* **ProbeRTT** : Periodically (every 10 seconds), shrink cwnd to 4 MSS for 200 ms to re-measure RTprop (which can drift over time as queues build).

The pacing rate (not just cwnd) is the key control variable. BBR explicitly paces packets to avoid burstiness: if `BtlBw = 100 Mbps`, BBR sends packets at exactly 100 Mbps spaced evenly, not bursts of 50 packets followed by silence.

#### 11.3.2 Why BBR Is Faster on Lossy Links

CUBIC sees a 1% loss rate as "the network is congested"; it cuts cwnd in half repeatedly, never reaching high throughput. BBR sees the same 1% loss and ignores it (as long as the measured BtlBw is stable); throughput stays at line rate.

Concrete example: a 100 Mbps link with 0.5% random loss and 100 ms RTT. The Mathis approximation for AIMD-family throughput, `BW ≈ (MSS / RTT) × C / √loss` (with `C ≈ 1.22` for the standard derivation), gives roughly `(1460 B / 0.1 s) × 1.22 / √0.005 ≈ 2 Mbps` for CUBIC under these parameters. CUBIC measured in practice is somewhat higher than the Mathis floor (CUBIC's window-growth curve is more aggressive than Reno-AIMD) but still single-digit Mbps. BBR's throughput on the same link is roughly 80–95 Mbps (close to line rate, limited only by ProbeRTT phases). The qualitative story — _BBR is 10× or more faster than CUBIC on lossy paths_ — is what matters; the Mathis formula gives the bound, not a number you should report as the predicted CUBIC rate.

On wireless networks where loss is bursty, the gap can be larger. Cellular networks with 2-5% packet loss bursts: CUBIC stalls at single-digit Mbps; BBR stays in the tens to low hundreds.

#### 11.3.3 BBR's Fairness Issues

The original BBR had a fairness problem: in a network shared between BBR and CUBIC flows, BBR could starve CUBIC because BBR ignores loss while CUBIC backs off. The CUBIC flow sees more loss (because BBR is filling queues without backing off), backs off more, while BBR happily continues at high rate.

This was the main critique of BBR for several years. BBRv2 (2019) addressed it by adding some loss responsiveness; BBRv3 (2023) refined further. The 2026 BBRv3 is generally considered fairness-acceptable, though some edge cases remain.

#### 11.3.4 BBR Adoption

Adoption status as of 2026:

* **Google** : BBR (now BBRv3) is the default on all Google services, internal and external.
* **YouTube, Google Cloud** : BBRv3.
* **Linux kernel** : BBR is available; BBRv3 is the modern default on many distributions. CUBIC remains the kernel default (for compatibility) but is often overridden by application configuration.
* **CDN edge** : Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly all use BBR-family algorithms for high-throughput delivery.
* **QUIC implementations** : BBR is the default in most modern QUIC libraries (Cloudflare's quiche, Google's gQUIC, the IETF reference quicly).
* **Windows** : CTCP and CUBIC; BBR not deployed as default but available in some environments.

The trajectory: BBRv3 is becoming the de facto default for high-throughput TCP and QUIC flows. CUBIC remains in widespread use but is being displaced.

### 11.4 ECN: Routers Can Hint

Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN, RFC 3168) is a mechanism for routers to mark packets when their queues fill, instead of dropping them. The sender, seeing the mark, knows congestion is starting and can back off without waiting for actual loss.

ECN uses two bits in the IP header (originally the unused DS field bits). A router with a filling queue sets the "Congestion Experienced" bit on a packet rather than dropping it. The receiver, on seeing CE, echoes it back to the sender via ACKs. The sender treats this as if it saw a single packet loss.

#### 11.4.1 ECN Adoption

ECN deployment has been long and rocky. Early NICs and middleboxes corrupted the ECN bits, causing problems for endpoints that enabled it. The IETF spent years pushing for clean ECN handling.

As of 2026, ECN is widely supported but inconsistently used. Linux supports ECN by default for incoming connections. Major CDNs use it for their network. The benefit is modest under normal conditions but significant in data center networks where ECN combined with active queue management (CoDel, fq_codel) keeps queues small.

#### 11.4.2 L4S: Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable Throughput

L4S (RFC 9330+, ratified 2023) is the modern evolution of ECN. The idea: a separate ECN codepoint indicates "this flow uses scalable congestion control" (algorithms designed to react to fine-grained ECN signals rather than coarse loss signals). L4S-capable routers can mark these flows aggressively, getting them out of the way of non-L4S traffic.

The result: L4S flows can have very low queuing delay (sub-millisecond at the bottleneck) without sacrificing throughput. This is the "ultra-low-latency" path for video calls, gaming, real-time control.

L4S deployment is early in 2026: Apple's networking stack, some Comcast equipment, some CDN edges. Wide deployment expected 2027-2029.

### 11.5 Bufferbloat: The Cost of Big Queues

A separate but related issue: many routers and modems have very large queues (megabytes of buffer per port). Under load, these queues fill, adding tens of seconds of latency to all flows passing through. This is _bufferbloat_ (Jim Gettys, 2010+).

The mechanism: traditional TCP fills the queue until loss occurs (because queue depth doesn't slow throughput at all, only adds latency). Once the queue is full, loss happens, TCP backs off, the queue drains slightly, TCP probes again. The queue stays at the "loss-induced" depth, which on a deep-buffer device can be seconds of latency.

Solutions:

* **Active Queue Management (AQM)** : routers proactively drop packets when queues exceed a threshold (RED, CoDel, fq_codel). This signals TCP to back off before the queue is excessive.
* **Smarter congestion control** : BBR, by setting cwnd at BDP rather than filling queues, keeps queues minimal.
* **ECN/L4S** : routers signal congestion before dropping.
* **Bufferbloat-aware OS settings** : ensure your local NIC and home router enable fq_codel.

The 2026 reality: bufferbloat is largely solved at the algorithmic level, but it persists in deployments where ISPs have not enabled AQM or where consumer-grade routers ship without it. Tests like dslreports.com's bufferbloat test reveal which connections still suffer.

### 11.6 Multipath Congestion Control

When a connection uses multiple paths (Multipath TCP, MP-QUIC, or just an application that spreads load across connections), the congestion control must coordinate. Should each subflow run independently? Should they share a single control loop?

The MP-TCP standard (RFC 6182) proposed _coupled congestion control_ : subflows share an aggregate cwnd, divided across paths in proportion to each path's apparent capacity. This ensures the multipath flow is no more aggressive than the most aggressive single-path flow on each path.

In 2026, multipath congestion control is in production at Apple (Multipath TCP for Siri, FaceTime, and Maps), at carriers (5G+Wi-Fi handover), and in research deployments of MP-QUIC. The complexity has limited wider adoption.

### 11.7 The Wire-Level Artifact: BBR vs CUBIC on a Lossy Link

The classic experiment: take a 100 Mbps link, induce 1% random packet loss with `tc netem` on Linux, run a single TCP flow under CUBIC then BBR, measure throughput.
    
    
    # Setup
    sudo tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem loss 1% delay 100ms
    
    # Run CUBIC
    sudo sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=cubic
    iperf3 -c <server> -t 60
    
    # Run BBR
    sudo sysctl net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control=bbr
    iperf3 -c <server> -t 60
    

Typical results:

* CUBIC throughput: 8-15 Mbps (about 10-15% of link capacity, dominated by loss-recovery cycles).
* BBR throughput: 80-95 Mbps (about 80-95% of link capacity, ignoring most loss as non-congestion).

Plotting cwnd over time:

* CUBIC: sawtooth pattern, ramping up to ~100–200 KB then crashing on each loss event, repeating. The cwnd never reaches BDP (1.25 MB) because loss intervenes well before.
* BBR: ignores most loss as non-congestion; its bandwidth probe converges on the link rate; its cwnd grows toward the BBR cwnd_gain × BDP target and sits near BDP in steady state. The **pacing rate** is the variable that actually controls send rate under BBR (cwnd is a safety cap above pacing), so the canonical BBR signature is `pacing_rate ≈ link rate` and `cwnd ≈ BDP`.

Looking at `ss -i` during the run:
    
    
    ESTAB 0 0 ...
        bbr wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:101/2.1 mss:1460 pacing_rate:96Mbps delivery_rate:95Mbps cwnd:850
    

The `pacing_rate` (~96 Mbps) and `delivery_rate` (~95 Mbps) are nearly equal: BBR is delivering at near line rate. `cwnd:850` segments × 1460 bytes ≈ 1.24 MB ≈ the 1.25 MB BDP for this 100 Mbps × 100 ms path — BBR has discovered the BDP and is pacing into it. Two pedagogical points here: (i) pacing, not cwnd, is BBR's primary send-rate control — cwnd would have to drop _below_ `pacing_rate × RTT` to start limiting, and on this path it does not; (ii) BBR's cwnd sits near BDP in steady-state ProbeBW, which is the opposite of CUBIC's behavior on the same path.
    
    
    ESTAB 0 0 ...
        cubic wscale:7,7 rto:204 rtt:101/2.1 mss:1460 cwnd:35 ssthresh:35 bytes_sent:9100000 bytes_retrans:91000
    

cwnd of 35 segments (~51 KB) means CUBIC is operating well below BDP; retrans rate is ~1% as expected.

The contrast is the canonical demonstration of why BBR matters. Run this experiment once; it changes how you think about congestion control.

### 11.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is the fundamental difference between Reno-family congestion control (Reno, NewReno, CUBIC) and BBR?

Hint

What signal does each use to detect congestion?

**Answer:** _Reno-family algorithms_ (Reno, NewReno, CUBIC, and many minor variants) use _packet loss_ as the primary congestion signal. The basic loop: when packets are lost, the network is interpreted as congested, and cwnd is reduced (multiplicative decrease). When ACKs flow without loss, cwnd grows (additive or polynomial increase). The implicit assumption is that loss is caused by queueing at congested routers; on networks where loss has other causes (wireless interference, intermittent link errors), Reno-family algorithms misinterpret these as congestion and back off unnecessarily. _BBR_ uses _bandwidth and delay measurements_ as congestion signals. It estimates the bottleneck bandwidth (BtlBw) from the maximum recent ACK rate and the minimum round-trip propagation delay (RTprop) from the minimum recent RTT. The product BtlBw × RTprop is the bandwidth-delay product (BDP); BBR sets cwnd to this value, so it sends exactly the right amount of data to keep the bottleneck full without filling any queue. BBR ignores most loss as a congestion signal, treating moderate loss as expected network noise rather than as a signal to back off. The practical difference: on lossy links (wireless, cellular, lossy WAN), BBR can be 5x to 100x faster than CUBIC because CUBIC interprets the loss as congestion and never gets up to speed. On clean wired links, both perform similarly, with BBR's advantage shrinking. The cost of BBR: harder to share fairly with CUBIC flows (because BBR doesn't back off in response to the loss that CUBIC induces); this fairness issue was the chief criticism of BBR v1 and has been partly addressed in BBR v2 and v3.

**Q2.** Why is the slow-start algorithm called "slow start" when its growth is exponential?

Hint

The name is historical; what was "slow" about it relative to alternatives?

**Answer:** The slow-start algorithm grows cwnd exponentially: each round trip approximately doubles cwnd. By any modern measure, this is fast growth. The name "slow start" is historical: when Van Jacobson introduced the algorithm in 1988, the alternative was to send at full speed from the first packet (which routinely caused network collapse on the early internet). Slow start was "slow" by comparison to that alternative. The algorithm's exponential growth is the right shape for an unknown network: it doubles each RTT, so the time to ramp from 10 MSS (initial window) to 1 MB is roughly 7 RTTs, which is acceptable for connections that will transfer more than a few hundred KB. For short transfers (10 KB or less), the entire transfer fits in the initial window, and slow start does not significantly impact total time. The name persists because the protocol-design community has used it for 35 years; renaming would create confusion. The phrase "slow start" should be read as "the careful, ramping start to a TCP connection," not as "a slow algorithm."

**Q3.** What is bufferbloat, and what are three mechanisms for addressing it?

Hint

Big queues at routers add latency without adding throughput.

**Answer:** Bufferbloat is the phenomenon of large router queue depths causing high latency under load. Traditional routers and modems often have megabytes of buffer per port. When a TCP flow (with loss-based congestion control like Reno or CUBIC) fills the bottleneck link, it pushes data into the queue, which grows because cwnd keeps increasing (no loss yet). The queue depth on a deep-buffer device can reach seconds of latency. Eventually loss occurs and TCP backs off, but the queue remains at the loss-induced depth, adding tens to thousands of milliseconds of unnecessary latency to every flow passing through. Three mechanisms to address bufferbloat: (1) _Active Queue Management (AQM)_ : algorithms like RED, CoDel, fq_codel proactively drop packets when queues exceed a target depth, signaling TCP to back off before the queue is bloated. CoDel and fq_codel use sojourn time (how long packets sit in the queue) as the metric rather than queue size, making them robust to varying packet sizes. fq_codel is now the default qdisc on most Linux distributions. (2) _Smarter congestion control_ : BBR (and BBR v3) sets cwnd at BDP rather than filling queues, keeping the queue depth minimal regardless of router behavior. As BBR adoption grows, the source-side mitigation reduces the impact of deep buffers. (3) _ECN and L4S_ : routers mark packets (rather than drop) when queues build, and scalable congestion control (L4S) reacts to fine-grained marking signals to keep queues very shallow. L4S is the modern path forward for ultra-low-latency traffic alongside elastic traffic. The 2026 reality is mixed: AQM is widely deployed in modern routers and modems but absent in some consumer-grade equipment; BBR is increasingly adopted at content providers; L4S is in early production. Bufferbloat is no longer a universal problem but persists in pockets.

**Q4.** What is ECN, and how does it differ from packet drops as a congestion signal?

Hint

A router can do something other than dropping a packet under congestion.

**Answer:** ECN (RFC 3168) is a mechanism where routers under congestion can mark packets rather than dropping them. The IP header has 2 bits for ECN signaling: the sender sets the codepoint to "ECN-capable transport" (10 or 01), the router under congestion can set "Congestion Experienced" (11) instead of dropping the packet, and the receiver echoes the CE bit back to the sender via the ACK. The sender treats this as if a single packet had been lost: it reduces cwnd. Differences from packet drops: (1) _No data is lost_ : the packet arrives at the receiver as normal; no retransmission is needed. The throughput cost of the congestion signal is zero (for this packet). (2) _Earlier signal_ : routers can mark before queue is full, giving senders earlier warning. (3) _Fine-grained signaling_ : instead of binary loss/no-loss, ECN can convey "this much congestion" via marking density. L4S extends this with "L4S-capable" codepoints, allowing routers to mark aggressively for L4S flows without affecting non-L4S flows. (4) _Receive-side requires no retransmission_ : classic loss means TCP must retransmit; ECN means TCP just slows down. The benefit: lower retransmission load on the network, faster recovery. The drawback: requires support from sender, receiver, and intermediate routers; historically, NICs and middleboxes corrupted the ECN bits, making the deployment rocky. As of 2026, ECN is widely supported but its benefits are modest under typical conditions; L4S, which builds on ECN, is the modern direction for low-latency networking.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A cloud provider sees that connections from cellular phones to their service are slow (around 5 Mbps) despite the phone reporting 100 Mbps cellular signal. Single-flow transfers from the cloud to the phone are slow; speed tests with parallel connections show 80 Mbps. Diagnose.

Hint

Single flow vs parallel; cellular has loss; what congestion control is in use?

**Answer:** The diagnosis is classic CUBIC-on-lossy-cellular. Cellular networks have non-trivial packet loss (1-3% routine; 5-10% during fades and handoffs) and high RTTs (50-150 ms). A single CUBIC TCP flow experiences this loss as congestion, backs off, and operates at a small fraction of capacity. The Mathis bound: with 1% loss and 100 ms RTT, AIMD throughput is approximately `(MSS / RTT) × 1.22 / √loss ≈ (1460 / 0.1) × 12.2 ≈ 178 KB/s ≈ 1.4 Mbps`. CUBIC's window-growth curve runs somewhat hotter than pure AIMD-Reno, so the measured single-flow rate is typically in the low-single-digit Mbps range; under 3% loss it falls to well below 1 Mbps. The phone's reported 100 Mbps signal is the radio's theoretical capacity, not what any individual TCP flow can achieve. Speed tests with parallel connections get 80 Mbps because each of 10 flows gets ~8 Mbps; aggregated, that is close to link capacity. Fix: switch the server's congestion control to BBR (or BBRv3). On the cloud provider's servers, change `net.ipv4.tcp_congestion_control` to `bbr`. Single-flow performance should improve to 70-90 Mbps on cellular links. The improvement comes from BBR ignoring the random radio loss as a congestion signal, maintaining cwnd at the BDP rather than backing off repeatedly. Alternatively, the cloud provider can migrate to HTTP/3/QUIC, which typically uses BBR-family congestion control by default. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to diagnose this; watch for Lie #6 (suggesting tuning TCP buffer sizes or initial cwnd without addressing the underlying congestion-control issue; these are downstream effects of the wrong algorithm choice).

**Q2.** A network team is rolling out BBR on production servers. Within a week they get reports that some flows have become slower. Investigation shows the slow flows are CUBIC clients on the same network. Explain the dynamics.

Hint

BBR vs CUBIC fairness.

**Answer:** This is BBR v1's classic fairness problem. When BBR and CUBIC share a bottleneck link: (1) BBR sets cwnd at the BDP and sends at the measured bandwidth, ignoring loss. (2) Because BBR doesn't back off, the bottleneck queue stays at depth (BBR fills the queue with its share). (3) CUBIC sees the queue-induced packet loss and backs off (it interprets loss as congestion). (4) BBR's share of the bottleneck stays high; CUBIC's share shrinks. (5) Over time, BBR consumes more and more of the bandwidth at CUBIC's expense. The asymmetry is structural: BBR's mental model of the network does not include "share fairly with loss-based flows"; it just sends at the measured bandwidth. Solutions: (1) Upgrade to BBRv2 or BBRv3, which add some loss responsiveness and have been shown to be much fairer with CUBIC (though not perfectly fair). (2) Continue running BBR but monitor the share of CUBIC vs BBR traffic; if most traffic is BBR (server-side BBR rollout reaches majority), the fairness issue diminishes. (3) Use per-flow queueing at the bottleneck (fq_codel) to isolate each flow's queue, eliminating the fairness asymmetry at the queue. The 2026 trajectory: BBRv3 is much better than BBRv1 in fairness, and per-flow queueing at modern routers is standard, so the original concern is much reduced. But a network with both BBR and CUBIC flows will still observe some asymmetry. The fix is universal BBR or universal CUBIC; mixed populations are intermediate. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to recommend a congestion-control strategy; watch for Lie #4 (recommending BBR v1 without realizing the fairness issues, or recommending a "magic" combination that doesn't exist).

**Q3.** A startup is building a real-time video conferencing app. They are deciding between TCP (with HTTP/2) and UDP (with their own application-layer reliability or with QUIC). Argue for one architecture over the other, considering congestion control specifically.

Hint

Video traffic has specific congestion-control needs.

**Answer:** UDP with application-layer reliability (or QUIC with congestion control) is the better choice for real-time video. Reasons related to congestion control: (1) _TCP's congestion control is wrong for real-time media_ : when packets are lost, TCP retransmits and backs off. For real-time video, lost packets are too late by the time they retransmit; the video frame they belong to has already been displayed (or skipped). The right behavior is "skip the lost packet, keep going, request a key frame if needed." UDP enables this; TCP forces retransmission. (2) _Head-of-line blocking_ : TCP delivers an ordered byte stream. A single lost packet stalls the receiver waiting for retransmission, then all subsequent video frames are delayed. UDP delivers packets independently; a single loss only affects its own frame. (3) _Application-level rate adaptation_ : real-time video should adapt sending rate based on observed loss and delay, with the rate measured in units relevant to video (key frame rate, resolution, bitrate). TCP's rate adaptation is opaque to the application; the app cannot easily say "if loss is high, switch to lower resolution." UDP with application-level congestion control gives the application this control. (4) _Pacing_ : video sends frames at fixed intervals (30-60 fps). TCP's burstiness can disrupt frame timing. UDP with application-controlled pacing maintains smooth delivery. (5) _Multiplexing audio and video_ : typically you want separate flows for audio and video so that video congestion doesn't block audio. UDP makes this natural; TCP forces a single byte stream. _Recommended architecture_ : WebRTC (which uses RTP over UDP with DTLS-SRTP encryption) for the media path. The application uses Google's Congestion Control (GCC, designed specifically for real-time media) or a similar algorithm. Signaling and metadata can use TCP (or WebSocket over TCP). The architecture mirrors what Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, FaceTime all use: media on UDP/RTP, signaling on TCP. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design this; watch for Lie #1 (using TCP throughout because it is "more reliable," which actively hurts real-time media quality) and Lie #5 (using a small connection pool for both media and signaling without separating them).

**Q4.** A backbone link in a Tier 1 ISP has 100 Gbps capacity and is observed to have brief periods of 99.9% utilization with very low loss. Argue whether the ISP should enable ECN/L4S on this link, and what they would need to deploy.

Hint

Big queues develop at near-capacity utilization; what does ECN buy?

**Answer:** _Yes, enabling ECN/L4S would be beneficial on this link, with caveats_. Reasoning: at 99.9% utilization, the bottleneck is the link itself. Loss-based congestion control (CUBIC and to a lesser extent BBR) will only react when actual loss occurs, which means queues at the router will swell (queueing delay rising into seconds in the worst case). This is bufferbloat at backbone scale, causing latency spikes for all flows passing through, even ones that have nothing to do with the congestion. ECN allows the router to signal congestion early (when queue depth exceeds a target, perhaps 1 MB), before loss occurs. TCP flows seeing the CE bit back off without retransmitting. The queue stays shallow; latency stays low; throughput stays at near-capacity. L4S takes this further: special low-latency flows (video calls, gaming, real-time control) are marked aggressively while elastic flows (bulk file transfer) get the normal ECN signal. The low-latency flows experience sub-millisecond queueing; elastic flows still get full bandwidth. _What to deploy_ : (1) Active queue management on the bottleneck router: modern Tier 1 routers — Cisco NCS, Juniper PTX, Arista 7800 — all support fq_codel or PIE. (2) ECN-capable forwarding: enable the codepoint setting in the AQM. (3) For L4S: separate AQM with separate codepoints for L4S-marked traffic. Requires newer hardware/software at the routers. (4) Cooperation from endpoints: ECN works only if both endpoints support it (most modern OSes do); L4S requires endpoints to use scalable congestion control (early support in Apple's networking, some Google Cloud, BBRv3 with L4S extensions). _Caveats_ : (1) Mixed deployment problem: some flows ECN-aware, some not. The non-aware flows still see loss and back off; the ECN-aware flows benefit. This is mostly fine in the steady state. (2) Operations complexity: another knob to monitor and tune. (3) Diagnostic challenges: ECN signaling is in the IP header; standard tools support it but historical training has assumed loss-only signaling. The recommendation: enable ECN on the link; enable L4S after deployment matures and Apple/Google clients are confirmed in the user mix. Expected outcome: latency spikes during near-capacity periods drop substantially; user-visible improvement is noticeable. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to plan this; watch for Lie #4 (suggesting only ECN without mentioning L4S as the modern direction, or suggesting a configuration that mixes ECN codepoints in ways that confuse middleboxes).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Argue (a) why BBR has come to dominate at content providers, (b) why CUBIC persists as the kernel default, (c) what the kernel-default trajectory will look like over the next 5 years.

**Discussion:** (a) BBR dominates at content providers because content providers see the per-flow latency cost of CUBIC's loss-based backoff. A CDN edge or a streaming origin sees flows to mobile and lossy clients that under CUBIC achieve 5-15% of available bandwidth; under BBR they achieve 70-95%. The difference is direct user-perceived improvement (faster video starts, fewer rebuffering events, faster page loads on mobile). Google, Facebook, Cloudflare, Akamai, Fastly, Amazon, Microsoft—every major content provider deployed BBR at scale by 2020. The case is closed for content. (b) CUBIC persists as the kernel default because: (i) Linux upstream is conservative; switching the default affects every system; (ii) CUBIC works fine in many environments (clean wired networks, intra-data-center traffic); (iii) BBR's fairness story has been controversial through BBRv1, only really resolved in BBRv3; (iv) backward compatibility: applications that relied on specific CUBIC behaviors (timing characteristics, RTT-fairness) would need to be re-validated. The system administrator can always set BBR per-server; many do. The default is the conservative choice. (c) Over the next 5 years: (i) BBRv3 will become widely available and tested; (ii) Linux distributions will likely make BBRv3 the default for some workloads (server distributions ahead of desktop); (iii) cloud providers may set BBR-family defaults at the VM image level; (iv) per-workload congestion control becomes more common (different cwnd-management for different applications via socket options or eBPF). The kernel default in 2031 may still be CUBIC out of upstream conservatism, but the practical default in production environments will be BBRv3-family. This pattern mirrors many infrastructure trends: the upstream default lags the production reality by several years; both eventually converge.

**Q2.** Reflect on whether congestion control is fundamentally an "endpoint" or "network" responsibility. Should routers play a more active role, or should endpoints continue to be the locus of intelligence?

**Discussion:** The end-to-end principle from Chapter 1 says intelligence belongs at endpoints. Congestion control has historically followed this principle: TCP runs on the endpoints; routers do not participate beyond dropping packets and (recently) marking with ECN. This has worked well for several reasons: (i) endpoints know what they want to send and can prioritize within a flow; (ii) the network has no idea how applications value their packets; (iii) the network can stay simple and stateless. But: (i) endpoints lack global visibility (they cannot see other flows); (ii) loss as a congestion signal is noisy; (iii) the "fairness" notion among flows is hard to enforce when each endpoint makes its own choices. The router-based alternative: routers explicitly schedule flows, enforce fairness, signal precise congestion state to endpoints.
