This has been proposed for decades (RED, ARED, FQ-CoDel, Network Service Mapping) and partly deployed. The synthesis: the modern model is hybrid. Routers do AQM (CoDel, fq_codel) to manage queues; signal congestion via ECN/L4S; rate-limit when needed. Endpoints respond with their own congestion control (CUBIC, BBR, scalable variants), choosing rate within the framework. Neither side has full control; both contribute. Future directions: more router-side intelligence (per-flow visibility, application-aware QoS at hyperscaler edges); also more endpoint-side intelligence (better measurement of RTT, BBR-like models, application-aware sending). The end-to-end principle holds in spirit (the application's intent lives at the endpoint) but the network plays a role too (early signals, fairness, queue management). By 2030 expect: more L4S deployment; more BBRv3 adoption; selective use of router-side rate limiting in some contexts. The pure end-to-end model and the pure network-managed model both lose to the practical hybrid.

**Q3.** Consider a future where machine-learning-based congestion control becomes feasible. Each flow's congestion control adapts in real time using a model of network behavior, possibly trained on the flow's own observation history. Argue whether this is a good idea and what could go wrong.

**Discussion:** ML-based congestion control is an active research area (Remy, PCC, several DRL variants) and has the potential to outperform hand-tuned algorithms on specific workloads. The benefits: an ML-trained CC could adapt to the specific network conditions of each user (mobile in a specific carrier, residential cable in a specific ISP, etc.) and learn the optimal sending rate without hand-coded thresholds. Potential problems: (1) _Adversarial dynamics_ : when many flows all run ML-based CC, they may converge to behaviors that are individually optimal but collectively bad (a tragedy-of-the-commons in bandwidth). Hand-designed algorithms are designed for the multi-flow case; ML-trained ones are typically trained on single-flow benchmarks. (2) _Distribution shift_ : training on one network environment, deploying on another, may produce wrong behavior. Mobile networks change over time; ML models trained yesterday may be wrong tomorrow. (3) _Lack of safety margins_ : hand-designed algorithms have provable properties (eventual convergence to capacity, fairness in the limit). ML-trained ones often do not, and may behave catastrophically in edge cases. (4) _Operational complexity_ : every flow now has model state; debugging becomes harder; updating the model requires retraining and redeploying. (5) _Regulatory/operational pressure_ : ISPs and content providers may resist deployment of ML-CC that they cannot audit. The realistic path: ML-CC will be useful in specific environments where the network's behavior is well-characterized (data center, specific carrier+region pairs) and where the operator owns both endpoints and intermediate links. ML-CC for general internet traffic is harder and probably 10+ years from production. Probably wrong to bet against it long-term; probably wrong to bet on it being the default by 2030.

### Chapter Summary

Congestion control is the hardest problem in transport protocol design: senders cannot directly see network state and must infer it from indirect signals. Reno-family algorithms (Reno, NewReno, CUBIC) use loss as the signal; AIMD (additive increase, multiplicative decrease) gives long-term fairness but underperforms on lossy links. BBR uses bandwidth and delay measurements directly, ignoring most loss; performance on lossy links is dramatically better, but fairness with CUBIC was a problem in v1 and is much improved in BBRv3.

ECN and the modern L4S extension let routers signal congestion explicitly, avoiding the loss-based feedback loop and enabling sub-millisecond queueing delays for latency-sensitive flows. Bufferbloat (deep router queues causing high latency under load) is largely addressed by AQM (CoDel, fq_codel), BBR's cwnd-at-BDP approach, and L4S deployments.

The wire-level artifact (BBR vs CUBIC on a 100 Mbps lossy link) is the canonical hands-on experiment. Running it once changes how you think about TCP performance.

The 2026 landscape: CUBIC is the kernel default and remains widely deployed; BBR (now BBRv3) is the de facto default at content providers and increasingly in QUIC stacks; L4S is emerging at the latency-sensitive edge. The trajectory points to BBR-family algorithms becoming dominant for high-throughput traffic and L4S becoming dominant for ultra-low-latency traffic over the next 5 years.

In Chapter 12 we step from the protocol's internals to the application-facing interface: the socket API. BSD sockets, epoll, kqueue, io_uring, AF_XDP. The socket API is how every application uses transport, and the modern alternatives (io_uring especially) are essential for high-throughput applications.

---

## Chapter 12: The Socket API and Modern Alternatives

We have spent the last three chapters on the transport protocols: TCP, UDP, QUIC, and how congestion control shapes their behavior. This chapter looks at the interface through which applications use them. The BSD socket API is the universal abstraction; `epoll` and `kqueue` and IOCP are the platform-specific event-notification primitives; `io_uring` is the modern Linux fast path; AF_XDP is the kernel-bypass alternative.

Why care? Because the choice of API has enormous performance implications. A traditional thread-per-connection server tops out at a few thousand connections. An epoll-based server handles 100,000 easily. An io_uring-based server can push a million. The protocol's wire performance is the same; the API's overhead is what changes.

This chapter walks the API stack from BSD sockets to the modern alternatives. We will see why `epoll` matters, why edge-triggered vs level-triggered semantics confuse people, what `io_uring` does that `epoll` cannot, where AF_XDP fits, and where the popular frameworks (libuv, Tokio, async-std, Go's netpoller) sit on this map. The wire-level artifact is a 50-line `io_uring`-based echo server compared to its `epoll` equivalent, with `strace` traces side by side.

By the end you should be able to look at any networking code and identify which API layer it sits on, predict its scaling profile, and reason about whether moving to a different API would help.

### 12.1 BSD Sockets: The Universal Foundation

The BSD socket API was introduced in 4.2BSD Unix in 1983. Forty years later it is still the universal abstraction for network programming. Every modern OS implements it. Every language has bindings to it. Every textbook teaches it.

The core primitives:
    
    
    int socket(int domain, int type, int protocol);
    int bind(int sockfd, const struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t addrlen);
    int listen(int sockfd, int backlog);
    int accept(int sockfd, struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t *addrlen);
    int connect(int sockfd, const struct sockaddr *addr, socklen_t addrlen);
    ssize_t send(int sockfd, const void *buf, size_t len, int flags);
    ssize_t recv(int sockfd, void *buf, size_t len, int flags);
    int close(int fd);
    

A typical TCP server:
    
    
    int sock = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    struct sockaddr_in addr = { ... };
    bind(sock, (struct sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr));
    listen(sock, 128);
    while (1) {
        int client = accept(sock, NULL, NULL);
        handle_client(client);  // probably in a new thread
        close(client);
    }
    

This works. It is simple. It scales to a few thousand connections if you use a thread per connection. It does not scale to a million.

#### 12.1.1 The Blocking-Call Problem

The basic socket API is _blocking_ : `accept()` blocks until a connection arrives; `recv()` blocks until data is available. If you have one thread, you can only handle one connection at a time.

Two approaches scale beyond one connection:

**Thread per connection** : spawn a new thread for each accepted connection. Each thread blocks on its own `recv()`. The kernel scheduler multiplexes threads onto CPU cores. Scales to a few thousand connections (limited by thread stack memory, kernel scheduling overhead, and per-thread CPU cost).

**Event-driven (single-threaded)** : use a non-blocking socket and a notification API (`select`, `poll`, `epoll`, `kqueue`, IOCP) to learn which sockets are ready. The single thread handles many sockets, processing each as it becomes ready. Scales to hundreds of thousands of connections on a single core.

Modern high-performance networking uses event-driven I/O, often with one event loop per CPU core and worker threads for CPU-intensive work.

#### 12.1.2 Non-Blocking Sockets

Setting a socket to non-blocking mode:
    
    
    int flags = fcntl(sock, F_GETFL, 0);
    fcntl(sock, F_SETFL, flags | O_NONBLOCK);
    

After this, `recv()` returns immediately even if no data is available: it returns -1 with `errno = EAGAIN` or `EWOULDBLOCK`. The application can poll, or use an event notification API.

### 12.2 select, poll, epoll, kqueue, IOCP

The classical event-notification APIs have evolved over decades.

#### 12.2.1 select (1983)

The original. `select()` takes three fd sets (read, write, exception), plus a timeout, and blocks until any fd is ready:
    
    
    fd_set readfds;
    FD_ZERO(&readfds);
    FD_SET(sock, &readfds);
    select(sock + 1, &readfds, NULL, NULL, NULL);
    if (FD_ISSET(sock, &readfds)) {
        recv(sock, buf, sizeof(buf), 0);
    }
    

Limitations:

* `fd_set` is typically 1024 fds (FD_SETSIZE). Larger sets require recompilation.
* The kernel scans the entire fd set on each call: O(N).
* The user must reset the fd_set before each `select()` call.

`select` survives for compatibility and for small fd counts. New code should not use it.

#### 12.2.2 poll (1986)

A small improvement: `poll()` takes an array of `pollfd` structs, each with an fd and events of interest. No fixed limit on fd count.
    
    
    struct pollfd fds[2];
    fds[0].fd = sock; fds[0].events = POLLIN;
    fds[1].fd = client; fds[1].events = POLLIN;
    poll(fds, 2, -1);
    

Still O(N) on the kernel side. Better than select but not by much.

#### 12.2.3 epoll — Linux 2002

Linux's scalable event notification. The kernel maintains a per-process set of "interest" (which fds are being watched, for which events). The application registers fds once, then calls `epoll_wait()` to get a list of ready fds. The kernel returns only the ready ones, not the entire set.
    
    
    int epfd = epoll_create1(0);
    struct epoll_event ev = { .events = EPOLLIN, .data.fd = sock };
    epoll_ctl(epfd, EPOLL_CTL_ADD, sock, &ev);
    
    while (1) {
        struct epoll_event events[64];
        int n = epoll_wait(epfd, events, 64, -1);
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            int fd = events[i].data.fd;
            handle_io(fd);
        }
    }
    

Scaling: `epoll_ctl` is O(log N) per call (typically called once per fd at registration); `epoll_wait` is O(M) where M is the number of ready fds (not N). For a server with 100,000 idle connections and a few active ones per millisecond, epoll handles them efficiently.

#### 12.2.4 kqueue (BSD, 2000)

The BSD equivalent of epoll. Used on FreeBSD, macOS. Similar scaling properties; the API is slightly different but conceptually identical:
    
    
    int kq = kqueue();
    struct kevent change = { .ident = sock, .filter = EVFILT_READ, .flags = EV_ADD };
    kevent(kq, &change, 1, NULL, 0, NULL);
    struct kevent events[64];
    int n = kevent(kq, NULL, 0, events, 64, NULL);
    

#### 12.2.5 IOCP — Windows 1994

Windows' I/O Completion Ports take a different approach: rather than "tell me when an fd is ready," they say "perform this I/O; tell me when it completes." Application submits operations; OS executes them; application receives notifications. This is the _completion model_ , while epoll/kqueue are the _readiness model_.

#### 12.2.6 Edge-Triggered vs Level-Triggered

epoll supports two modes:

**Level-triggered (default)** : `epoll_wait()` returns whenever the fd is ready. If you don't read all the data, the fd remains ready, and the next `epoll_wait()` returns it again.

**Edge-triggered (EPOLLET flag)** : `epoll_wait()` returns only on a state change (transition from not-ready to ready). If you don't read all the data, the fd remains ready, but `epoll_wait()` will not notify you again until something changes (more data arrives, or you've read everything and new data arrives).

Edge-triggered is faster (fewer epoll_wait calls per fd) but requires careful handling: you must read until `EAGAIN` to drain the socket completely. Level-triggered is more forgiving.

Modern high-performance code uses edge-triggered with proper draining; reactive frameworks (Tokio, async-std) abstract the details.

### 12.3 io_uring: The Modern Linux Path

`io_uring` (introduced in Linux 5.1 in 2019) is the modern Linux fast-path I/O API. It is the most significant change to Linux I/O since `epoll`.

The model: the application and kernel share two ring buffers (a submission queue and a completion queue), both in shared memory. The application submits I/O operations by writing to the submission queue; the kernel processes them asynchronously and writes results to the completion queue. The application reads completions.

No system calls per operation; no copying; no readiness/draining dance. The kernel polls the submission queue (or is notified periodically); the application polls the completion queue (or is notified). Throughput is dramatically higher than epoll for I/O-intensive workloads.

#### 12.3.1 The Basic API
    
    
    struct io_uring ring;
    io_uring_queue_init(64, &ring, 0);
    
    // Submit a read
    struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(&ring);
    io_uring_prep_read(sqe, fd, buf, sizeof(buf), offset);
    io_uring_submit(&ring);
    
    // Wait for completion
    struct io_uring_cqe *cqe;
    io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
    int result = cqe->res;
    io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);
    

The `liburing` library (helper APIs) abstracts the ring-buffer details. The actual io_uring operations cover not just network I/O but also file I/O, async fsync, splice, openat, accept, connect, send, recv, and many others.

#### 12.3.2 What io_uring Buys You

(1) _No system call per operation_ : submit many operations in one batch; receive many completions in one batch. The kernel can be configured to poll the submission queue without any application-initiated system calls.

(2) _Native asynchronous I/O_ : previous Linux async I/O (`aio`) was incomplete and slow; io_uring is the first first-class async I/O on Linux.

(3) _Unified API for many operations_ : the same ring can handle reads, writes, network I/O, file I/O, fsync, splice, etc. Composing complex I/O patterns is straightforward.

(4) _Zero-copy options_ : with the right flags, io_uring can read or write directly into application memory without an extra copy.

(5) _High throughput_ : at 100 Gbps with small packets, io_uring is the only way to keep up on x86 CPUs. epoll-based servers fall behind around 10-25 Gbps.

#### 12.3.3 The Performance Profile

For a simple TCP echo server:

* thread-per-connection: 5,000 connections, ~100k RPS.
* epoll: 100,000 connections, ~500k RPS.
* io_uring: 1,000,000 connections, ~2-3M RPS.

The numbers depend heavily on workload; small-message servers see the biggest io_uring win; large-message servers see less. For modern high-rate servers (financial systems, real-time messaging, large game backends), io_uring is increasingly the choice.

#### 12.3.4 io_uring Adoption

As of 2026:

* _Web servers_ : nginx, HAProxy, Envoy all support io_uring as an opt-in I/O backend.
* _Databases_ : PostgreSQL added io_uring support; MySQL/MariaDB consider it; FoundationDB and TigerBeetle use it.
* _Languages and frameworks_ : Rust's tokio-uring crate; Go's standard library opts into io_uring for some operations; Python's `liburing` / `iouring` bindings (packages, not crates — Rust terminology); Node.js considering it.
* _Caveats_ : io_uring is Linux-only; portable code needs a fallback to epoll. macOS has no equivalent (kqueue with similar semantics is older).

### 12.4 AF_XDP: Kernel Bypass at the Socket Layer

AF_XDP (eXpress Data Path, Linux 4.18, 2018) is a different beast. It is not a faster epoll; it is kernel bypass: the application receives raw Ethernet frames directly from the NIC, with the kernel involved minimally.

The use case: hyperscaler-scale packet processing where the kernel's network stack is the bottleneck. DPDK does similar things in user space; AF_XDP does it via a kernel-cooperative API.

#### 12.4.1 The Model

The application:

  1. Creates an AF_XDP socket.
  2. Allocates a UMEM region (a chunk of memory for packet buffers).
  3. Configures the NIC's XDP program to redirect specific packets to the AF_XDP socket.
  4. Receives raw frames from the UMEM by polling rings.
  5. Transmits raw frames the same way.

Throughput: line-rate on 100 Gbps NICs from a single CPU core. Latency: sub-microsecond when polling.

#### 12.4.2 The Tradeoffs

The benefits: extreme throughput and predictable latency.

The costs: (1) The application must implement the entire TCP/IP stack in user space (or use a library like the Linux Foundation's f-stack, mTCP, or a DPDK-style framework). (2) The NIC must be AF_XDP-capable, which most modern enterprise NICs are but consumer ones are not. (3) The kernel still does some work (XDP program execution); cooperation between kernel XDP and user-space AF_XDP requires care.

AF_XDP is the right tool for special workloads: DDoS scrubbing, market data feeds, packet capture appliances. It is the wrong tool for general-purpose servers.

### 12.5 The Async Framework Layer

Most applications do not interact with epoll or io_uring directly. They use async frameworks that abstract the event-loop details. Each language and runtime has its own:

#### 12.5.1 libuv (Node.js, Julia, others)

libuv is the cross-platform event loop underlying Node.js. It uses epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, IOCP on Windows. Provides callbacks-based and promise-based APIs.

Node.js's "non-blocking I/O" pitch is essentially libuv abstracted to JavaScript. The single-threaded model with the event loop is what makes Node.js scale to many concurrent connections.

#### 12.5.2 Tokio (Rust)

Tokio is the dominant Rust async runtime. Built on epoll (with tokio-uring optionally on io_uring). Uses Rust's async/await for ergonomic concurrent code. Each task is a state machine compiled by the async transform.

Tokio's `async fn` is the standard pattern for I/O code in Rust. The runtime schedules tasks across worker threads; each thread runs an epoll loop. Performance is competitive with C-level epoll-based servers in microbenchmarks, with significantly better safety guarantees.

#### 12.5.3 async-std (Rust)

An alternative to Tokio with similar goals; less widely adopted.

#### 12.5.4 Go's Netpoller

Go integrates async I/O into its runtime: every goroutine doing I/O is automatically scheduled onto a netpoller (epoll on Linux). The application writes blocking-style code with `net.Dial` and `(*Conn).Read`; the runtime handles the asynchrony transparently. This is the "best of both worlds" claim of Go: simple sequential code with efficient async runtime.

The cost: Go's runtime is opinionated; you cannot easily integrate io_uring (Go has its own scheduling); you have less control than in Rust+Tokio.

#### 12.5.5 Python's asyncio

Python's asyncio provides async/await over a base event loop. Performance is much lower than C/Rust/Go because of Python's interpreter overhead, but adequate for many I/O-bound applications. asyncio is the standard library; alternatives (uvloop, trio, anyio) provide variations.

#### 12.5.6 The Common Pattern

All these frameworks share the structure:

* One event loop per CPU core (or one per process).
* Async-style application code (callbacks, promises, async/await, or goroutines).
* I/O multiplexing via epoll/kqueue/IOCP (or io_uring in newer Rust/Linux).
* Optional thread pool for CPU-bound work.

The performance hierarchy: pure-C epoll > Rust+Tokio ≈ Go-netpoller > Node.js > Python-asyncio. The convenience hierarchy is roughly the reverse. The right choice depends on the workload.

### 12.6 The Wire-Level Artifact: io_uring vs epoll Echo Server

A simple TCP echo server using io_uring (with liburing):
    
    
    #include <stdio.h>
    #include <stdlib.h>
    #include <stdint.h>
    #include <string.h>
    #include <unistd.h>
    #include <sys/socket.h>
    #include <netinet/in.h>
    #include <arpa/inet.h>
    #include <liburing.h>
    
    #define BUFSZ 4096
    enum op { OP_ACCEPT = 1, OP_READ = 2, OP_WRITE = 3 };
    
    struct conn {
        int fd;
        char buf[BUFSZ];
        enum op pending;
    };
    
    /* Encode (op, conn*) into the 64-bit user_data field. */
    static inline __u64 ud_pack(enum op op, struct conn *c) {
        return ((__u64)op << 56) | (__u64)(uintptr_t)c;
    }
    static inline enum op ud_op(__u64 ud)       { return (enum op)(ud >> 56); }
    static inline struct conn *ud_conn(__u64 ud) {
        return (struct conn *)(uintptr_t)(ud & 0x00FFFFFFFFFFFFFFULL);
    }
    
    static void prep_accept(struct io_uring *ring, int listen_fd) {
        struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
        io_uring_prep_accept(sqe, listen_fd, NULL, NULL, 0);
        io_uring_sqe_set_data64(sqe, ud_pack(OP_ACCEPT, NULL));
    }
    
    static void prep_read(struct io_uring *ring, struct conn *c) {
        struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
        io_uring_prep_recv(sqe, c->fd, c->buf, BUFSZ, 0);
        c->pending = OP_READ;
        io_uring_sqe_set_data64(sqe, ud_pack(OP_READ, c));
    }
    
    static void prep_write(struct io_uring *ring, struct conn *c, int len) {
        struct io_uring_sqe *sqe = io_uring_get_sqe(ring);
        io_uring_prep_send(sqe, c->fd, c->buf, len, 0);
        c->pending = OP_WRITE;
        io_uring_sqe_set_data64(sqe, ud_pack(OP_WRITE, c));
    }
    
    int main(void) {
        int listen_fd = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
        int opt = 1;
        setsockopt(listen_fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_REUSEADDR, &opt, sizeof(opt));
        struct sockaddr_in addr = {
            .sin_family = AF_INET,
            .sin_port   = htons(8080),
            .sin_addr   = { .s_addr = htonl(INADDR_ANY) },
        };
        bind(listen_fd, (struct sockaddr*)&addr, sizeof(addr));
        listen(listen_fd, 128);
    
        struct io_uring ring;
        io_uring_queue_init(256, &ring, 0);
        prep_accept(&ring, listen_fd);
    
        for (;;) {
            io_uring_submit(&ring);
            struct io_uring_cqe *cqe;
            io_uring_wait_cqe(&ring, &cqe);
            __u64 ud = cqe->user_data;
            int res = cqe->res;
    
            switch (ud_op(ud)) {
            case OP_ACCEPT: {
                prep_accept(&ring, listen_fd);          /* re-arm accept */
                if (res < 0) break;
                struct conn *c = calloc(1, sizeof *c);
                c->fd = res;
                prep_read(&ring, c);
                break;
            }
            case OP_READ: {
                struct conn *c = ud_conn(ud);
                if (res <= 0) { close(c->fd); free(c); break; }   /* EOF or error */
                prep_write(&ring, c, res);                         /* echo */
                break;
            }
            case OP_WRITE: {
                struct conn *c = ud_conn(ud);
                if (res < 0) { close(c->fd); free(c); break; }
                prep_read(&ring, c);                               /* read next */
                break;
            }
            }
            io_uring_cqe_seen(&ring, cqe);
        }
        return 0;
    }
    

Three things to notice. First, every completion re-arms the next operation in the state machine: accept re-arms accept _and_ prepares the new connection's first read; each read enqueues the corresponding write; each write enqueues the next read. Without these re-arms, the ring goes idle and `wait_cqe` blocks forever — a common first-pass mistake. Second, the `user_data` field carries both an operation tag and a pointer to the per-connection state, so a single completion loop handles all three operation types without a separate `epoll`-style fd-to-state lookup. Third, this loop is single-threaded; for production throughput you would batch submissions, use a worker pool, and consider `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to amortize syscall cost further.

The equivalent epoll-based version is roughly 30% longer and has explicit event-mask management plus a manual fd → state hash table. Both versions handle 100,000+ connections; io_uring with proper batching reaches 2x or more the throughput at high RPS.

Running `strace -c` on both shows the difference: io_uring does almost no system calls during the steady state (everything happens through shared-memory rings); epoll at 1 million RPS makes millions of `epoll_wait`/`read`/`write` syscalls per second. The win compounds as RPS climbs.

### 12.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Distinguish between the readiness model (epoll, kqueue) and the completion model (IOCP, io_uring). Why is the completion model becoming more popular?

Hint

Who initiates the I/O?

**Answer:** In the _readiness model_ , the application says "tell me when this fd is ready to read/write." The OS notifies; the application then performs the actual I/O operation. The classic example is epoll: epoll_wait tells the application that fd X is ready; the application then calls read() to actually transfer data. In the _completion model_ , the application says "perform this I/O for me; tell me when it's done." The OS itself executes the I/O and notifies the application of the result. Windows IOCP and io_uring are completion-model APIs. The completion model is becoming more popular because: (1) It avoids the readiness-then-do-it dance; the I/O is initiated and completed atomically. (2) It enables zero-copy operations more cleanly (the OS can write directly into application buffers). (3) It scales better at very high I/O rates because the application can batch many submissions and process many completions per system call. (4) It naturally supports operations that don't fit the readiness model (e.g., async file I/O where "ready to read" doesn't quite make sense for disk operations). The readiness model has a long history and is good enough for many workloads, but completion-model APIs (io_uring on Linux, IOCP on Windows) are the modern direction. The completion model is also the only model that natively supports asynchronous file I/O on Linux.

**Q2.** What is the difference between level-triggered and edge-triggered semantics in epoll? Which is the default, and why does edge-triggered require careful coding?

Hint

What signals the application that an fd is "ready" again after the first notification?

**Answer:** _Level-triggered_ (the default in epoll): the fd is reported as ready as long as there is data available to read (or space available to write). If you call `epoll_wait()` and an fd has data, but you only read half of it, the next `epoll_wait()` call will report the same fd as ready again. The OS keeps notifying you until you've handled all the data. _Edge-triggered_ (when EPOLLET flag is set): the fd is reported only on a _state transition_ from "not ready" to "ready." Once notified, you must keep reading until you get EAGAIN. If you stop reading midway, the OS does not notify you again until something changes (more data arrives, or you've drained the buffer and new data comes). Edge-triggered is faster because it produces fewer kernel notifications, but it requires the application to "drain" each fd to completion in each notification: read in a loop until EAGAIN. If the application doesn't, it can hang waiting for a notification that never comes. Edge-triggered is the standard for high-performance servers; level-triggered is the standard for simpler or more forgiving code. Most modern async frameworks (libevent, libuv, Tokio) use edge-triggered internally because they manage the draining for the application.

**Q3.** What is `io_uring`, and what does it do that `epoll` cannot?

Hint

Two ring buffers in shared memory; no syscall per operation.

**Answer:** `io_uring` (introduced in Linux 5.1 in 2019) is the modern Linux async I/O API. Its architecture: the application and kernel share two ring buffers in mapped memory, a submission queue and a completion queue. The application submits I/O operations by writing entries to the submission queue (no system call needed); the kernel processes them asynchronously and writes completions to the completion queue (no system call needed for the application to read). What it does that epoll cannot: (1) _True asynchronous I/O, including for file operations_ : epoll only works for fds that support non-blocking I/O (network sockets, pipes); io_uring can perform async reads from disk, async fsyncs, async opens, etc. (2) _Submission and completion without system calls_ : at high I/O rates, epoll-based code makes many system calls per second (epoll_wait, read, write); io_uring with the right configuration can run for long periods with no system calls at all. (3) _Operation batching_ : hundreds of I/O operations can be submitted in one batch; the kernel processes them efficiently. epoll requires individual operations per notified fd. (4) _Native operation chaining_ : a read followed by a write (e.g., a proxy) can be expressed as a linked pair of operations; the kernel handles the chain without returning to the application. (5) _Higher absolute throughput_ : at peak, io_uring delivers 2-3x the throughput of epoll for small-packet workloads. The cost: io_uring is Linux-only (not portable); requires Linux 5.1+ (5.13+ for the most useful features); has a learning curve for the ring-buffer API; security model has been the subject of refinements over the years (some early features were restricted in later kernels due to misuse concerns).

**Q4.** Why don't most applications use AF_XDP, given its dramatic performance advantage?

Hint

What does the application have to do that the kernel normally does?

**Answer:** AF_XDP delivers raw Ethernet frames to user space, bypassing the kernel's network stack entirely. The application receives raw bytes; the application must implement TCP, IP, ARP, ICMP, etc. itself, or use a library (mTCP, f-stack, Seastar) that does. The benefit: peak performance. The costs: (1) _Complexity_ : the application is responsible for protocol correctness across edge cases that the kernel handles routinely. Implementing a TCP stack from scratch is a multi-year effort; most teams cannot do it. (2) _Functionality loss_ : standard tools (tcpdump, ss, netstat) do not work for traffic that bypasses the kernel; debugging requires custom tooling. (3) _Maintenance burden_ : every TCP option, every new protocol feature, every middlebox compatibility issue must be re-implemented and maintained in user space. (4) _NIC support_ : AF_XDP requires NIC driver support, which is increasingly common but not universal. (5) _Scaling boundaries_ : the application takes over a NIC interface or queue; it cannot share that interface with regular kernel traffic without careful configuration. The right use cases for AF_XDP: special-purpose appliances that own their NIC entirely (DDoS scrubbers, packet capture, market data feeds, custom load balancers). Wrong use cases: general-purpose web servers, databases, application servers. For these, io_uring delivers most of the performance benefit without the operational cost. The result: AF_XDP serves a real but narrow market.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A team is benchmarking a TCP echo server and observes that throughput plateaus at 200,000 RPS even when CPU is 50% utilized. Walk through the diagnosis.

Hint

The CPU isn't saturated; something else is.

**Answer:** _Diagnosis path_ : (1) Check the kernel's TCP statistics: `ss -s` shows TCP connection counts; `netstat -s` shows segment counts and errors. Look for TIME_WAIT exhaustion (covered in Chapter 9), accept-queue overflow, retransmissions. (2) Check the application's event-loop saturation: profile with `perf top` to see where CPU is spent. If it's spent in `epoll_wait` or kernel system calls rather than application logic, the system-call overhead is the bottleneck. (3) Check the NIC's interrupt rate: `cat /proc/interrupts | grep eth0`. If a single core is handling all interrupts (50% utilization on one core, idle others), enable RPS (Receive Packet Steering) or use a NIC with RSS (Receive-Side Scaling) to spread interrupts across cores. (4) Check the network card's offload state: `ethtool -k eth0` shows whether GRO (Generic Receive Offload), GSO (Generic Segmentation Offload), TSO (TCP Segmentation Offload), and others are enabled; if disabled, the CPU does work that hardware could. (5) Check kernel parameters: `net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog`, `net.core.somaxconn`, `net.core.netdev_max_backlog`. Default values are often too small for high-RPS workloads. (6) Try a different API: if the server uses epoll, try io_uring. The reduced syscall overhead may unlock additional throughput. (7) Profile with `bpftrace` or `perf` to find specific bottlenecks: the JIT compilation in async runtimes, lock contention, allocator overhead. _Most likely culprit at 200K RPS plateau with 50% CPU_ : one or more of (a) interrupt affinity stuck on one core, (b) accept-queue / SYN-cookies, (c) per-connection allocator overhead. The path is methodical: capture metrics, identify what is hot, change one thing, re-measure. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to diagnose this; watch for Lie #2 (suggesting random kernel-parameter tuning without checking what's actually saturated; the "throw `sysctl` at it" anti-pattern).

**Q2.** A startup is choosing a runtime for a new microservice that will handle 10,000 concurrent connections, mostly idle. The team is comfortable with Rust, Go, and Node.js. Argue for each option's tradeoffs.

Hint

Performance per core, developer productivity, ecosystem.

**Answer:** _Rust + Tokio_ : best performance (single-core can handle 100,000+ connections, low memory per connection, no GC pauses); high development cost (Rust's borrow checker and async ergonomics are demanding); excellent for performance-critical services; harder to hire for. _Go_ : very good performance (goroutines per connection are cheap; Go's runtime handles many concurrent goroutines efficiently); easier development (goroutine model is simpler than async/await); good ecosystem (gRPC native, many libraries, simple deployment); some overhead from the runtime and GC (acceptable for most services); easy to hire for. _Node.js_ : good performance for I/O-bound work (libuv is mature; the V8 engine is fast for JavaScript); easiest development for many teams (familiar JavaScript syntax; vast NPM ecosystem); single-threaded by default (need cluster mode or worker threads for CPU-bound work); GC pauses can be noticeable at very high RPS; runtime overhead is higher than Rust or Go for the same logic. _Recommendation for 10K concurrent connections, mostly idle_ : Go is the sweet spot. Performance is more than adequate (Go can handle 100K connections per server easily); development velocity is high; the ecosystem is mature for microservices (Kubernetes-native, gRPC, OpenTelemetry, etc.); operational simplicity is good (single binary, no runtime to install). Rust is overkill unless the service is performance-critical or memory-constrained. Node.js is fine but Go's combination of performance and simplicity edges it out. If the team has strong existing expertise in one language, that often dominates the choice; new teams should pick Go for microservices in 2026. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to recommend; watch for Lie #5 (recommending a "thread-per-connection" model that scales much worse than goroutines/async; or pretending Node.js can do CPU-bound work efficiently in a single thread).

**Q3.** Walk through how an HTTP server using io_uring would handle 1 million concurrent WebSocket connections, each receiving a small message once per minute. Identify the resource constraints.

Hint

Memory per connection, event-loop cost, kernel data structures.

**Answer:** _Per-connection memory_ : each WebSocket connection has TCP state (socket structure in kernel ~3 KB), TLS state if encrypted (~10-20 KB), application-level state (read/write buffers, parser state, ~5-10 KB), and io_uring-related state (negligible per connection). Total: 20-40 KB per connection. For 1 million connections: 20-40 GB of memory. Achievable on modern servers with 64 GB or more RAM but not trivial; tuning to reduce per-connection state is important. _Kernel fd table_ : 1 million file descriptors. `ulimit -n` must be set to at least 1M; the kernel's fd table grows dynamically but the default limit is 4096 or 65536; admins must raise it. _Conntrack table_ : if a stateful firewall is in front, the conntrack table must be sized for 1M entries; default is 65536; raise via `/proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_max`. _Event loop cost_ : with messages once per minute, the per-connection event rate is 1/60 = 0.017 events per second; aggregate event rate across 1M connections is ~16.7K events per second. io_uring handles this easily; epoll would also handle it (event rate is low). _Wakeup efficiency_ : io_uring's batched completion model means thousands of events can be processed per system call. With 16.7K events/sec, this is roughly one batch per second per worker thread; very efficient. _Connection migration / churn_ : WebSocket connections are long-lived but not eternal. Some clients reconnect every few minutes; budget for 1-10% reconnect rate per second. _TLS overhead_ : if the WebSockets are encrypted, TLS terminations consume CPU; consider TLS offload to a separate process or DPU. _Resource constraints summary_ : memory (20-40 GB for 1M idle connections) is the dominant cost; CPU is light at this event rate; kernel fd table and conntrack table need tuning; storage and network bandwidth are negligible. Achievable on a single 64 GB server with 32 CPU cores. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design this; watch for Lie #5 (assuming the kernel's default fd limit is sufficient without raising it; the default is 1024 or 4096 on most distributions, way too low for 1M connections).

**Q4.** A team is profiling a Go service and finds that 30% of CPU is in `runtime.netpoll`. They want to understand if this is normal or a problem. Diagnose.

Hint

30% in netpoll could be reasonable or could be a sign of polling at the wrong rate.

**Answer:** Go's `runtime.netpoll` is the function that does the epoll_wait call internally and dispatches readable/writable goroutines. 30% CPU in netpoll could be reasonable or pathological depending on context. _Reasonable scenarios_ : (1) High I/O throughput: a server processing many small messages per second, where each message triggers a netpoll round-trip. At 100K+ RPS with small messages, 20-40% in netpoll is normal. (2) Many concurrent connections each generating few events: similar argument. _Pathological scenarios_ : (1) The application is calling `time.Sleep(...)` or other timer-based operations frequently, causing netpoll to wake up but not have any real work. (2) The application is using context.WithTimeout aggressively, causing many timer wheel entries that netpoll iterates over. (3) Excessive goroutine creation: each goroutine doing one I/O and exiting, with high churn. (4) Many sockets with little traffic: netpoll iterates through fds even when most are idle. _Diagnosis_ : (1) Profile with `pprof.Lookup("goroutine")`: count goroutines; if there are hundreds of thousands and most are blocked on I/O, this is normal. (2) Profile with `pprof.Lookup("heap")`: check if allocation rate is high (high churn). (3) Use `go tool trace` for a trace recording; look at the GC pause times, goroutine scheduling, network I/O events. (4) Compare to a reference implementation in another language; if Go is 2x slower than a reasonable C/Rust equivalent for the same workload, netpoll overhead is unusually high. _Fix paths_ : (1) Reduce I/O rate: batch operations; reduce small-message churn. (2) Reduce goroutine creation: use worker pools rather than spawning per-message goroutines. (3) Tune GOMAXPROCS and Go runtime parameters. (4) Consider profile-guided optimization (Go 1.20+) for specific hot paths. (5) Consider switching critical I/O to direct syscalls or a Cgo-bound library if Go's runtime is the bottleneck (last resort; loses Go's ergonomic benefits). The decision is contextual: at 100K RPS, 30% in netpoll is fine. At 1K RPS with the same metric, something is off. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to interpret the metric; watch for Lie #6 (concluding netpoll is "too high" without measuring the comparison baseline; raw percentage metrics without context are misleading).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Reflect on whether `io_uring` will replace `epoll` for most production workloads, or whether they will coexist for a long time. What forces drive each direction?

**Discussion:** Both will coexist for a long time, with io_uring slowly taking share. Forces favoring continued epoll use: (1) epoll is portable across all Linux versions (decade+ of compatibility); io_uring requires 5.1+ for basic features, 5.13+ for most modern features. Production systems with older kernels (LTS distributions from 2019-2020) cannot use io_uring effectively. (2) Stability and proven-ness: epoll has 20+ years of production deployment; io_uring has had several security-related restrictions added in its first few years. Some operators are cautious. (3) Application complexity: io_uring's ring-buffer API is more complex than epoll's straightforward API; library wrappers (liburing, tokio-uring) reduce this but the conceptual model is still richer. (4) The performance gap is workload-dependent: at moderate I/O rates (the majority of production workloads), epoll and io_uring perform similarly; the io_uring win is at very high I/O rates. Forces favoring io_uring growth: (1) Cloud and content providers handle very high I/O rates; io_uring delivers user-visible benefits. (2) Modern libraries (Rust's tokio-uring, Go's eventual full migration, language standard libraries adding io_uring backends) make the API easier. (3) Newer Linux distributions support io_uring out of the box; the kernel-version barrier diminishes over time. (4) New features in io_uring (file I/O, network registers, eBPF integration) make it strictly more capable. The trajectory: by 2030, io_uring is the default I/O backend for new high-performance applications on Linux. epoll persists for portability, simplicity, and legacy code. Both APIs are simultaneously present in mature applications, with io_uring on Linux and epoll/kqueue on macOS/BSDs.

**Q2.** Argue (a) why the asynchronous programming model (async/await, callbacks, coroutines) has displaced thread-per-connection for high-concurrency servers, (b) whether this is a permanent shift or temporary, (c) what hybrid approaches make sense.

**Discussion:** (a) Async/await displaced thread-per-connection because of cost: each thread requires (i) several KB of kernel state (task_struct, kernel stack), (ii) typically 8 MB of user stack (or less if tuned, but never zero), (iii) overhead for context switches between threads. At 100,000 concurrent connections, thread-per-connection costs ~800 GB just in user stacks (impossible) and many context switches per second (saturating CPU). Async/await with one thread per CPU core spreads I/O across many coroutines on each thread, each coroutine using bytes rather than KBs of state; context switches between coroutines are cheaper than between threads. The performance gap is multiple orders of magnitude. (b) Permanent or temporary? Permanent for the foreseeable future. The hardware reality (memory bandwidth, cache hierarchies, NUMA effects) makes per-connection thread state expensive in ways that are not improving. The trend (many concurrent connections per server) accelerates as workloads move to microservices and connection counts grow. Async models will continue to dominate. (c) Hybrid approaches: (i) _Goroutine model (Go)_ : extremely lightweight threads scheduled by a user-space runtime; effectively async/await but with sequential-looking code. Best of both worlds for many workloads. (ii) _Async-style I/O with thread pool for CPU work_ : typical Node.js, Tokio, async-std pattern. Most code is async; CPU-bound work is delegated to a worker pool. (iii) _DPDK/AF_XDP for the data plane, kernel for control plane_ : hyperscaler pattern where high-throughput data movement uses kernel bypass while configuration and management uses standard APIs. (iv) _eBPF-based programs for hot paths_ : certain types of packet filtering and processing can happen in the kernel before reaching user space, eliminating the user-space cost. The async model wins for general-purpose servers; specialized fast paths (kernel bypass, eBPF) win for the highest-rate workloads.

**Q3.** Consider the future of networking APIs in a world where DPUs handle much of the per-packet processing (Chapter 4). What does this mean for socket programming, and will the API as we know it survive?

**Discussion:** The socket API survives, but its meaning shifts. In a DPU-centric architecture: (1) The host CPU still uses a socket-like API (a stream of bytes for TCP, datagrams for UDP, streams for QUIC). The application is unchanged. (2) The DPU handles the low-level packet processing: TCP/IP, TLS termination, connection tracking, packet filtering. The host CPU's sockets are connections to the DPU's logical endpoints, not to the wire directly. (3) The kernel becomes a thin layer between the application's socket and the DPU's offload. Some implementations use VirtIO or similar para-virtualization to communicate with the DPU; others use shared-memory rings (effectively io_uring extended to talk to the DPU rather than the NIC). (4) Operations like TLS handshake, congestion control, and packet retransmission happen on the DPU; the host CPU just sees application bytes. The socket API remains the universal language for application networking. The kernel and DPU implementation details change underneath. Specifically: (a) `recv()` is still recv(); under the hood, the DPU may have already done the TLS decryption and TCP reassembly. (b) `send()` is still send(); the DPU handles TLS encryption and TCP segmentation. (c) Advanced operations (zero-copy, scatter-gather) become more important and may use io_uring's interface to express them to the DPU. (d) Some applications might use a different interface for direct DPU access (similar to how some applications use AF_XDP today), bypassing the socket abstraction for special-purpose workloads. The forecast for 2030-2035: socket APIs remain the standard interface; io_uring or its successors are the implementation; DPUs absorb the per-packet work. Most application code looks the same as today. The kernel network stack becomes simpler over time as more functions move to the DPU.

### Chapter Summary

The socket API is the universal foundation for network programming, unchanged in its core shape since 1983. Event notification has evolved through select, poll, epoll, kqueue, and io_uring; each generation enabling higher connection counts and higher throughput. Modern Linux servers use either epoll (mature, portable to all Linux versions) or io_uring (faster, requires Linux 5.1+).

The choice of event-notification API has profound performance implications. Thread-per-connection tops out at thousands of connections; epoll handles hundreds of thousands; io_uring handles millions. AF_XDP bypasses the kernel for special-purpose hyperscaler workloads (DDoS scrubbing, market data, packet capture). DPDK does the same in pure user space.

Async frameworks (libuv, Tokio, Go's netpoller, asyncio) abstract the event-loop details. Each is tied to a programming model: callbacks, async/await, goroutines. The performance hierarchy roughly mirrors the language's runtime overhead: C/Rust at the top, Go close behind, Node.js moderate, Python lower. The convenience hierarchy is roughly reversed; pick based on workload requirements.

io_uring is the modern Linux fast path: shared-memory rings, asynchronous I/O including for file operations, syscall-free operation at high rates. Adoption is growing rapidly; by 2030 expect io_uring to be the default backend for new high-performance servers.

The wire-level artifact (io_uring vs epoll echo server with strace traces) shows the practical difference: io_uring eliminates per-operation syscalls during the steady state.

Chapter 13 takes us into the application layer: DNS, the protocol that translates names into addresses. We will see classic DNS, DoH/DoT/DoQ, EDNS extensions, and service discovery in cloud-native systems.

---

## Chapter 13: DNS, DoH/DoT/DoQ, and Service Discovery

Names are how humans use the internet. Addresses are how computers use it. The protocol that translates between them is DNS, and it is one of the most under-appreciated pieces of internet infrastructure: invisible when working, catastrophic when not.

This chapter develops DNS from first principles: the hierarchy of zones, the recursive resolution process, the record types, the EDNS extensions, the modern encrypted variants (DoH, DoT, DoQ), and the 2024-2026 privacy story. We also touch service discovery in cloud-native systems, which extends DNS-like ideas to ephemeral microservices. The wire-level artifact is a `dig +trace` walk-through showing recursive resolution end-to-end, and a `curl --doh-url` query encrypted via DoH.

By the end you should be able to read a DNS query and response in tcpdump, walk the recursive resolution path for any name, reason about TTLs and caching, and articulate the privacy implications of plaintext vs encrypted DNS.

### 13.1 The DNS Hierarchy

DNS is a globally distributed hierarchical database. The hierarchy maps directly to the structure of domain names. Reading a name right-to-left:
    
    
    www.example.com.
    ↑    ↑       ↑
    hostname  zone  TLD  root
    

The trailing dot represents the root. The root delegates to top-level domains (TLDs): `.com`, `.org`, `.net`, country codes like `.uk` and `.jp`, plus thousands of generic TLDs (`.app`, `.dev`, `.io`, etc.). Each TLD is operated by a registry: Verisign for `.com`, Public Interest Registry for `.org`, ccTLD authorities for country codes.

Below TLDs, _registrars_ sell domains to registrants. The registrant for `example.com` operates the zone, delegating subdomains as desired: `www.example.com`, `mail.example.com`, etc. Subdomains can be further delegated to other authorities.

#### 13.1.1 Zones and Delegation

A _zone_ is a contiguous portion of the namespace under one administrative authority. The `.com` zone is administered by Verisign; the `example.com` zone is administered by example.com's owner. Zones are connected by _delegation_ records: in the `.com` zone, there is an NS record for `example.com` pointing to the name servers for the `example.com` zone.

A zone is served by one or more authoritative name servers. There are typically at least two for redundancy. The authoritative servers know the contents of their zone but nothing else; they respond authoritatively for their own zone and refer queries about other zones to those zones' name servers.

#### 13.1.2 The 13 Root Name Servers (Sort Of)

DNS has 13 root name server identities (labeled `a.root-servers.net` through `m.root-servers.net`). Each identity is actually anycast: hundreds of physical servers around the world all announce the same IP for each root identity. The 13 logical identities expand to over 1,500 physical servers.

The roots respond authoritatively for the root zone, which contains NS records for all TLDs. They are the starting point for any DNS resolution that can't be answered from cache.

### 13.2 The Resolution Process

A typical resolution: a user types `www.example.com` into their browser. The browser asks the OS resolver. The OS resolver asks a _recursive resolver_ (typically the home router's, the ISP's, or `1.1.1.1` / `8.8.8.8` configured manually). The recursive resolver, if it doesn't have the answer cached, walks the hierarchy:

  1. Query a root server for `www.example.com`. Root responds: "I don't know, but `.com` is at servers X, Y, Z" — and, crucially, includes the IP addresses of X, Y, Z in the same reply. Those IP-address records are _glue records_ : address records the parent zone publishes for nameservers that live inside (or just below) the parent's own zone, so the resolver does not have to do a separate lookup just to find the next nameserver. Glue is the small leaf of cleverness that keeps DNS from looping on itself.
  2. Query a `.com` server for `www.example.com`. The `.com` server responds: "I don't know, but `example.com` is at servers M, N" — again with glue if M and N are themselves under `.com`.
  3. Query `example.com`'s authoritative server for `www.example.com`. The server responds: "www.example.com is at IP address 93.184.216.34."
  4. Recursive resolver returns the answer to the client and caches it for the record's TTL.

Each step is a single UDP query and response, typically 50-200 bytes. Total resolution time is the sum of the round trips, often dominated by the slowest hop. A cold resolution can take 100-500 ms; cached subsequent queries are sub-millisecond.

#### 13.2.1 Caching and TTLs

Every DNS record has a _Time-To-Live_ (TTL), in seconds. The TTL tells the resolver how long it can cache the record before re-querying. Typical TTLs:

* Root and TLD records: hours to days (very stable).
* Common services (CDN edges): 60-300 seconds (allows quick failover).
* Long-stable records (corporate websites): 86400 seconds (1 day).
* DDoS protection records: 30-60 seconds (rapid failover).

The TTL is a tradeoff: low TTLs allow fast response to changes; high TTLs reduce query load on authoritative servers. Most operators choose TTLs in the 300-3600 range.

#### 13.2.2 The Recursive Resolver

The recursive resolver is the workhorse. It maintains caches (typically tens of millions of records); knows the root server addresses (the _hint zone_); walks the hierarchy on cache misses; serves the answer to clients. Popular recursive resolvers:

* **Public** : Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`, Google's `8.8.8.8` and `8.8.4.4`, Quad9's `9.9.9.9`, OpenDNS, Comodo Secure DNS.
* **ISP-operated** : most ISPs run their own resolvers; some are slow or filtered; many users override.
* **Self-hosted** : enterprises and tech-savvy users run their own resolvers (unbound, BIND, Knot Resolver, PowerDNS).

The choice of resolver matters: a fast nearby resolver with good caching can shave hundreds of milliseconds off page load times. A privacy-respecting resolver (some public ones promise no logs) differs from an ISP resolver that may log every query.

### 13.3 DNS Record Types

A short tour of common record types:

* **A** : maps a name to an IPv4 address. `www.example.com A 93.184.216.34`.
* **AAAA** : maps a name to an IPv6 address. `www.example.com AAAA 2606:2800:220:1:248:1893:25c8:1946`.
* **CNAME** (Canonical Name): an alias from one name to another. `www.example.com CNAME example.com`.
* **MX** (Mail Exchanger): name and priority of mail servers for the domain.
* **TXT** : arbitrary text data; used for SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain ownership verification.
* **NS** : nameservers authoritative for a zone (delegation records).
* **SOA** (Start of Authority): metadata about the zone (primary nameserver, admin contact, serial number, refresh intervals).
* **PTR** (Pointer): reverse mapping (IP to name).
* **SRV** : name and port of a service (e.g., `_sip._tcp.example.com SRV 0 5 5060 sipserver.example.com.`).
* **CAA** (Certificate Authority Authorization): which CAs may issue certs for the domain.
* **HTTPS** (RFC 9460, 2023): combines A, AAAA, ALPN, and other connection parameters in one record; used for QUIC/HTTP/3 discovery.
* **SVCB** (RFC 9460): generalization of HTTPS for other service types.
* **DNSSEC records** (RRSIG, DNSKEY, DS, NSEC, NSEC3): cryptographic signatures and proof of non-existence.

#### 13.3.1 DNS over UDP and DNS over TCP

DNS originally used only UDP port 53. The reasoning: queries are small, latency matters, and UDP avoids handshake overhead. The maximum DNS-over-UDP message size was 512 bytes (per RFC 1035).

DNS-over-TCP (also port 53) was the fallback for large responses (zone transfers, large response sets). Many operators historically blocked DNS-over-TCP, which caused problems for large responses.

EDNS0 (RFC 6891) extends UDP message size to 4096 bytes or larger via an OPT record in the query. Modern resolvers and authoritative servers all support EDNS0.

#### 13.3.2 EDNS Client Subnet (ECS)

A controversial EDNS extension (RFC 7871) where the recursive resolver tells the authoritative server "the client I'm asking for is in network X." This lets authoritative servers give location-aware responses: a query for a CDN's hostname returns the nearest edge.

The privacy concern: ECS leaks the client's general location to authoritative servers. Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` does not send ECS by default; Google's `8.8.8.8` does for some queries; the practice varies.

### 13.4 DNS Security: DNSSEC and Encrypted Transports

DNS was designed with no security model. Queries and responses are plaintext UDP; anyone on the path can read or modify them. This made DNS one of the most attack-friendly protocols.

#### 13.4.1 DNSSEC

DNSSEC (RFC 4033 et al., 2005) adds cryptographic authentication to DNS responses. Each zone signs its records with a private key; responses include signature (RRSIG) records; resolvers verify against the public key (DNSKEY) of the zone, which is itself signed by the parent zone via a DS record. The chain of trust extends from the root to each zone.

DNSSEC validates that a response is authentic; it does not encrypt the query or response. An attacker can still see what name was queried and what response was returned; they cannot forge or modify.

DNSSEC adoption has been spotty. As of 2026, perhaps 30-40% of `.com` domains are signed; for some TLDs (`.gov`, `.bank`) signing is mandatory; for many TLDs the deployment is partial. Recursive resolvers can be configured to validate or to bypass DNSSEC. Cloudflare, Google, Quad9 all validate by default.

#### 13.4.2 DNS over HTTPS (DoH)

DoH (RFC 8484, 2018) sends DNS queries over HTTPS. The query is encoded in an HTTPS GET or POST request to a well-known URL on a DoH-enabled resolver. The response is JSON or DNS wire format.

Encryption protects the query and response from network observers. Authentication (via TLS certificates) prevents man-in-the-middle attacks. The HTTPS path also blends DNS traffic with other web traffic, making it harder to identify and block.

DoH adoption: major resolvers (1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9) all support DoH. Major browsers (Firefox, Chrome, Edge, Safari) can use DoH instead of OS resolver. Mobile OSes increasingly use DoH.

#### 13.4.3 DNS over TLS (DoT)

DoT (RFC 7858, 2016) sends DNS queries over TLS on port 853. Similar privacy properties to DoH but a different protocol; uses the standard DNS wire format inside TLS rather than HTTPS framing.

DoT is more common at the OS level (Android supports DoT system-wide); DoH is more common at the application level (browsers use DoH).

#### 13.4.4 DNS over QUIC (DoQ)

DoQ (RFC 9250, 2022) sends DNS queries over QUIC, gaining the same properties as DoT plus QUIC's faster handshakes and connection migration. Adoption is early in 2026 but growing on the resolver side (1.1.1.1 and others advertise DoQ availability). Client-side deployment is uneven: Android has DoQ support via custom apps; Apple's "Encrypted DNS" configuration on iOS/macOS still ships DoH and DoT only as of 2026, not DoQ.

#### 13.4.5 The Browser-vs-OS DoH Fight

When a browser uses DoH and ignores the OS resolver, several controversies arise: (1) The user's IT department (enterprise, school) loses visibility into DNS queries, which may be required for security or filtering. (2) The browser is now in the position of choosing the DNS resolver, which is a significant trust question. (3) Some networks (corporate, hotel Wi-Fi with captive portals) rely on the OS resolver to handle local names; the browser bypassing this can break things.

Firefox introduced "DoH by default" in 2019 with `1.1.1.1` as the default resolver and faced significant pushback. Chrome's approach is more conservative: DoH is offered but the OS resolver is preferred unless the user opts in explicitly. The 2026 reality is mixed: each browser has its own policy; users have some control but not full visibility.

### 13.5 Service Discovery in Cloud-Native Systems

DNS provides global name resolution. Cloud-native systems have an additional need: discovering ephemeral microservices that come and go on demand. The traditional DNS model (TTL caching, slow updates) doesn't fit.

#### 13.5.1 The Service-Discovery Problem

A Kubernetes cluster has, say, 100 services, each with 5-50 pod replicas, each pod's IP changing on restart. Clients need to find the right pod for a given service, with the routing updating in seconds when pods come or go.

Traditional DNS would work if TTLs were ~30 seconds and the authoritative source updated in real time. In practice, cloud-native systems use DNS as the discovery layer but combine it with other mechanisms.

#### 13.5.2 Kubernetes DNS

In Kubernetes, every service has a stable DNS name (e.g., `my-service.default.svc.cluster.local`). The cluster's DNS service (CoreDNS in modern setups) resolves this to either a single virtual IP (Service ClusterIP) or to the set of pod IPs (Headless Service).

For the virtual-IP case (Service), the request to that IP is load-balanced (via kube-proxy or eBPF) to one of the backing pods. The application sees a single virtual IP; the underlying pod set can change without disrupting DNS.

For the headless case, DNS returns all pod IPs; clients balance themselves.

#### 13.5.3 Service Mesh Discovery

Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd, Cilium Service Mesh) maintain richer service-discovery information: not just IP addresses but also versions, traffic-splitting rules, retry policies, mTLS identity. The mesh's control plane pushes this to per-pod sidecars (Envoy proxies); the sidecars handle the actual routing.

DNS is still used at the application layer (the application looks up `my-service` and gets a virtual IP), but the actual routing decision is made by the sidecar based on richer information. See Chapter 20 for service mesh depth.

### 13.6 The Wire-Level Artifact: `dig +trace` and `curl --doh-url`

A `dig +trace example.com` walks the hierarchy explicitly:
    
    
    $ dig +trace example.com
    
    . 86400 IN NS a.root-servers.net.
    . 86400 IN NS b.root-servers.net.
    ... (13 root servers)
    
    com. 172800 IN NS a.gtld-servers.net.
    com. 172800 IN NS b.gtld-servers.net.
    ... (13 .com servers)
    ;; Received 836 bytes from 198.41.0.4#53(a.root-servers.net) in 8 ms
    
    example.com. 172800 IN NS a.iana-servers.net.
    example.com. 172800 IN NS b.iana-servers.net.
    ;; Received 561 bytes from 192.5.6.30#53(a.gtld-servers.net) in 12 ms
    
    example.com. 86400 IN A 93.184.216.34
    ;; Received 56 bytes from 199.43.135.53#53(a.iana-servers.net) in 18 ms
    

Three queries (root, TLD, zone), each visible. The IP, the response time, and the cached state are all explicit. Reading a `dig +trace` is the canonical hands-on DNS exercise.

A DoH query via curl:
    
    
    $ curl --doh-url https://1.1.1.1/dns-query -v https://example.com/
    

The HTTPS request to `1.1.1.1` carries the DNS query; the encrypted response carries the answer. From a network observer's perspective, only the HTTPS traffic is visible; the DNS query is hidden.

### 13.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** Walk the recursive resolution process for `www.example.com`. Name each query and what it returns.

Hint

Three layers of delegation: root, TLD, zone.

**Answer:** (1) The recursive resolver queries a root server for `www.example.com`. The root server responds with NS records for `.com` (the next level down the hierarchy) and glue (the A/AAAA records for those NS servers). (2) The resolver queries a `.com` server (chosen from the NS records returned in step 1) for `www.example.com`. The `.com` server responds with NS records for `example.com` plus glue. (3) The resolver queries an `example.com` server for `www.example.com`. The authoritative server responds with the A (or AAAA, or CNAME) record. The resolver caches each response according to its TTL and returns the final answer to the client. Each query is a UDP datagram, typically 50-200 bytes; total latency is the sum of the three round trips, often 100-300 ms for a cold lookup, sub-millisecond when cached.

**Q2.** What is the difference between DoH, DoT, and DoQ?

Hint

Different transports for encrypted DNS; same overall idea.

**Answer:** All three are encrypted variants of DNS, addressing the privacy and integrity problems of plaintext DNS over UDP. The differences are in the transport: _DoT (DNS over TLS, RFC 7858)_ : DNS queries inside TLS on TCP port 853. The standard DNS wire format is encapsulated in TLS records. Adopted by Android and some OSes for system-wide DNS. _DoH (DNS over HTTPS, RFC 8484)_ : DNS queries inside HTTPS (HTTP/2 typically) on TCP port 443. The query is encoded as a JSON object or DNS wire format inside an HTTPS request. Adopted by major browsers and increasingly by mobile OSes. The advantage: HTTPS traffic blends with general web traffic, harder to identify and block. _DoQ (DNS over QUIC, RFC 9250)_ : DNS queries inside QUIC on UDP port 853 (or some implementations use 443). Combines DoT-style framing with QUIC's faster handshakes and connection migration. Newest of the three; gaining adoption in 2024-2026. Functionally, all three protect against the same threats: passive eavesdropping (an ISP cannot see queries) and active man-in-the-middle (an attacker cannot modify responses without breaking TLS). The differences are operational: DoH integrates well with browsers; DoT integrates well with OS-level resolvers; DoQ promises lower latency once widely deployed.

**Q3.** Why do DNS records have TTLs, and what is the tradeoff in setting TTL values?

Hint

Trade caching efficiency against responsiveness to change.

**Answer:** TTL (Time-To-Live) tells a recursive resolver how long it can cache a record before re-querying. The tradeoff: _Low TTL_ (30-300 seconds): the record can change rapidly without leaving stale data in caches; useful for CDN edge IPs, DDoS-protection failover, load-balanced services with frequent rebalancing. The cost is higher load on authoritative servers (more re-queries) and potentially worse cache hit rates at recursive resolvers. _High TTL_ (86400 seconds = 1 day, or higher): the record is stable, cached widely, low query load on authoritative servers. The cost is that planned or unplanned changes propagate slowly (caches around the world hold the old value for up to the TTL). Operators choose based on stability of the record: stable corporate websites use 1-day TTLs; dynamic CDN endpoints use 60-second TTLs; root and TLD records use multi-day TTLs (rarely change). A common pattern: set TTL high under normal operation; reduce TTL temporarily before a planned migration so caches start to expire; perform the migration; restore the high TTL. The total propagation time is roughly the original TTL plus the new TTL.

**Q4.** Why was the original DNS UDP message size limited to 512 bytes, and how does EDNS0 work around the limit?

Hint

The IPv4 minimum MTU; fragmentation reliability.

**Answer:** The original DNS spec (RFC 1035, 1987) limited UDP messages to 512 bytes because the IPv4 minimum guaranteed MTU was 576 bytes, leaving 512 bytes for UDP payload (after IP and UDP headers). Any larger message could be fragmented at the IP layer, and IP fragmentation has long had reliability issues: some routers drop fragments, some firewalls block them, reassembly is buggy in some implementations. The DNS designers chose to limit DNS-over-UDP to 512 bytes for reliability; larger responses required the requester to retry over TCP. As DNS responses grew (DNSSEC signatures, IPv6 records, longer TXT records), the 512-byte limit became restrictive. EDNS0 (RFC 6891) addresses this: the requester includes an OPT pseudo-record in the query indicating the maximum UDP response size it can receive (typically 4096 bytes, though some networks support more). The authoritative server can return a response up to that size; if it would exceed, it sets the TC (truncated) flag, prompting the requester to retry over TCP. Modern resolvers and authoritative servers all support EDNS0 and routinely send responses larger than 512 bytes over UDP. The reliability issues with large UDP responses have been mitigated by careful path-MTU discovery and better router behavior, though some operators still see EDNS0 issues in specific networks.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A company's website goes offline because their DNS provider has an outage. Customers cannot reach the site even though the web servers are running. What strategies could the company have employed to mitigate this?

Hint

Multiple DNS providers, longer TTLs, anycast.

**Answer:** Mitigation strategies: (1) _Use multiple DNS providers (secondary DNS)_ : configure two or more authoritative DNS providers (e.g., AWS Route 53 and Cloudflare DNS). Both publish the same records; recursive resolvers query whichever is reachable. If one provider's network has an outage, the other handles queries seamlessly. The cost is operational complexity (keeping both in sync) and double DNS provider fees. (2) _Use anycast DNS_ : major DNS providers run anycast networks, so even one provider has many physical nameservers worldwide; an outage at one location doesn't take everyone offline. This is mostly automatic when using a major provider but worth confirming. (3) _Lower the TTL temporarily before incidents are detected_ : not really feasible since outages are unpredictable; useful only for planned migrations. (4) _Cache pinning at the client side_ : not standard but some applications cache DNS responses longer than the TTL when the authoritative server is unreachable, with a fallback grace period. (5) _Use a CDN as the front-end_ : many CDNs (Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai) provide DNS plus content delivery; if the CDN's DNS is down, the CDN provides the static fallback. (6) _Don't rely on a single DNS provider for your global authority_ : this is the consolidated lesson of multiple high-profile DNS outages (Dyn 2016, AWS Route 53 occasionally). The defense-in-depth principle: redundancy in DNS just as in other critical infrastructure. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design DNS architecture; watch for Lie #2 (no fallback strategy: relying on a single provider's SLA without backup) and Lie #4 (suggesting outdated mechanisms like increasing TTL after an outage starts, which doesn't help because caches already have the records).

**Q2.** A new web service wants HTTPS records (RFC 9460) to advertise HTTP/3 support. Walk through what the records should look like and what they enable.

Hint

HTTPS records replace the older alt-svc-discovery dance.

**Answer:** An HTTPS record (record type 65) carries connection parameters for the service, including supported ALPNs (HTTP versions), addresses, and optional parameters. Example zone configuration:
    
    
    example.com.        300 IN HTTPS 1 . alpn=h3,h2 ipv4hint=93.184.216.34 ipv6hint=2606:2800:220:1::1
    www.example.com.    300 IN HTTPS 1 . alpn=h3,h2
    

Field by field: priority (1, with lower being higher priority); target name (`.` means use the queried name itself, otherwise an alternative); parameters in key=value form. The `alpn` parameter lists supported ALPNs in priority order: `h3` means HTTP/3 over QUIC; `h2` means HTTP/2 over TLS. The `ipv4hint` and `ipv6hint` are optimizations: the client can use these IPs immediately without an extra A/AAAA lookup. What this enables: (1) The client (browser, mobile app) queries HTTPS records when it doesn't know which transport to use. Receiving "h3,h2" tells it HTTP/3 is available; it can attempt QUIC directly rather than fall back from HTTP/2. (2) Eliminates the "first connect to HTTP/2, get an alt-svc header, then switch to HTTP/3" roundtrip used by older browsers. (3) Supports any future ALPN values, enabling new protocols to be deployed by advertising in HTTPS records. Adoption: Chrome, Firefox, Safari, recent iOS/Android all use HTTPS records when available. Major CDNs publish HTTPS records on their customer domains automatically (Cloudflare, Fastly). The result: faster HTTP/3 adoption with less round-trip overhead. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to set up HTTPS records; watch for Lie #4 (using older alt-svc HTTP headers as the only mechanism, missing the modern DNS-based approach) and Lie #3 (confusing HTTPS DNS records with the HTTPS protocol—they're related but distinct concepts).

**Q3.** A network engineer suspects DNS spoofing is causing customers to be redirected to a malicious site. List the diagnostic steps and the mitigations available.

Hint

Use DoH or DoT for protected lookups; verify via DNSSEC; capture and inspect DNS traffic.

**Answer:** _Diagnostic steps_ : (1) Compare lookups across multiple resolvers: from a fresh client (not the suspected compromised network), query the same name via `1.1.1.1`, `8.8.8.8`, `9.9.9.9`, and the suspected ISP resolver. If results differ, one of them is incorrect. (2) Compare against authoritative: `dig +trace` the name to ensure you're seeing the authoritative response, not a spoofed one. (3) Check DNSSEC: if the domain is signed, validate the response (modern dig shows AD flag for validated responses). A failed validation suggests spoofing or DNSSEC misconfiguration. (4) Capture DNS traffic on the suspected network with tcpdump; look for unexpected responses, responses from the wrong source, response races (multiple responses for the same query). (5) Check the certificate of the destination: if the user is being redirected to a malicious site, the TLS certificate will not match (assuming the user's browser doesn't fall victim to MITM). _Mitigations_ : (1) Switch to DoH or DoT on all clients to encrypt DNS queries; the recursive resolver cannot be transparent to the network. (2) Configure DNSSEC validation on the resolver. (3) Use a trusted public resolver (`1.1.1.1`, `9.9.9.9`) rather than the ISP's resolver. (4) For corporate networks: deploy DoH or DoT to a known-good resolver from all clients; block plaintext DNS at the firewall. (5) Enable DoT/DoH at the OS level if possible (Android, recent iOS, Windows 11). (6) For high-value services, pin certificates in the application to prevent fraudulent certificate acceptance even if DNS is spoofed. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to plan the response; watch for Lie #4 (relying on DNSSEC alone for protection, but if the network blocks DNSSEC validation responses, this fails; encrypted transport is more robust).

**Q4.** A high-traffic service is seeing slow DNS resolution times for first-time clients (200-500ms before any HTTP traffic). The DNS records are correct. What is going on, and how to fix?

Hint

The first-time-resolution cost is the cold resolution; what can you do to warm it up?

**Answer:** _Diagnosis_ : 200-500ms is consistent with cold-cache DNS resolution: a recursive resolver that hasn't seen the name before must query root, TLD, and authoritative servers, each adding latency. For a global service with many recursive resolvers worldwide, "first-time" clients can mean "first client at this resolver in the last cache lifetime," which can happen frequently if the TTL is short or the resolver's cache is small. _Fixes_ : (1) _DNS preloading_ : in the application, perform DNS lookups for known dependencies during startup so resolutions are cached when actual requests happen. Browsers do this via `<link rel="dns-prefetch">` and `<link rel="preconnect">` hints in HTML; mobile apps can pre-resolve at app startup. (2) _Anycast nameservers_ : ensure authoritative nameservers are anycast (most managed DNS providers do this). The cold resolution then has fewer round-trip-to-Asia issues. (3) _Increase TTL on stable records_ : if records change rarely, TTLs of 3600 to 86400 reduce cache misses. (4) _Use HTTPS records (RFC 9460)_ : bundles A, AAAA, ALPN, and connection hints into one query, reducing the number of DNS round trips needed before HTTPS connection setup. (5) _Reduce dependency on DNS for the critical path_ : services can ship their DNS lookups along with the app (mobile apps embed initial connection IPs in the binary; web apps preload critical resources). (6) _Edge anycast_ : if the service is at a CDN, the CDN's anycast IP is announced by edges close to users; even cold DNS resolves to a nearby IP. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to improve DNS performance; watch for Lie #2 (suggesting lower TTLs to "fix" cold resolution, when lower TTLs actually increase cold-resolution frequency).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Argue (a) whether DNS encryption (DoH/DoT/DoQ) is a clear win for users or has notable downsides, (b) what the role of the OS resolver should be in 2026 and beyond, (c) what happens when DNS is fully encrypted but the network's QoS or security tools depend on seeing queries.

**Discussion:** (a) DNS encryption is a clear win for individual user privacy: ISPs and on-path observers can no longer harvest the lookups for advertising, surveillance, or filtering. It is a partial win for security: man-in-the-middle attacks are foiled if certificate validation is robust. The downside: parental controls, school filters, enterprise security tools that depend on DNS visibility lose their primary signal. Some networks (corporate, school) require knowing what users are accessing for legitimate reasons. (b) The OS resolver should remain the primary path but be configurable to use encrypted transport. Windows 11, recent macOS, Android all support DoH/DoT system-wide. The OS resolver respects the user's configured policy (which resolver, which transport) and applications use it. Applications (especially browsers) that override the OS resolver bypass user/admin policy, which is contentious. (c) When DNS is fully encrypted and the network cannot see queries: legitimate use cases need new approaches. Corporate networks: deploy DoH/DoT to a managed corporate resolver that the company controls (running its own DNS server, performing the logging/filtering at that server). Schools and parental control: similar approach; deploy a DNS-filtering resolver via DoH. ISPs are caught between privacy-respecting users (who want encryption) and regulatory or business requirements (DPI, content filtering, advertising). The 2026 reality: a slow transition where encrypted DNS becomes the default but managed-network resolvers handle visibility. By 2030 expect the picture to be settled: managed environments deploy their own resolvers; consumer ISPs offer DoH/DoT to consumers; passive observers lose visibility.
