The deeper insight: DNS is one of the last protocols where the network had visibility for free; encrypting it shifts power to endpoints, which is the same direction TLS pushed everything else.

**Q2.** Reflect on whether DNS, fundamentally a 1980s protocol, is well-suited to the 2026 internet. What features would a DNS designed today look like?

**Discussion:** DNS has aged remarkably well: the hierarchy, the recursive resolution, the caching model, the record-type extensibility all still work at internet scale 40 years later. Things that have been added: EDNS0 (modern message sizes), DNSSEC (authentication), encrypted transports (DoH/DoT/DoQ), HTTPS/SVCB records (extensibility for new use cases), new record types as needed. The protocol has been backward-compatibly extended dozens of times. If designing today: (1) Encryption would be the default (no plaintext UDP fallback). (2) The hierarchy would be similar but with cleaner trust delegation (DNSSEC-style chain of trust, but built-in not retrofitted). (3) Service discovery would be more first-class (rich service-locator records rather than the SRV+A combination). (4) Resolution would parallelize better (query multiple authoritative servers in parallel; return the first response). (5) DNS would integrate with discovery for cloud-native systems (a single protocol for global and cluster-local discovery, not a separate Kubernetes DNS). (6) Privacy-respecting resolvers would be assumed (resolvers don't keep logs of which client asked for what, with cryptographic enforcement). Probably retain: hierarchy, caching, TTLs, the record-type model. Probably drop: many legacy record types (HINFO, MINFO, etc.), the 512-byte UDP limit (already worked around by EDNS0). The practical reality: we're not designing today's DNS; we're incrementally evolving the 1980s DNS. The evolution is slow but durable; new features ship every few years; the protocol remains universally interoperable. The 2040 DNS will look much like the 2026 DNS, but with more encryption, more cloud-native integration, and probably some new record types we haven't conceived yet.

**Q3.** Consider service discovery in a future where billions of IoT devices each need to find each other. Will DNS scale, or will alternative mechanisms be needed?

**Discussion:** Scale challenges: (1) The number of unique names: billions of IoT devices imply billions of names. The current DNS handles ~hundreds of millions of domains; can it scale 10-100x? Probably yes, with careful zone sharding and efficient implementations. (2) Update rates: ephemeral devices (a sensor that joins and leaves rapidly) need their records to update at second-scale, not minute-scale. DNS's TTL model has lower bounds (cache pressure if TTL < 30s); cloud-native systems use this poorly. (3) Discovery: a device should be able to find services nearby (the nearest light controller, the local weather sensor); pure name-based DNS doesn't support spatial proximity queries well. (4) Privacy: IoT devices revealing their name to every recursive resolver is a privacy nightmare. _Alternative mechanisms emerging_ : (i) _mDNS / Bonjour_ : link-local multicast DNS for finding devices on the same network. Already deployed for printers, AirPlay, smart-home devices. Doesn't scale beyond a single subnet. (ii) _DNS-SD (Service Discovery)_ : extensions to DNS for finding services by type within a zone; complements mDNS for managed zones. (iii) _Service meshes and registries_ : Kubernetes-style discovery within a defined cluster. Doesn't scale to "all IoT devices everywhere" but works within an administrative domain. (iv) _Content-centric networking_ (CCN, NDN): rebuild the internet's discovery model around content names rather than location names. Research, not deployed. (v) _Distributed hash tables_ : peer-to-peer service-discovery layers (Kademlia, Chord). Used in some IoT protocols (Matter for smart home includes DHT-based discovery). The likely trajectory: DNS scales to billions of names in the 2020s-2030s with optimizations. mDNS+DNS-SD handles local discovery. Cluster-internal discovery uses Kubernetes-like service registries. Truly global IoT discovery is still being figured out; expect a mix of solutions rather than a single winner. The deeper insight: DNS is the universal "find by name" protocol; service discovery for ephemeral systems is a different problem with different tradeoffs.

### Chapter Summary

DNS is the protocol that turns names into addresses. The hierarchy (root → TLD → zone) maps directly to the structure of names; recursive resolvers walk this hierarchy on cache misses. Records have TTLs; caching is the protocol's primary optimization. Modern variants (DoH, DoT, DoQ) encrypt queries; DNSSEC authenticates responses; EDNS0 extends message sizes; HTTPS records (RFC 9460) accelerate HTTP/3 deployment.

The recursive resolver is the unsung workhorse: Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1`, Google's `8.8.8.8`, Quad9's `9.9.9.9` together handle a substantial fraction of global DNS traffic. The choice of resolver matters for performance (closer resolver = faster lookups) and privacy (some operators log queries; some don't).

Encrypted DNS transports (DoH, DoT, DoQ) are increasingly default in browsers, mobile OSes, and some desktop OSes. They protect against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks but reduce visibility for legitimate network management. The 2026 reality is mixed: encryption growing, managed networks adapting with their own resolvers.

Service discovery in cloud-native systems extends DNS-like ideas but with richer semantics (versions, traffic splitting, retry policies). Kubernetes DNS plus service meshes provide a layer beyond raw DNS for ephemeral microservices.

The wire-level artifact (`dig +trace` plus DoH via curl) is the canonical hands-on DNS exercise. Reading a trace once cements every concept in the chapter.

Chapter 14 starts Part VI: HTTP. We will trace HTTP semantics across versions (1.1, 2, 3), see what survives unchanged and what evolves at the wire, and meet Reza Hashemi's first decision: HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for Loom's API.

## Chapter 14: HTTP Semantics and Wire Evolution (1.1 → 2 → 3)

HTTP is the application protocol that ate the internet. What started in 1991 as a simple text protocol for serving hypertext documents now carries every flavor of internet traffic: API calls, video streaming, file transfer, real-time messaging, IoT telemetry, AI inference requests. The semantics of HTTP have remained surprisingly stable across 30+ years (methods, status codes, headers, MIME types) while the wire format has evolved dramatically (text-based HTTP/1.1 → binary-framed HTTP/2 → QUIC-based HTTP/3).

This chapter develops HTTP from two angles. First, the _semantics_ : methods, headers, status codes, caching, content negotiation. These are stable across versions. Second, the _wire evolution_ : HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking → HTTP/2's binary framing and multiplexing → HTTP/3's stream-per-request on QUIC. Each version solved real problems and introduced new ones.

We meet Reza Hashemi, our backend engineer protagonist at Loom, who must pick HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 for the company's main API. The wire-level artifact is the same `GET /index.html` request traced across all three versions, byte-by-byte.

By the end you should be able to read an HTTP request and response in any wire format, reason about which HTTP features survive across versions, and articulate the cost/benefit of picking each version for a new service.

### 14.1 HTTP Semantics: What Survives Across Versions

The semantics of HTTP are version-independent. Whether the bytes on the wire are HTTP/1.1 text, HTTP/2 binary frames, or HTTP/3 QUIC streams, the conceptual operations are the same.

#### 14.1.1 Methods

The HTTP methods, from RFC 9110 (the 2022 consolidation of HTTP semantics):

* **GET** : retrieve a resource. Idempotent (safe to retry).
* **HEAD** : like GET but returns only headers, no body. Idempotent.
* **POST** : submit data to a resource (often creates a new resource). NOT idempotent.
* **PUT** : replace a resource. Idempotent.
* **PATCH** : partially update a resource. NOT idempotent by default; some implementations make it so.
* **DELETE** : remove a resource. Idempotent.
* **OPTIONS** : query supported methods and CORS information. Idempotent.
* **CONNECT** : establish a tunnel (used by HTTPS proxies). Note: WebSocket over HTTP/1.1 uses the _Upgrade_ mechanism (RFC 6455), not CONNECT; WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) and HTTP/3 (RFC 9220) uses the _Extended CONNECT_ form. The two are easy to conflate but produce different wire shapes.
* **TRACE** : echo the request (mostly disabled for security reasons).

Idempotency matters because retries are common: clients retry on failure; CDNs and proxies retry on certain errors. Idempotent methods can be retried freely; POST and PATCH may not. The retry rules are encoded in the methods.

#### 14.1.2 Status Codes

The well-known three-digit codes in five families:

* **1xx** : informational. `100 Continue`, `101 Switching Protocols` (used in WebSocket upgrade).
* **2xx** : success. `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content`, `206 Partial Content` (range requests).
* **3xx** : redirection. `301 Moved Permanently`, `302 Found` (temporary), `304 Not Modified` (cache validation), `307 Temporary Redirect` (preserves method), `308 Permanent Redirect`.
* **4xx** : client error. `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden`, `404 Not Found`, `429 Too Many Requests`.
* **5xx** : server error. `500 Internal Server Error`, `502 Bad Gateway`, `503 Service Unavailable`, `504 Gateway Timeout`.

The semantics of each code are stable. New codes are added rarely (`451 Unavailable For Legal Reasons` in 2015; `425 Too Early` for HTTP 0-RTT in 2018). The taxonomy is durable.

#### 14.1.3 Headers

Headers carry metadata about the request or response. They are key-value pairs. The key set is partly standardized (Host, Content-Type, Authorization, etc.) and partly custom (X-Custom, X-Forwarded-For).

Standard request headers include: `Host` (mandatory in HTTP/1.1+), `User-Agent`, `Accept` (content negotiation), `Authorization`, `Cookie`, `Referer`, `If-None-Match` (conditional GET), `Range` (partial content).

Standard response headers include: `Content-Type`, `Content-Length`, `Cache-Control`, `Set-Cookie`, `ETag`, `Location` (for redirects), `Last-Modified`, `Strict-Transport-Security` (HSTS), `Content-Security-Policy`.

Headers are the extensibility point of HTTP. New features are usually added via new headers; the protocol versions stay stable, and any participant that doesn't understand a header ignores it.

#### 14.1.4 Caching

HTTP has a caching model embedded in the protocol:

* **Cache-Control** : response header indicating cacheability: `max-age=3600` (cache for 1 hour), `no-cache` (revalidate before use), `no-store` (don't cache at all), `public`/`private` (shared vs single-user caches).
* **ETag** and **If-None-Match** : conditional GET. The server's ETag is an opaque tag for the current resource version; the client sends `If-None-Match: <etag>` to ask "is this still current?"; the server returns `304 Not Modified` if so, or the new content with a new ETag if changed.
* **Last-Modified** and **If-Modified-Since** : timestamp-based conditional GET (legacy mechanism, replaced by ETags but still supported).
* **Vary** : indicates which request headers affect the response (e.g., `Vary: Accept-Encoding` means responses differ by encoding; caches must key on encoding).

The caching model is what makes CDNs effective: an edge server can serve a response from cache for hours without consulting the origin.

#### 14.1.5 Content Negotiation

The client tells the server what it wants via `Accept*` headers; the server picks the best match.

* `Accept: text/html, application/json` — content type preference.
* `Accept-Language: en-US, fr` — language preference.
* `Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd` — compression methods supported.

The server picks one and returns it; responds with `Content-Type` and `Content-Encoding` headers reflecting the choice.

#### 14.1.6 Idempotency and Safety

Methods classified along two axes:

* **Safe** : read-only, no side effects. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS.
* **Idempotent** : multiple identical requests have the same effect as one. GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE.

Non-safe, non-idempotent: POST, PATCH (typically).

The semantic guarantees inform retry behavior: clients and proxies retry idempotent requests freely; non-idempotent requests should not be retried automatically unless the client provides explicit idempotency keys (a common API pattern: `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>` header that lets the server deduplicate retries).

### 14.2 HTTP/1.1: The Original Wire Format

HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112) is the text-based protocol that dominated until 2015. A request looks like:
    
    
    GET /index.html HTTP/1.1
    Host: example.com
    User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 ...
    Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,*/*
    Connection: keep-alive
    
    

(blank line terminates headers; body follows if present)

A response:
    
    
    HTTP/1.1 200 OK
    Date: Mon, 17 May 2026 14:00:00 GMT
    Content-Type: text/html
    Content-Length: 1234
    Connection: keep-alive
    Cache-Control: max-age=3600
    
    <html>...</html>
    

Plain ASCII text. Header lines end in `\r\n`; blank line separates headers from body; the body's length is given by `Content-Length` or chunked transfer encoding.

#### 14.2.1 The Connection Model

In HTTP/1.0, each request required a fresh TCP connection (connect, request, response, close). HTTP/1.1 introduced persistent connections (`Connection: keep-alive`), allowing many requests over one connection.

Within a connection, HTTP/1.1 supported _pipelining_ : send multiple requests back-to-back without waiting for responses. Responses must come back in order. In practice, pipelining had compatibility issues with proxies (which couldn't always reorder responses correctly) and was disabled by default in most browsers.

So in practice: HTTP/1.1 sends one request, waits for the response, sends the next request, etc. The connection is reused but not parallelized.

#### 14.2.2 Head-of-Line Blocking at HTTP/1.1

A page might load 50 resources (HTML, CSS, JS, images, fonts). Over one HTTP/1.1 connection, these are serialized: each request waits for the previous response to complete. Loading the page takes the sum of all per-resource RTTs and processing times.

Browsers worked around this by opening multiple TCP connections in parallel (typically 6 connections per origin in classic browsers). This parallelizes 6 resources at a time but requires 6 sets of TCP+TLS handshakes; the resources are still serialized within each connection. Domains are sharded to get more parallelism: a page might load resources from `static1.example.com`, `static2.example.com`, etc., each domain getting its own 6 connections.

The result: HTTP/1.1 page loads are I/O-bound, dominated by handshakes and per-resource serialization. This is the inefficiency HTTP/2 set out to fix.

#### 14.2.3 Compression Limits

HTTP/1.1 supports compression of message bodies (`Content-Encoding: gzip`). Headers are NOT compressed. Repeated cookies, user-agent strings, accept headers, all sent in full with every request. On modern web pages with large cookies and many requests, headers can dominate request size.

### 14.3 HTTP/2: Binary Framing and Multiplexing

HTTP/2 (RFC 9113, originally RFC 7540 in 2015) replaces the text format with binary frames and multiplexes many requests over one connection.

#### 14.3.1 Frames

HTTP/2 messages are split into binary frames, each with a small header:
    
    
    +-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
    | Length (24 bits) | Type | Flags | StreamID |
    +-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
    | Frame payload (variable)              |
    +-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
    

Frame types include: DATA (request/response body), HEADERS (request/response headers, compressed with HPACK), SETTINGS (connection parameters), PING (keepalive), GOAWAY (graceful shutdown), WINDOW_UPDATE (flow control), PRIORITY (stream prioritization), CONTINUATION (large headers).

#### 14.3.2 Streams and Multiplexing

A connection contains multiple _streams_ , each carrying one request-response pair (in the simplest case). Streams are identified by 31-bit stream IDs (client-initiated streams use odd IDs; server-initiated use even). Many streams can be in flight simultaneously; their frames are interleaved over the connection.

The result: a single TCP connection can carry hundreds of concurrent requests, each with its own state. Page loads parallelize naturally.

#### 14.3.3 HPACK: Header Compression

Headers in HTTP/2 are compressed using HPACK (RFC 7541): a custom encoding designed for HTTP headers. Common headers (`:method`, `:scheme`, `:authority`, `:path`, `:status`) get short representations; repeated headers (cookies, user-agent) are referenced from a shared table. Compression ratios of 10:1 are typical for modern web traffic.

#### 14.3.4 Server Push (Deprecated)

HTTP/2 introduced _server push_ : the server could send resources the client hadn't asked for yet (e.g., the CSS the client will need after parsing the HTML). The idea was to eliminate the "first request, parse, second request" round trip.

In practice, server push was hard to use correctly: the server didn't know what the client had cached, often pushing unnecessary data. HTTP/2 server push is deprecated as of 2022 (Chrome removed support; other browsers followed). RFC 9113 leaves it in the spec but marks it as not recommended.

#### 14.3.5 Head-of-Line Blocking Returns

HTTP/2 multiplexing solves head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer: many requests in flight, each independent. But it sits on TCP, which has its own head-of-line blocking: if a TCP segment is lost, all streams in the connection stall waiting for retransmission.

This is the limitation that motivated HTTP/3.

### 14.4 HTTP/3: HTTP over QUIC

HTTP/3 (RFC 9114, 2022) is HTTP semantics carried over QUIC instead of TCP. The protocol-level differences:

#### 14.4.1 Mapping HTTP/2 onto QUIC

HTTP/3 inherits HTTP/2's frame-based design but maps frames onto QUIC streams rather than a single TCP byte stream. Each HTTP request gets its own QUIC stream; frames within a request flow over that stream.

The benefit: a packet loss in one stream doesn't block other streams. Per-stream head-of-line blocking is gone.

#### 14.4.2 QPACK: HTTP/3's HPACK

HTTP/2's HPACK requires header ordering between requests (the dynamic table is shared and ordered). For HTTP/3 over QUIC with concurrent streams, this becomes problematic: streams might process headers out of order. QPACK (RFC 9204) solves this by separating the dynamic-table updates onto their own stream, with explicit ordering primitives.

#### 14.4.3 Connection Setup

HTTP/3 uses QUIC's handshake: 1 RTT for new connections, 0 RTT for resumed connections (with replay-safety constraints). HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP needs 2 RTTs.

#### 14.4.4 Connection Migration

HTTP/3 inherits QUIC's connection migration: the client's IP can change without breaking the connection. For mobile users handing off between Wi-Fi and cellular, this is a major user-experience improvement.

### 14.5 Reza's Decision: HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 for Loom

Reza Hashemi, senior backend engineer at Loom (a fictional real-time collaborative product), is choosing the HTTP version for the company's main API.

Loom's traffic profile:

* Real-time messaging via WebSocket (a separate decision; covered in Chapter 16).
* REST/JSON API for non-real-time operations: about 60% GETs (cacheable), 30% POSTs/PUTs (state-changing), 10% other.
* 70% of users on mobile networks (cellular or Wi-Fi); 30% on desktop wired or Wi-Fi.
* Average request: 2-5 KB. Typical response: 5-20 KB. Some larger responses for document loads (up to 200 KB).
* Reza's stack: Cloudflare Workers (which support HTTP/3 natively), Durable Objects, Postgres backend.

Reza's analysis:

_HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP (current baseline)_ :

* Pro: mature, broadly supported, debugging tools mature.
* Pro: works on every network including the small fraction that block UDP.
* Con: head-of-line blocking on lossy mobile networks.
* Con: 2-RTT handshake for new connections.

_HTTP/3 over QUIC over UDP_ :

* Pro: 1-RTT handshake (faster initial requests); 0-RTT for repeat connections.
* Pro: connection migration (mobile users on the move).
* Pro: no head-of-line blocking (better on lossy networks).
* Con: blocked on some restrictive networks (~5-10% of traffic).
* Con: less mature observability (qlog vs tcpdump).
* Con: server-side CPU cost noticeably higher (typical reports are in the 10-30% range for HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2 on the same workload, dominated by user-space TLS+QUIC crypto versus in-kernel TCP; numbers vary widely with workload and TLS hardware acceleration).

Reza's decision: deploy HTTP/3 with HTTP/2 fallback. Cloudflare's `1.1.1.1` already does this for its own services; Workers handle the dual-stack automatically. The 5-10% of traffic on UDP-blocked networks falls back to HTTP/2 with minimal latency penalty (the client tries QUIC first; after 100-200ms timeout, switches to HTTP/2).

Validation metrics for the rollout (similar to Jin's in Chapter 10):

* p50 connection setup: should drop from ~150ms to ~75ms.
* p99 connection setup: should drop from ~500ms to ~250ms.
* Mobile users' bounce rate (page loads abandoned in <2s): should drop by 1-3%.
* CDN egress cost: should stay flat or rise <5% due to QUIC's slightly larger headers.

Reza ships the migration over 6 weeks. The metrics confirm expectations. The company's "Loom feels fast" customer feedback improves slightly. The decision is judged a success.

We will see Reza again in Chapter 15 (HTTP/3 and QUIC end-to-end), Chapter 16 (WebSocket Hibernation), and Chapter 21 (cache-key engineering for Loom).

### 14.6 The Wire-Level Artifact: Same GET, Three Versions

A simple HTTP request: `GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: example.com\r\n\r\n`.

**HTTP/1.1 over TCP (bytes after TCP+TLS handshake)** :
    
    
    GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\n
    Host: example.com\r\n
    User-Agent: curl/8.0.0\r\n
    Accept: */*\r\n
    \r\n
    

~80 bytes plaintext (encrypted inside TLS), readable in `tcpdump -A` if TLS is disabled.

**HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP** :

Binary frame format. The HEADERS frame containing the same request:
    
    
    00 00 1c 01 05 00 00 00 01    [frame header: length=28, type=HEADERS, flags=END_STREAM(0x01)+END_HEADERS(0x04)=0x05, R=0, stream=1]
    82                            [:method: GET (HPACK static table index 2)]
    85                            [:path: /index.html (HPACK static table index 5)]
    87                            [:scheme: https (HPACK static table index 7)]
    41 88 9d 29 ad 17 18 63 c7 8f [:authority: example.com (literal with incremental indexing, name index 1, Huffman value 8 bytes)]
    40 0a 75 73 65 72 2d 61 67 65 6e 74 ...
                                  [user-agent: curl/8.4 (literal, not indexed)]
    ...
    

(The HPACK static table is fixed by RFC 7541 Appendix A. Index 2 is `:method GET`; index 5 is `:path /index.html`; index 7 is `:scheme https`. An indexed-header-field representation encodes one of these as a single byte with the high bit set, so `0x82`, `0x85`, `0x87` respectively. The fourth and fifth lines show literal representations for headers whose _names_ are in the static table but whose _values_ are not — those use the incremental-indexing or literal-without-indexing forms with longer encodings.)

Compressed via HPACK; roughly 50-60 bytes for the equivalent of HTTP/1.1's 80 bytes. The frame is wrapped in TLS records.

**HTTP/3 over QUIC** :

Inside a QUIC stream, a similar binary HEADERS frame compressed via QPACK. The QUIC stream is encapsulated in QUIC packets (with their own framing). The encrypted bytes look opaque in tcpdump; you need qlog to decode them.

Side-by-side latency for a typical first-page load on 100ms RTT mobile:

Phase | HTTP/1.1+TLS | HTTP/2+TLS | HTTP/3+QUIC | HTTP/3 0-RTT  
---|---|---|---|---  
TCP handshake | 100ms | 100ms | (in QUIC) | (in QUIC)  
TLS handshake | 100ms | 100ms | (in QUIC) | (in QUIC)  
QUIC handshake | - | - | 100ms | 0ms  
HTTP request | 100ms | 100ms | 100ms | 0ms  
HTTP response | (start) | (start) | (start) | (immediate)  
**Time to first byte** | **300ms** | **300ms** | **200ms** | **~100ms**  
  
These are theoretical lower bounds. Real-world numbers vary with congestion, server processing time, and so on. The QUIC improvement is real and substantial for mobile traffic.

### 14.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What semantics survive across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3? What changes?

Hint

Methods, status codes, headers stay; wire format changes.

**Answer:** _Semantics that survive (i.e., the same in all versions)_ : (1) The set of methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, PATCH, etc.) and their idempotency/safety guarantees. (2) The status code taxonomy (1xx, 2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx) and the specific codes (200 OK, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error, etc.). (3) Header names and their meanings (Host, Content-Type, Cache-Control, Authorization, Cookie, etc.). (4) Caching semantics (Cache-Control directives, ETag, conditional requests via If-None-Match). (5) Content negotiation (Accept, Accept-Language, Accept-Encoding). (6) URL structure (scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment). (7) MIME types (text/html, application/json, image/png). _Wire format that changes_ : (1) HTTP/1.1 is plaintext over TCP with line-based framing; HTTP/2 is binary frames over a single TCP connection with multiplexing; HTTP/3 is binary frames over QUIC streams. (2) Headers are uncompressed in HTTP/1.1, HPACK-compressed in HTTP/2, QPACK-compressed in HTTP/3. (3) HTTP/2's server push was specified but is now deprecated; HTTP/3 inherits this. (4) Connection setup: HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use TCP (with HTTPS adding TLS on top); HTTP/3 uses QUIC (with TLS 1.3 integrated). (5) Head-of-line blocking: present in HTTP/1.1 (serial responses) and HTTP/2 (TCP-level), absent in HTTP/3 (per-stream independence). The application programmer rarely sees the wire format differences; they program against HTTP semantics via libraries (curl, fetch, requests, axios) that abstract the wire details. The same `fetch()` call works across all three versions, with the library negotiating the protocol.

**Q2.** Explain head-of-line blocking in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3.

Hint

Where does blocking happen, and what mitigates it?

**Answer:** _HTTP/1.1_ : head-of-line blocking happens at the HTTP layer. Each request is serialized on a connection; the next request cannot be sent until the current response completes. Browsers mitigate this by opening multiple TCP connections to the same origin (typically 6) and by sharding domains across multiple subdomains. The mitigation is partial; large pages with many resources still suffer. _HTTP/2_ : head-of-line blocking is eliminated at the HTTP layer through stream multiplexing. Many requests can flow concurrently over one connection. But HTTP/2 sits on TCP, which still has its own head-of-line blocking: a single lost TCP segment stalls all streams in the connection until the retransmission arrives, because TCP must deliver bytes in order. So HTTP/2's HOL blocking is at the transport layer, not the application layer. On clean networks, this is rare; on lossy mobile networks, this is common and costly. _HTTP/3_ : head-of-line blocking is eliminated at both layers. QUIC streams are independent; a loss in one stream does not block other streams. Each request flows over its own QUIC stream; concurrent requests are truly independent. This is the principal motivation for HTTP/3's existence: take the HTTP/2 multiplexing model and put it on a transport that doesn't reintroduce blocking.

**Q3.** What is HPACK, and why does QPACK exist?

Hint

HPACK assumed ordered frames; QPACK handles concurrent streams.

**Answer:** HPACK (RFC 7541) is HTTP/2's header compression algorithm. The design: a static table of well-known headers (`:method`, `:scheme`, `:status`, `cache-control`, etc., with common values) plus a dynamic table that grows as the connection sees new header values. Both sender and receiver maintain synchronized copies of the dynamic table; when a header is sent, it can be referenced by index into the table rather than spelled out. Compression ratios of 10:1 or better are typical for modern web traffic with many cookies and repeated headers. HPACK works in HTTP/2 because the streams' frames arrive in order on a single TCP connection; the sender and receiver process them in the same order, keeping the dynamic table in sync. QPACK (RFC 9204) is HTTP/3's header compression. It exists because HTTP/3 over QUIC has _concurrent streams_ with no guaranteed ordering between them. If HTTP/3 used HPACK as-is, two concurrent streams could arrive at the receiver in different orders than they were sent, causing the dynamic table to desync. QPACK addresses this by separating the dynamic-table updates onto their own special streams (one for encoder-to-decoder updates), with explicit ordering. The header frames on regular streams reference the dynamic table; if a reference is to a table entry that the decoder hasn't processed yet, the decoder waits for that entry's update. The cost is a small amount of additional complexity; the benefit is correct header compression in a multi-stream concurrent transport. Both HPACK and QPACK use Huffman coding for literal strings, achieving similar compression ratios.

**Q4.** Why was HTTP/2 server push deprecated?

Hint

The server doesn't know what the client has cached.

**Answer:** HTTP/2 server push allowed the server to proactively send resources to the client without waiting for the client's explicit request. The intent: when the server returns an HTML page, it could push the CSS and JS files the client would need next, saving one round trip. In practice, server push had multiple problems: (1) _The server doesn't know what the client has cached_ : pushing a file the client already has wastes bandwidth and may displace useful cached data. The "Push Cache Digest" mechanism was proposed to communicate the client's cache state to the server, but was never widely deployed. (2) _Resource priority confusion_ : pushing a low-priority resource ahead of a high-priority client request could starve important requests. The priority system was complex and inconsistently implemented. (3) _Diminishing returns_ : HTTP/2's multiplexing already reduced the cost of fetching multiple resources; the additional savings from server push were small for most use cases. (4) _Implementation complexity_ : server push required application-level logic to identify what to push and when, deployment complexity in CDNs and edge servers, and client-side handling. The complexity was high relative to the benefit. (5) _Better alternatives emerged_ : the 103 Early Hints status code (RFC 8297) provides a similar performance benefit by sending hints about resources the client should fetch, without speculatively transferring data. The client then makes its own requests, with the benefit of knowing what to fetch earlier in the pipeline. The deprecation: in 2022, Chrome removed server push support. Other browsers followed. RFC 9113 (the HTTP/2 revision) retains the spec but marks server push as not recommended. HTTP/3 inherits this status. The lesson: protocol features that look good on paper can fail in practice if the operational complexity exceeds the benefit. Server push was elegant; the 103 Early Hints status code is pragmatic.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** Reza Hashemi's API decision: argue for or against deploying HTTP/3 for the API. Use the metrics from §14.5 plus your own reasoning.

Hint

Mobile audience + lossy networks favor HTTP/3.

**Answer:** _Argument for HTTP/3_ : (1) 70% of users on mobile networks, where HTTP/3's improvements are largest: faster handshake, no head-of-line blocking on lossy paths, connection migration across network handoffs. (2) The expected p50 reduction in connection setup time (from 150ms to 75ms) directly improves perceived API responsiveness. (3) p99 improvements (500ms to 250ms) help the tail latency that is most disruptive to user experience. (4) Cloudflare Workers handle the dual-stack automatically; the engineering cost is low. (5) The 5-10% of users on UDP-blocked networks fall back to HTTP/2 cleanly; no regression. (6) The 15% CPU cost is acceptable for an API server; in fact, Cloudflare Workers absorb most of this cost. (7) Future-proofs the stack: HTTP/3 is the modern direction; deploying now sets up for further protocol evolutions. _Argument against HTTP/3_ : (1) Some risk of unknown issues on specific carriers or network configurations; thorough testing required. (2) Operational tooling (debugging, monitoring) is less mature for HTTP/3 than HTTP/2; engineers may need to learn qlog. (3) The 15% CPU cost on origin servers may not be negligible at very high scale. (4) Maintaining two protocol stacks (HTTP/3 + HTTP/2 fallback) is operational complexity. _Decision_ : deploy HTTP/3. The benefit for mobile users is real and measurable; the engineering cost is bounded; the fallback handles edge cases. This matches what Cloudflare, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others have done for their own services. Most companies in 2026 should be moving to HTTP/3 for new services. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to analyze; watch for Lie #3 (recommending HTTP/2 because "HTTP/3 is too new" when the latter has been in production at hyperscale since 2018) and Lie #4 (recommending TLS 1.2 configurations that don't apply to QUIC).

**Q2.** A developer is writing a REST API client that sometimes retries failed requests. Which methods can the client safely retry, and which require additional caution?

Hint

Idempotency.

**Answer:** _Safe to retry without caution (idempotent)_ : GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT, DELETE. These methods are defined to have the same effect whether executed once or many times. Multiple retries of a GET fetch the same data; multiple retries of a DELETE leave the resource deleted; multiple retries of a PUT leave the resource at the specified state. _Requires caution (not idempotent)_ : POST, PATCH. POST typically creates a new resource (a new entity each retry); PATCH typically applies a partial update (depending on the patch semantics, may not be idempotent). Retrying these can cause: duplicate resources, double charges, double messages, double deletions if the original succeeded but the response was lost. _Best practices_ : (1) For non-idempotent operations, include an `Idempotency-Key` header (a UUID generated by the client). The server stores recently-seen idempotency keys with their results; a retry with the same key returns the original result without re-executing. Stripe pioneered this pattern; many APIs now use it. (2) For idempotent operations, retry with exponential backoff and jitter to avoid synchronized retries from overwhelming the server. Initial backoff of 100-200ms, doubled each retry, with up to 50% jitter, max 5-10 retries. (3) Distinguish retriable failures (5xx server errors, network errors, 429 rate limits) from non-retriable failures (4xx client errors, especially 400 Bad Request, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, where retrying produces the same error). (4) Use Retry-After header from 503 and 429 responses to know when to retry. (5) For long retries, monitor and alert on cascading failure (many retries amplifying load on a struggling service). _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to write retry logic; watch for Lie #6 (no jitter or exponential backoff, leading to synchronized retry storms) and Lie #2 (retrying all 4xx errors, when 400/401/403/404 should not be retried because retry will not succeed).

**Q3.** A web application serves static files (CSS, JS, images). The team wants to maximize cacheability. Design the Cache-Control strategy.

Hint

Different resource types have different cacheability characteristics.

**Answer:** _For immutable, versioned static assets_ (e.g., `/static/js/app-a3b8c.js` where the hash is in the URL): `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. The `max-age=31536000` is 1 year; `immutable` tells the cache the content will never change (so it doesn't bother revalidating). This is the gold standard for hash-named asset URLs; the file can be cached effectively forever. _For changeable assets without versioning_ (e.g., `/index.html`): `Cache-Control: public, max-age=300, must-revalidate`. The 5-minute max-age balances freshness with performance; `must-revalidate` requires the cache to check with the origin once expired (using ETag) rather than serve stale. _For user-specific or private content_ : `Cache-Control: private, max-age=0, no-cache`. Private prevents shared caches (CDNs) from caching; `no-cache` forces revalidation every time. _For API responses (mostly fresh)_ : `Cache-Control: no-cache` plus an ETag header. The browser caches the response; on subsequent requests, sends `If-None-Match: <etag>`; server responds 304 Not Modified if unchanged, returning small validation response rather than full body. _For sensitive data_ : `Cache-Control: no-store`. Forbids any caching, including in memory. Use for authentication tokens, payment info, etc. _Implementation considerations_ : (1) Use unique URLs for unique resource versions (hash-in-filename). This is the single most impactful caching practice. (2) Set ETag from a strong hash of the content (e.g., SHA-256 prefix). (3) Use Vary header when responses differ by request headers (e.g., `Vary: Accept-Encoding` for compressed responses). (4) Set Cache-Control consistently across all responses; don't rely on browser defaults. (5) For CDN caching specifically, use `s-maxage` to set CDN cache lifetime independently from browser cache lifetime. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design caching; watch for Lie #4 (recommending outdated headers like Pragma: no-cache, which is HTTP/1.0 legacy and ignored by modern proxies) and Lie #2 (omitting Vary header, leading to wrong cached responses for different Accept-Encoding clients).

**Q4.** A user reports that a website is slow on their mobile phone. Their wired desktop loads in 1.5s; phone takes 6s. The site uses HTTP/1.1. Diagnose and recommend.

Hint

HTTP/1.1's specific weaknesses on mobile.

**Answer:** _Diagnosis_ : HTTP/1.1 has multiple weaknesses on mobile that combine to produce the slowdown: (1) Per-connection serialization: each TCP connection serves requests one at a time. With 50 resources and 6 parallel connections, each connection handles ~8 resources serially. Cellular RTT of 80-150ms means each resource costs at least one RTT; 8 resources × 100ms = 800ms minimum per connection. (2) Handshake costs: 6 TCP+TLS handshakes per origin at startup, each costing 2 RTT = 200ms, so 6 × 200ms = 1.2s before any resource can be fetched. (3) Header overhead: HTTP/1.1 sends full headers per request, no compression. With cookies and modern headers, request headers can be 1-2 KB; 50 requests × 1.5 KB = 75 KB just for headers. On mobile uplink at 1-10 Mbps, this is hundreds of milliseconds. (4) Cellular network loss patterns: bursty loss triggers TCP retransmissions; HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking compounds with TCP's. _Recommendations_ : (1) _Upgrade to HTTP/2 or HTTP/3_. HTTP/2 alone provides multiplexing (one TCP connection handles all requests) and HPACK (header compression). HTTP/3 adds QUIC's faster handshake and no head-of-line blocking on lossy networks. Expected improvement: 2-4x faster page loads on mobile. (2) _Use a CDN_ : serves resources from edge servers close to the user, reducing RTT. Most CDNs support HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 by default. (3) _Reduce resource count_ : bundle multiple small files into larger ones; inline critical CSS; use sprite sheets for icons. The "many small files" pattern is HTTP/1.1-specific anti-pattern; HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 handle many small files efficiently. (4) _Optimize image delivery_ : WebP, AVIF, or modern formats are 30-50% smaller than JPEG; lazy-load below-fold images. (5) _Use service workers_ for caching: aggressive caching of static resources reduces network dependency on repeat visits. _Expected outcome after upgrades_ : mobile page load drops from 6s to 1.5-2s. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to suggest optimizations; watch for Lie #3 (recommending HTTP/1.1 optimizations like domain sharding, which is now anti-pattern with HTTP/2; or suggesting HTTP/2 server push, which is deprecated).

#### Think Deeper

**Q1.** Argue (a) why HTTP semantics have proven so stable across 30+ years, (b) whether they will continue to be stable or will fragment as new use cases emerge, (c) what the next major HTTP extension is likely to be.

**Discussion:** (a) HTTP semantics have been stable because they were well-designed for the resource-oriented use case: name a resource by URL, perform an operation (GET, POST, etc.), receive a status code and content. This model fits an enormous range of applications (documents, APIs, files, streams). The extensibility points (headers, methods, status codes) accommodate new needs without breaking existing ones. The protocol designed for fetching hypertext documents in 1991 turned out to be the right abstraction for almost everything that came later. (b) Continued stability is likely, with selective additions. The current model has been validated by 30 years and trillions of HTTP transactions per day; replacing it would require enormous coordination. But specific application domains may diverge into specialized protocols: real-time messaging (WebSockets, server-sent events), media streaming (DASH/HLS), real-time bidding (RTBP), interactive systems (WebRTC for media; WebSocket for control). These coexist with HTTP rather than replacing it. (c) Likely next major extensions: (i) _HTTP for IoT_ : protocols like CoAP and MQTT serve IoT today; some integration with HTTP semantics is likely. (ii) _Decentralized HTTP_ : protocols like IPFS, content-addressed storage extending HTTP to address content by hash rather than by URL. (iii) _AI-aware HTTP_ : headers and methods for LLM streaming, partial responses, tool-use protocols. The Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google AI APIs are already extending HTTP in custom ways. (iv) _Better multiplexing for video_ : media-over-QUIC (MoQ, an IETF draft from 2024 onward) adds video-specific framing on top of QUIC. (v) _Continued evolution of HTTP/3 itself_ : more efficient extension mechanisms, better congestion control, deeper integration with applications. The protocol's evolution is incremental and will remain so; abrupt replacement is unlikely.

**Q2.** Reflect on whether the HTTP/1.1 -> HTTP/2 transition was a clear net positive or whether the operational complexity (server push, prioritization, multiplexing) outweighed the benefits. What would have been a simpler alternative?

**Discussion:** HTTP/2 was a net positive for the web's performance but introduced complexity that has been gradually pruned. The benefits: massive multiplexing (essentially infinite parallel requests per connection); HPACK header compression (often 10x smaller); reduced connection setup overhead. The complexity: server push (deprecated 2022); priority signaling (complex, inconsistently implemented); stream-level flow control (interacts in subtle ways with TCP); HPACK's stateful dynamic table (works but is the source of various edge cases). A simpler alternative would have been "HTTP/1.1 with multiplexing": keep the text protocol, add a simple stream-id prefix per message, allow many in flight, use gzip on header lines. This would have captured most of the benefits with less complexity. The IETF chose binary framing because: (i) parsing efficiency at scale (binary is faster to parse than text); (ii) it forced upgrade conversations (HTTP/1.1 with extensions would have languished as legacy); (iii) it set up the framework for HTTP/3's eventual stream-based design. With hindsight, the binary-framing decision is mixed. The benefit is real but the cost was higher than expected, and some of the complexity (server push, prioritization v1) didn't pay off. HTTP/2's deprecated features are evidence of design overshoot. HTTP/3 is doing better: simpler design, focused on the wins (multiplexing without HOL blocking), letting the protocol do less.

**Q3.** Consider HTTP's role in the AI era. Will the resource-oriented model (URLs identifying things, methods operating on them) extend gracefully to AI agent workflows? Or will a new protocol be needed?

**Discussion:** HTTP can extend to AI workflows, with some stretching. The current pattern is: AI APIs are HTTP services. You POST a request with a model, prompt, and parameters; you GET or stream back a response. The semantics fit. Things that strain HTTP: (1) _Long-running operations_ : an AI agent doing a multi-step task may take minutes. HTTP's request-response model with a 30-second default timeout is awkward. Workarounds: long polling, server-sent events, WebSockets, callbacks via webhooks. (2) _Streaming responses_ : token-by-token generation is naturally streaming; HTTP/1.1's chunked encoding handles this, but client libraries had to learn to handle it. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 streams are clean for this. (3) _Bidirectional communication_ : agent workflows often involve back-and-forth between models and tools. Pure request-response is awkward; WebSockets work; some specialized protocols emerging (Anthropic's MCP, OpenAI's tool-use mechanisms). (4) _State-heavy interactions_ : agent conversations are stateful; HTTP is stateless. Workarounds: explicit session tokens, conversation IDs. (5) _Resource modeling_ : AI conversations don't fit cleanly into resource-oriented thinking. A conversation is more like a chat than a document. HTTP's status codes and headers don't quite capture the semantics. The 2026 reality: HTTP is the substrate for AI APIs; specific AI services build their own conventions on top; some new protocols emerging (MCP, MoQ-style streaming, agent-to-agent protocols). The likely future: HTTP remains the underlying transport; richer AI-specific protocols live on top (similar to how gRPC lives on HTTP/2). The resource-oriented model survives but is augmented; truly novel protocols may emerge for narrow use cases (multi-agent communication, real-time multi-modal AI). HTTP probably persists as "the transport" but not as "the agent communication standard." The pattern recurs: HTTP is the substrate, specific use cases get specialized layers on top.

### Chapter Summary

HTTP semantics (methods, status codes, headers, caching, content negotiation) have been remarkably stable for 30+ years. The wire format has evolved through three major generations: HTTP/1.1 (text, single-request-at-a-time per connection, head-of-line blocking), HTTP/2 (binary frames, multiplexing, HPACK header compression, but still TCP HOL blocking), and HTTP/3 (QUIC streams, no HOL blocking, faster handshakes, connection migration).

HTTP/2's headline features (multiplexing, HPACK, prioritization) solved real problems but introduced complexity. Some features (server push) have been deprecated. HTTP/3 is HTTP/2's logical successor with the TCP-level HOL blocking eliminated by moving to QUIC.

Reza Hashemi's decision (HTTP/2 vs HTTP/3 for Loom's API) illustrates the practical tradeoffs: HTTP/3 is the modern direction with measurable benefits for mobile users; HTTP/2 fallback handles the small minority on UDP-blocked networks. The decision matches the industry trajectory.

The wire-level artifact (the same GET request traced across HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and HTTP/3) shows how the same operation manifests differently at each version. The semantics are the same; the wire bytes differ dramatically.

Chapter 15 goes deeper into HTTP/3 and QUIC end-to-end: connection migration, qlog observability, 0-RTT replay safety, ALPN negotiation, MTU and fallback discipline. Jin Park returns; his LTE-to-Wi-Fi handoff is the case study for connection migration.

## Chapter 15: HTTP/3 and QUIC End-to-End

Chapter 10 introduced QUIC; Chapter 14 placed HTTP/3 on the wire-evolution timeline. This chapter goes end-to-end: a real HTTP/3 connection from QUIC handshake to first response byte, with qlog/qvis observability, connection migration as a daily feature, the 0-RTT replay safety constraint as the canonical gotcha, HTTP/2 trailers and gRPC as the place where production teams trip, and the ALPN, MTU, and fallback rules for a real deployment.

We follow Jin Park's LTE-to-Wi-Fi handoff scenario in detail. The wire-level artifact is a real HTTP/3 deployment checklist plus a captured `curl --http3` test and a qlog dump.

By the end you should be able to operate HTTP/3 in production: deploy it, monitor it, debug it, fall back gracefully when needed.

### 15.1 Tracing a Real HTTP/3 Connection

A fresh HTTP/3 connection from a mobile client to a server:
    
    
    T+0ms      Client sends QUIC Initial packet (CRYPTO frame with ClientHello, plus stream 0 with HTTP/3 SETTINGS)
    T+~80ms    Server sends QUIC Initial (ACK + ServerHello) + Handshake (Cert, CertVerify, Finished)
    T+~80ms    Client sends QUIC Handshake (Finished) + 1-RTT (HTTP/3 request HEADERS on stream 0)
    T+~160ms   Server sends 1-RTT (HTTP/3 HEADERS for response, plus DATA frames)
    

Compared to HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP (which would have taken 240ms total for the same trace), QUIC saves one RTT for new connections. For repeat connections with 0-RTT, the request goes in the first packet, and the response arrives at T+80ms; that is a 160ms improvement.

The connection is identified by a _connection ID_ (CID), a variable-length value (0–20 bytes per RFC 9000 §5.1; 8 bytes is the common deployment choice). Each side chooses the CIDs it wants its peer to use when addressing packets to it; both sides can rotate CIDs during the connection. The server's load balancer can route on the CID rather than the 4-tuple, which means the connection can survive a client IP change.

#### 15.1.1 Stream-per-Request

In HTTP/3, each request-response pair runs on its own QUIC stream (typically a client-initiated bidirectional stream, IDs 0, 4, 8, 12, ...). Within a stream:

  1. Client sends HEADERS frame (compressed via QPACK).
  2. Server responds with HEADERS frame (response status and headers).
  3. Server sends DATA frame(s) with the response body.
  4. Optionally, server sends HEADERS frame as trailers (for gRPC-style trailing metadata).
  5. Server marks the stream complete by setting FIN on the last frame.

Multiple requests run as concurrent streams. A drop on one stream's packets does not block other streams. This is the principal HTTP/3 win over HTTP/2.

#### 15.1.2 Frame Types

HTTP/3 frame types (RFC 9114):

* **HEADERS** (type 0x01): request or response headers, compressed via QPACK.
* **DATA** (type 0x00): request or response body bytes.
* **CANCEL_PUSH** (type 0x03): related to server push (deprecated).
* **SETTINGS** (type 0x04): connection-level settings.
* **PUSH_PROMISE** (type 0x05): server push (deprecated).
* **GOAWAY** (type 0x07): graceful shutdown.
* **MAX_PUSH_ID** (type 0x0D): server push (deprecated).

Most modern traffic is HEADERS and DATA frames; the rest are control. SETTINGS is exchanged once at connection setup to negotiate per-connection parameters (max header table size, etc.).

### 15.2 qlog and qvis: Observability

Standard tcpdump captures show encrypted QUIC packets; you cannot read them without the keys. The qlog format (`draft-ietf-quic-qlog-main-schema` and `draft-ietf-quic-qlog-quic-events`; aligned with RFC 9000 events but a separate specification) is the canonical observability format: a JSON log file emitted by the QUIC implementation containing every packet, frame, key derivation, congestion event, and stream operation.

A qlog file is structured as (current schema; events are objects, not positional tuples):
    
    
    {
      "qlog_version": "0.4",
      "qlog_format": "JSON",
      "traces": [{
        "vantage_point": {"type": "client"},
        "events": [
          {"time": 0,  "name": "transport:packet_sent",     "data": {...}},
          {"time": 80, "name": "transport:packet_received", "data": {...}}
        ]
      }]
    }
    

(Older drafts used a 3-tuple `[time, category, event_name, data]`; you may still encounter it in archived traces. Current `qvis` ingests the object form.)

Each event has a timestamp, category, type, and payload. Tools like qvis (visualization for qlog) consume the file and produce timeline views, sequence diagrams, throughput plots.

#### 15.2.1 What qlog Shows

For each connection:

* Packet send/receive timeline with packet types and sizes.
* Stream lifecycle (open, data, FIN, close).
* Congestion control state (cwnd, RTT estimates).
* Loss events and retransmissions.
* Key derivations and key updates.
* Connection migration events.
* Application-level frames (HTTP/3 HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS).

For debugging a slow connection or a failed deployment, qlog is essential. Cloudflare, Google, and Apple all generate qlog for their internal QUIC traffic; many implementations expose qlog to users for client-side debugging.

#### 15.2.2 Where qlog Is Limited

qlog is endpoint-side only. A network observer sees QUIC packets but cannot decode the content; the network's perspective is opaque. This is by design (encryption protects against ossification), but it makes some traditional network operations (DPI-based security, traffic analysis) hard or impossible.

The standard advice for operating QUIC: deploy endpoint-side observability (qlog at the server, qlog at the client when accessible, application-level metrics). Network-side observability is restricted to "this much UDP/443 traffic for this many seconds" without further detail.

### 15.3 Connection Migration: Jin's LTE-to-Wi-Fi Handoff

Jin Park's mobile app, now on HTTP/3, is in the middle of a session. The user walks into a café; the phone associates with the café's Wi-Fi. The phone's IP changes from a carrier-CGNAT 10.x.x.x to a Wi-Fi 192.168.x.x.

In a TCP-based connection, this would have killed the session: TCP identifies connections by 4-tuple; the new IP doesn't match; the kernel cannot deliver packets to the right socket. Application-level reconnection is required.

In HTTP/3, QUIC's connection migration handles this:

  1. The phone's next QUIC packet uses the new IP+port but the same connection ID.
  2. The server sees a packet with a known connection ID arriving from a new IP.
  3. The server _path-validates_ the new address: sends a small QUIC PATH_CHALLENGE frame to the new address, expects a PATH_RESPONSE.
  4. Once the new path is validated, the server updates its routing for this connection. Application data continues uninterrupted.

Total disruption: typically 100-200ms for the validation, but no application-level reconnection. The user's chat message in progress doesn't fail; their video call doesn't drop; their photo upload doesn't restart.

#### 15.3.1 The Server-Side Mechanics

QUIC servers maintain a _connection ID to connection_ mapping. When a packet arrives from a new IP but a known CID, the server looks up the connection state and routes to the right handler. The path validation is a small additional step.

Server implementations typically issue _multiple_ connection IDs per connection (the server tells the client "use any of these CIDs"), so the client can rotate CIDs as it migrates to prevent linkability across paths. The connection identity is durable; the on-wire identifier changes with each migration.

#### 15.3.2 What Doesn't Migrate

Connection migration handles the common case but has limits:

* _NAT mapping changes that don't involve the client's IP changing_ : most CGNAT timeouts are transparent to QUIC because the client's IP didn't actually change; only the public-mapped port did. QUIC handles this through the same mechanism: the next packet from the same CID arrives from a different source port; the server treats it like a migration.
* _Server-side IP changes_ : less common but supported (QUIC has NEW_CONNECTION_ID and similar frames).
* _Connection ID exhaustion_ : if the server runs out of new CIDs to offer the client (rare with proper implementation), migration may fail.

In practice, connection migration works well on mobile networks. Jin's case is the canonical example: Wi-Fi to LTE handoff, LTE to Wi-Fi handoff, both transparent.

### 15.4 0-RTT Replay Safety in Production

0-RTT lets a returning client send application data with the very first packet. Saves an RTT. Has replay risk.

#### 15.4.1 What Can Be Replayed

An attacker who captures a 0-RTT packet (e.g., on a Wi-Fi network the attacker controls) can replay it later. The server, finding the PSK still valid, accepts and processes the data.

If the request is `GET /index.html`, this is harmless (the response is the same; replay just causes the server to send the response twice). If the request is `POST /api/transfer { amount: 100, to: "Alice" }`, the replay causes a duplicate transfer.

#### 15.4.2 The HTTP Method Restriction

HTTP/3 mandates that 0-RTT is only used for "safe" HTTP methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE are forbidden over 0-RTT. The library enforces this; if an application tries to send a POST in 0-RTT, the library either upgrades to 1-RTT or rejects the request.

The reasoning: the method itself signals intent. GET retrieves; replaying the GET retrieves again, harmless. POST has side effects; replaying may cause duplicate side effects.

#### 15.4.3 The Server-Side Replay Window

A more aggressive defense: the server maintains a deduplication window of recent 0-RTT requests (typically a few seconds). If the same request hash appears twice within the window, it is rejected as a replay.

This is implemented by some servers (Cloudflare, for instance) but not universally. The basic HTTP method restriction is the floor; the deduplication window is additional defense.

#### 15.4.4 What Goes Wrong in Practice

Common production mistakes:

* The application's HTTP framework permits 0-RTT for POST inadvertently (bug in the framework).
* A custom HTTP method (PROPFIND, MKCOL, etc.) is used without considering 0-RTT semantics.
* The application uses "GET with a side effect" patterns (e.g., `GET /endpoint?action=delete`). 0-RTT replays this; the side effect happens twice.

The mitigation discipline: design APIs to be idempotent at the application level (idempotency keys); never put state-changing operations behind GET; verify that 0-RTT is gated on the right HTTP methods at the library/middleware level.

### 15.5 HTTP/2 Trailers and gRPC

HTTP/2 (and HTTP/3) supports _trailers_ : headers sent at the end of a response, after the body. This was a minor feature in HTTP/2; in gRPC, it is load-bearing.

#### 15.5.1 What Trailers Are

A normal HTTP response:
    
    
    HEADERS: status=200, content-type=application/json
    DATA: { "result": "..." }
    [stream FIN]
    

A response with trailers:
    
    
    HEADERS: status=200, content-type=application/grpc
    DATA: <serialized gRPC message>
    HEADERS: grpc-status=0, grpc-message=
    [stream FIN]
    

The final HEADERS frame carries trailers, in this case the gRPC status code and message. The application gets the status only after the response body is fully delivered.

#### 15.5.2 Why gRPC Uses Trailers

gRPC streams responses with potentially varying lengths. At the end, gRPC reports a status (success/failure, with optional error details). Trailers fit this pattern: the status is known only after the response is generated, sent at the end as metadata.

The benefit: the server can stream a response of unknown length and report success only after generating it. The HTTP/2 trailer mechanism handles this cleanly.

#### 15.5.3 Where Trailers Bite

Trailers are not universally supported. Specifically:

* Many older HTTP/2 implementations (including some load balancers, proxies, and middleboxes) drop trailers or convert them to leading headers. gRPC traffic through such middleware fails.
* HTTP/1.1 supports trailers via chunked encoding (RFC 7230) but few implementations care.
* WebSocket and other long-lived protocols cannot easily use trailers.

In practice, gRPC requires a HTTP/2 stack that handles trailers correctly. AWS ALB had trailer-handling issues for years (fixed circa 2019-2021); some service meshes need careful configuration. When gRPC stops working, "are trailers being preserved through the proxy" is one of the first things to check.

#### 15.5.4 gRPC over HTTP/3

gRPC over HTTP/3 inherits the trailer behavior. QUIC's per-stream HEADERS-DATA-HEADERS pattern works the same way. The same trailer-preservation question applies to any HTTP/3-aware proxy or load balancer.

### 15.6 ALPN, MTU, and Fallback Discipline

Deploying HTTP/3 in production requires three operational disciplines.

#### 15.6.1 ALPN Negotiation

ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) is the TLS extension that lets the client and server agree on which protocol to use over the TLS connection. For HTTP/3, the ALPN value is `h3`. For HTTP/2, it is `h2`.

In QUIC, ALPN is included in the ClientHello during the initial handshake. The client offers a list (`h3`, `h3-29` for older draft versions); the server picks one. If the server doesn't speak any of the offered ALPNs, the connection fails.

For a server to offer HTTP/3, it must advertise `h3` in its ALPN list. Failure to do so causes clients to fall back to HTTP/2.

#### 15.6.2 MTU and Path-MTU Discovery

QUIC packets are UDP datagrams; they are subject to path-MTU constraints. A QUIC implementation must:

  1. Start with a conservative UDP-payload size (RFC 9000 mandates ≥ 1200 bytes for QUIC Initial packets). At 1200 bytes of UDP payload, the total on-wire frame is roughly 1242 bytes over IPv4 (1200 + 8 UDP + 20 IPv4 + 14 Ethernet) and 1262 bytes over IPv6 (1200 + 8 UDP + 40 IPv6 + 14 Ethernet) — both well under the standard 1500-byte Ethernet MTU.
  2. Probe larger UDP-payload sizes by sending **PING frames inside padded packets** of the candidate size. There is no `PATH_MTU` frame in QUIC; DPLPMTUD reuses PING + padding. If the ACK comes back, the path supports that size.
  3. Handle PMTUD black holes (when a router silently drops oversized packets); time out and shrink.

The 1200-byte default is the minimum required to fit the QUIC initial packets. Larger MTUs (1280-1500 typical) yield better throughput. Modern QUIC implementations do DPLPMTUD (RFC 8899) to probe path MTU.

#### 15.6.3 Fallback to HTTP/2

When QUIC fails (UDP blocked, server doesn't speak h3, NAT issues), the client falls back to HTTP/2 over TLS over TCP. The fallback discipline:

  1. Client attempts QUIC connection.
  2. If no response within ~100ms, in parallel start a TCP+TLS+HTTP/2 connection.
  3. The first successful connection wins; the other is abandoned.

This is the "race-and-fallback" pattern. It adds slight overhead for QUIC-successful cases (the parallel TCP attempt that wasn't needed) and saves a lot of time when QUIC fails (no waiting for QUIC timeout).

The DNS HTTPS record (Chapter 13) accelerates this further: the client knows in advance whether the server supports QUIC, so it can attempt QUIC first with confidence.

### 15.7 The Wire-Level Artifact: A Real HTTP/3 Deployment Checklist
    
    
    [Server-side]
    ☐ TLS 1.3 certificate (TLS 1.2 not allowed with QUIC)
    ☐ ALPN: list includes "h3"; also lists "h2" for fallback
    ☐ UDP/443 firewall allows inbound
    ☐ Load balancer routes UDP/443 to QUIC servers (or terminates QUIC and re-originates HTTP/2 backwards)
    ☐ Connection-ID-based load balancing (if multiple QUIC servers)
    ☐ qlog generation enabled for diagnostics
    ☐ Path validation tested for connection migration scenarios
    
    [DNS]
    ☐ A and AAAA records for the service
    ☐ HTTPS (RFC 9460) record with alpn=h3,h2 and ipv4hint/ipv6hint
    ☐ TTLs set appropriately
    
    [Client-side test]
    $ curl --http3 -v https://example.com/
    * Connected to example.com (203.0.113.50) port 443 (#0)
    * using HTTP/3
    * Server certificate verified
    > GET / HTTP/3
    > Host: example.com
    > User-Agent: curl/8.x
    > Accept: */*
    < HTTP/3 200
    < content-type: text/html
    < content-length: 1234
    < 
    <html>...
    

A successful `curl --http3` test indicates the server is reachable via QUIC. A qlog from the curl client (or from the server) shows the full handshake and request flow.

For production rollout, a typical phased approach:

  1. Week 1-2: deploy QUIC server software, test internally.
  2. Week 3-4: enable HTTP/3 for a small percentage of users (1-5%) via feature flag.
  3. Week 5-8: gradual ramp to 100% with monitoring.
  4. Week 9+: full production; monitor for regressions.

Monitoring during rollout: percentage of HTTP/3 successful connections (should be 85-95% in 2026), latency improvements (p50, p99), CPU/memory cost on servers, any application-level errors that correlate with HTTP/3 paths.

### 15.X Exercises

#### Concept Check

**Q1.** What is connection migration in HTTP/3, and how does it work?

Hint

Connection IDs identify connections, not 4-tuples.

**Answer:** Connection migration is HTTP/3's (via QUIC's) ability to continue a connection across changes to the client's IP address. The mechanism: QUIC long-header packets (and short-header packets after handshake) carry a connection ID (CID) — variable-length 0-20 bytes per RFC 9000, typically 8 bytes — in cleartext. The connection is identified by this CID, not by the 4-tuple (source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port). When a client's IP changes, the next packet from the new IP carries the same CID. The server: (1) Sees a packet with a known CID arriving from a new IP. (2) Validates the new path by sending a PATH_CHALLENGE to the new address and expecting a PATH_RESPONSE (this prevents an attacker from spoofing IP addresses to redirect traffic). (3) Once validated, updates its internal routing to send response packets to the new IP. The application sees no disruption; in-flight requests complete normally. For mobile users handing off between Wi-Fi and cellular (Jin's case), this eliminates the visible reconnection that TCP-based applications experience. The cost: a brief delay for path validation (typically 100-200ms); slight server-side state (the server must maintain mappings between connection IDs and active paths). The benefit: dramatically better user experience on mobile, where network changes are routine. Some QUIC servers issue multiple connection IDs per connection (telling the client "you can use any of these"); the client can rotate CIDs as it migrates to make the new path unlinkable from the old, preserving privacy.

**Q2.** What is the 0-RTT replay safety problem in HTTP/3, and how is it mitigated?

Hint

The same as in Chapter 10; here look at HTTP-level details.

**Answer:** In QUIC's 0-RTT mode, a returning client can send application data in the very first packet, encrypted under a pre-shared key derived from a previous session. An attacker who captures the 0-RTT packet can replay it later; the server, finding the PSK still valid, will accept and process the data. If the data triggers a state-changing operation (POST that transfers money, DELETE that removes a resource), the operation can be duplicated. HTTP/3 mitigations: (1) _HTTP method restriction_ : HTTP/3 mandates that 0-RTT is only used for "safe" methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS). The HTTP/3 library enforces this; requests using POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE are either upgraded to 1-RTT or rejected. The reasoning: safe methods are idempotent by definition; replay produces the same effect. (2) _Server-side deduplication_ : some servers (Cloudflare, for instance) maintain a deduplication window of recent 0-RTT requests; the same request hash within the window is rejected as replay. (3) _Application-level idempotency_ : critical operations should use idempotency keys (a client-supplied UUID; the server deduplicates by key). This protects against replay even outside of 0-RTT scenarios. The discipline: design APIs so state-changing operations use POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE (which the HTTP/3 stack will refuse to 0-RTT); use idempotency keys for any operation that must be safe to retry. Common mistakes: putting side effects behind GET (a 0-RTT replay of a "GET /admin/delete" will execute the deletion twice); using a custom HTTP method that doesn't appear in the safe list and getting unexpected 0-RTT behavior.

**Q3.** What are HTTP/2 (and HTTP/3) trailers, and why are they essential for gRPC?

Hint

Trailers are headers sent at the end of the response.

**Answer:** Trailers in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are header frames sent at the _end_ of a response, after the response body. The flow is: HEADERS (initial response headers, status code) → DATA (response body bytes) → HEADERS (trailers, sent only after the body is complete) → stream FIN. The trailers can include metadata that is only known after the response is fully generated. gRPC uses trailers to convey its protocol-level status: `grpc-status` (a numeric status code), `grpc-message` (a human-readable error string if applicable), and `grpc-status-details-bin` (binary status details for richer error information). gRPC has these reasons to use trailers: (1) The full response status is known only after the response body is fully sent; trailers let it be sent at the right moment without buffering the entire response. (2) Streaming responses can run for a long time (server-streaming or bidirectional-streaming gRPC); trailers report the final status when the stream ends. (3) Including the gRPC status in the leading HEADERS would require knowing the success/failure before generating any response body, which defeats streaming. The "where trailers bite": many HTTP middleboxes and proxies don't preserve trailers correctly. They drop them, or convert them to leading headers (which corrupts gRPC), or buffer the whole response (which defeats streaming). When gRPC mysteriously fails through a proxy, the proxy's trailer handling is one of the first things to investigate. As of 2026, major cloud load balancers (AWS ALB, GCP HTTPS Load Balancer, Cloudflare) handle trailers correctly; older middleboxes or custom proxies may not.

**Q4.** What is the "race-and-fallback" pattern for HTTP/3 vs HTTP/2 client behavior?

Hint

Parallel connection attempts.

**Answer:** Race-and-fallback is the client-side discipline for selecting between HTTP/3 (over UDP/QUIC) and HTTP/2 (over TCP/TLS) when the server supports both but the network's QUIC capability is uncertain. The mechanism: (1) The client begins by attempting an HTTP/3 connection (QUIC handshake to UDP/443). (2) After a short delay (typically 100-200ms), the client begins a parallel HTTP/2 attempt (TCP handshake + TLS handshake to TCP/443). (3) Whichever connection succeeds first is used for the request. The other connection is closed. The benefit: if QUIC works (the common case in 2026, around 85-95% of networks), the parallel HTTP/2 attempt is wasted but only by 100-200ms of overhead. If QUIC is blocked (5-15% of networks: corporate firewalls blocking UDP, restrictive Wi-Fi, etc.), the HTTP/2 fallback completes within 200-400ms total, vs. waiting for QUIC timeout which can take 5-30 seconds. The DNS HTTPS record (Chapter 13) further optimizes this: the client knows in advance whether the server supports QUIC, allowing it to start the QUIC attempt without speculation. Modern browsers (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) and HTTP libraries (curl, reqwest, hyper) all implement race-and-fallback. The key tuning parameter is the delay before starting the HTTP/2 attempt: too short and you waste bandwidth on parallel TCP+TLS handshakes; too long and the fallback feels slow when QUIC fails. 100-200ms is the production sweet spot. Race-and-fallback is invisible to applications; the HTTP library handles it transparently.

#### Application Problems

**Q1.** A team is deploying HTTP/3 behind an existing load balancer. The load balancer is a Layer 7 (HTTP-aware) proxy that does not understand HTTP/3 yet. Design the architecture.

Hint

Terminate QUIC somewhere; talk HTTP/2 to the backend.

**Answer:** _Architecture options_ : (1) _Upgrade the load balancer to HTTP/3-aware_ : AWS ALB, GCP HTTPS Load Balancer, Cloudflare, Fastly all support HTTP/3 as of 2025. If the load balancer is a managed service from a major cloud provider, this is the simplest path: enable HTTP/3 in the configuration and the load balancer handles the protocol negotiation and back-end translation. (2) _Add an HTTP/3-aware proxy in front of the load balancer_ : Envoy 1.20+, HAProxy 2.6+, Nginx with the OpenSSL+QUIC patch can terminate HTTP/3 on the edge. The proxy receives HTTP/3 from clients, terminates QUIC, sends HTTP/2 over TCP to the existing load balancer. The load balancer is unchanged. (3) _Layer 4 (TCP/UDP) load balancing with HTTP/3 servers behind_ : instead of an L7 proxy, use L4 load balancing (HAProxy in TCP mode, nginx stream module, NLB on AWS). The load balancer routes UDP/443 to backend servers that speak HTTP/3 natively. Connection-ID-based affinity ensures the same QUIC connection always reaches the same backend. The backend handles all HTTP/3 termination and application logic. _Decision factors_ : (a) If the application uses gRPC, deeper HTTP/2 awareness in the load balancer (for trailers, etc.) may be important; an L7 load balancer is preferable. (b) If you need to do HTTP/3-aware features (cache key derivation, A/B testing based on HTTP/3 status), terminating HTTP/3 at the load balancer makes sense. (c) If you want to keep architectural simplicity and trust the application's HTTP/3 implementation, L4 load balancing with HTTP/3-native backends is cleanest. (d) Connection-ID-based load balancing is essential for L4 setups; ensure the load balancer supports it. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to design the architecture; watch for Lie #5 (assuming L4 load balancing will just work without considering connection-ID routing) and Lie #4 (suggesting older load balancer versions that don't support HTTP/3 because the LLM's training is outdated).

**Q2.** A gRPC service is reporting intermittent errors when accessed through a corporate proxy. The error is "trailers not received" on roughly 5% of requests. Diagnose.

Hint

Trailers are fragile; what could be dropping or mishandling them?

**Answer:** _Diagnosis_ : the corporate proxy is most likely interfering with gRPC trailers. Possible mechanisms: (1) The proxy is HTTP/1.1-only and doesn't pass HTTP/2 trailers through. Most enterprise proxies were designed for HTTP/1.1; some convert HTTP/2 streams back to HTTP/1.1 internally, losing trailers in the conversion. (2) The proxy is HTTP/2-aware but has a trailer-handling bug: it drops trailers, sends them as leading headers (corrupting gRPC), or buffers the response and converts to a non-streaming form. (3) The proxy is doing TLS interception (MITM with a corporate CA); the interception breaks the HTTP/2 framing in some edge case. (4) Connection-multiplexing issues: the proxy multiplexes many gRPC streams over fewer backend connections, and the trailer handling races with stream cleanup. _Diagnosis steps_ : (1) Bypass the proxy (if possible, even temporarily) and confirm the gRPC service works directly. (2) Capture HTTP/2 traffic in front of and behind the proxy; compare to see what is transformed. (3) Check the proxy version and changelog for known trailer issues. (4) Try a different proxy (open-source Envoy or HAProxy in pure mode) to isolate whether it's the proxy-as-such or the specific proxy product. (5) Look at the application-level gRPC errors: are they specific to certain RPC methods? Certain user groups? _Mitigation options_ : (1) Upgrade or reconfigure the proxy to handle HTTP/2 trailers correctly. (2) Move the gRPC service outside the proxy's path; have clients hit it directly (with appropriate auth and routing). (3) Add a layer of HTTP/2-aware reverse proxy (Envoy) in front of the gRPC service, on the inside of the corporate network; this ensures HTTP/2 termination before the broken proxy. (4) Switch to gRPC-Web for HTTP/1.1-friendly transport (loses streaming features); pragmatic but reduces functionality. (5) Engage the vendor; many enterprise proxy vendors have HTTP/2 fixes available, but they require explicit enablement. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to diagnose; watch for Lie #3 (assuming HTTP/2 server push has anything to do with this; trailers are a different feature) and Lie #1 (mixing up TCP and HTTP/2 layer issues; trailers are an HTTP/2 concept).

**Q3.** Jin Park's LTE-to-Wi-Fi handoff with HTTP/3: walk through what the user sees and what the network observes, second-by-second.

Hint

Migration happens in the protocol; what's the latency profile?

**Answer:** _T=0_ : User is on LTE; phone IP is 10.x.x.x (CGNAT private), public mapping 198.51.100.5:54321. QUIC connection to server is active; HTTP/3 stream in progress (uploading a 5 MB photo). _T=0.5s_ : User walks into the café. Phone associates with the café Wi-Fi network; gets a new IP 192.168.1.42; Wi-Fi connection is fully up at the OS level. _T=0.6s_ : Phone's networking stack notices the new IP; the QUIC implementation in the phone's HTTP/3 library detects the IP change. Phone sends the next QUIC packet from the new IP, using the same connection ID as before. The packet contains the next chunk of the upload data. _T=0.7s_ (one RTT after sending from new IP): Server receives the packet from the new source IP. Server looks up the connection ID; finds the active connection. Server sends a PATH_CHALLENGE frame to the new IP. _T=0.8s_ : Phone receives the PATH_CHALLENGE; responds with PATH_RESPONSE. _T=0.9s_ : Server receives PATH_RESPONSE; validates the new path. Server begins sending response data to the new IP. _T=1.0s onward_ : Connection continues normally on Wi-Fi. The upload completes; the user sees the photo upload progress continue without interruption. _What the user sees_ : a brief pause (~200-400ms) in the upload progress bar around T=0.5-1.0s; no error; no need to retry; the upload completes. From the user's perspective, the network transition was nearly seamless. _What the network observes_ : from the LTE network's perspective, the QUIC connection's packets stop arriving at T=0.5s. The CGNAT may keep the mapping briefly (for the timeout) but eventually clears it. From the Wi-Fi network's perspective, new UDP/443 traffic starts at T=0.6s; the packets carry an apparent random connection ID. From the server's perspective, the connection identity is stable, just the IP changed. _Comparison to TCP_ : with HTTP/2 over TCP, the LTE connection would have been killed at T=0.5s (server still tries to send to LTE IP but the IP is no longer reachable; TCP eventually times out). The application would have to detect the failure, re-establish a connection from the new IP (TCP handshake + TLS handshake = 200-400ms), and resume the upload from scratch (or with some application-level checkpointing). The QUIC version saves an interrupted experience for the user. _AI-collaboration sub-question_ : ask an LLM to describe migration; watch for Lie #1 (confusing TCP semantics with QUIC; describing TCP-style "connection reset" behavior for QUIC) and Lie #5 (mishandling the connection state transition; QUIC's connection is durable across the migration, not "reconnected").
